8946e511190b3292: BERLIN: Germany's consumer protection association said on Tuesday it would take legal action against Meta and the makers of Ray-Ban over data privacy concerns linked to AI-powered smart glasses.
Ramona Pop, head of the Federation of German Consumer Organisations (vzbv), said the wearable devices "make it possible to record images and audio unnoticed".
"Smart glasses create significant data protection risks both for bystanders and for users themselves," she said.
The vzbv argued that potential buyers of the glasses were not sufficiently informed that their use could breach the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
"Products must be designed in such a way that people can use them in compliance with data protection rules and the rights of third parties remain protected," said Pop.
Smart glasses are being sold by various eyewear manufacturers in cooperation with technology companies, with the capacity to take photos, videos and audio recordings, as well as livestreams.

Manufacturers say LED lights on the glasses prevent people nearby from being filmed without their knowledge, but consumer advocates argue that this is insufficient to protect consumers from unwanted recordings.
"A tiny white blinking light just a few millimetres in size is not enough to signal to people in public spaces that they are being filmed," said Pop.

The association said it had filed a lawsuit against Ray-Ban manufacturer EssilorLuxottica in a Berlin court and planned to take similar action against US tech giant Meta, which owns WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram.
Neither company was immediately available for comment.

f40a593c250a0893: RIYADH: The Saudi capital's tallest skyscraper was struck for a second time in days on Tuesday, injuring 11 people, as the coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis denounced a "terrorist attack".

Three separate witnesses said the strike targeted the 80-storey Public Investment Fund (PIF) Tower, which houses the kingdom's sovereign wealth fund and dominates Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD).
The building was attacked last Thursday and is one of several high-profile targets hit since hostilities with the Iran-backed Houthis resumed in July.
"One of the towers in the financial centre was targeted in a cowardly terrorist attack," coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said in a social media post, without naming the building.
"The relevant authorities are currently inspecting the attack site."
Saudi Arabia's civil defence agency later said 11 people were injured in the attack, which it blamed on the Houthis.
The Saudi Press Agency said Indians, Nepalese and Egyptians, as well as Saudis, were among the wounded.
A source briefed on the attack told AFP that several people were in the tower repairing damage caused when the building was struck last week.
The source said at least two of the 11 injured were in critical condition after sustaining severe burns.
An attack on the PIF is symbolic, as the fund is driving efforts to diversify the oil-reliant Saudi economy — a project that has been complicated by the Middle East war and Houthi strikes.
US CONDEMNATION
A tower belonging to state oil giant Aramco in KAFD was hit earlier this month, while Riyadh's international airport was repeatedly struck in October, with one attack killing 14 people.
A fourth witness told AFP that a vehicle fitted with a loudspeaker had warned pedestrians in the area to take cover on Tuesday. No warning was sent to mobile phones about any threats to the capital.
Afterwards, police cars blocked some entrances to the gleaming financial district, a showpiece of Saudi Arabia's modernisation under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the de facto ruler.
A waiter at a KAFD restaurant told AFP: "We just reopened a while ago.
"They evacuated all of us, telling us a tower has been hit. They closed the streets and they banned people from passing in streets or entering."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in a call with his Saudi counterpart on Tuesday, condemned attacks on the kingdom's infrastructure, without specifically mentioning the latest incident.

"Secretary Rubio spoke today with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud. The Secretary condemned the Iran-backed Houthi terrorist attacks on Saudi civilian and energy infrastructure," the State Department said in a statement.
WEEKS OF VIOLENCE
Last week, Saudi officials said an attack on a tower in the financial district damaged several floors and two adjacent buildings but caused no casualties.
Although authorities did not identify the building, photos released by the civil defence agency appeared to show shattered glass and other exterior damage to the PIF Tower.
The Houthis claimed responsibility but did not announce any fresh attacks on Tuesday.
Standing 385 metres high, the PIF Tower is the most prominent landmark of KAFD, a showcase for Saudi Arabia's economic ambitions.
With imposing skyscrapers, luxury shops and green spaces, the district also hosts the headquarters of the Saudi stock exchange, along with multinationals such as Goldman Sachs.
The Houthis have stepped up attacks against Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, striking military, civilian and oil infrastructure.

A major attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport forced the suspension of flights for two weeks. Several events have been cancelled, including the Future Investment Initiative financial conference, dubbed "Davos in the desert".
In response, a Saudi-led military coalition fighting on behalf of Yemen's government has been striking Houthi targets in the impoverished country.
On Tuesday, local officials said a coalition air strike on buses and trucks killed 26 people in Lahj province. Government forces blamed the Houthis for the attack.
Britain on Tuesday sanctioned the Houthis and four of its top officials "for deliberately attempting to undermine stability".
The Saudi-led coalition intervened in Yemen in early 2015 after the Houthis had captured the capital, Sanaa, and forced the internationally recognised government to flee to Aden.

5f58be54b1dd7d8b: ROME: Jannik Sinner risks missing the Australian Open after confirming on Tuesday that he has undergone surgery on his troublesome right knee.

The five-time Grand Slam champion has not played a match since winning Wimbledon for the second time in July, with less than two months until the start of the first major tournament of the season in Melbourne.
"Over the past few months, together with my team we've tried everything to treat my injury without surgery," Sinner said in a statement.
"After some very encouraging progress early on, my knee unfortunately didn't respond as we had all hoped, that's why today I underwent a minor surgery to improve the condition of my iliotibial band."

The procedure, which had been reported earlier in the day by broadcasters RAI and Sky Sport, and sports daily La Gazzetta dello Sport, was performed by knee injury specialist Lasse Lempainen at a clinic in Finland.
Another knee specialist, Fabrizio Terrone at the Isokinetic centre in Turin, told Sky Sport that Sinner's absence could last "at least three to four months."
That means the earliest Sinner might be back on court with a racket in hand would be during the American hard-court swing, at Indian Wells and Miami Masters.
The 25-year-old admitted recently that the worst injury of his career left him barely able to move.
"The worst part for me about this injury is that I cannot compete, I cannot play tennis," said Sinner in a recent video.
"Also my life outside of tennis is a bit more limited because of a simple fact that I cannot do things that I really like, because I want to protect my knee."

Sinner, a two-time champion at the Australian Open which begins on January 17, recently said that he will make his comeback at the "Six Kings Slam" tournament in Saudi Arabia, which has been rescheduled for late December due to the conflict with Yemen's Houthis.

But that now looks impossible and a difficult start to 2027 seems in store for the man who has in recent years risen to be, alongside Spanish star Carlos Alcaraz, the pre-eminent force in men's tennis.
Sinner was having a brilliant campaign before being stopped by his knee problem, with five Masters 1000 titles going alongside his triumph at Wimbledon.
The Italian's 94 percent winning record in 2026 is the best of his career, even beating his figures from the previous two seasons in each of which he won two Grand Slams and the ATP Finals.

He suffered a major disappointment at the French Open when, leading Argentina's Juan Manuel Cerundolo by two sets and 5-1 ahead in the third, he succumbed to heat stroke and was eliminated in the second round.

Sinner recently lost top spot in the men's world rankings to losing Wimbledon finalist Alexander Zverev, who has taken advantage of injury problems for both Sinner and Alcaraz to win Roland Garros and the US Open.
81f33bb6b49fdbda: NEW YORK: A US jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei of stealing trade secrets on Tuesday, but acquitted it of a more serious racketeering allegation, media reported.
The world's leading telecoms equipment manufacturer, Huawei has been targeted by the Trump administration, which alleges that it poses a risk of spying on behalf of the Chinese government.
The United States has previously urged countries not to use Huawei infrastructure for the rollout of new 5G mobile networks.
The verdict followed an 11-week trial at a federal court in Brooklyn, during which Huawei had strenuously denied wrongdoing, The New York Times reported.
The equipment manufacturer was accused of attempting to recruit employees of US telecoms firms and obtaining technological information from them in the process.
That data allegedly enabled Huawei to develop products similar to those of its competitors, which it then sold at lower prices, according to the original indictment.
Huawei even launched an internal programme offering bonuses to employees who obtained industrial secrets from competitors, prosecutors had claimed.
Jurors found Huawei guilty of 10 of the 12 criminal counts it faced, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets, conspiracy to defraud the United States and bank fraud, The Times reported.
They acquitted the company of racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice.

A WOMAN who fell into a coma after an accident in Kluang on Nov 19 has given others a chance at life, with her family agreeing to donate her heart, lungs and liver.
The family of Nurul Natasya Ahmad Jaafar, 36, decided to donate her organs after she was pronounced dead at Sultanah Aminah Hospital (HSA) here on Sunday.

HSA paid a final tribute to Nurul Natasya with a "Walk of Honour", with doctors and medical personnel lining up hospital corridors as her body was wheeled out, while green lights illuminated the building as a symbol of gratitude and respect for her final gift of life.
The Fire and Rescue Department deployed a helicopter to transport the organs from HSA to Subang, Selangor, before they were taken to the National Heart Institute in Kuala Lumpur.
HSA described Nurul Natasya's final act as a powerful reminder that one person's generosity could give others another chance at life.
Her death drew an outpouring of condolences and tributes on social media, with many describing her family's decision as an enduring act of charity.
Nurul Natasya was laid to rest at the Kampung Cahaya Baru Muslim cemetery in Masai on Monday.
b879995cf1e26209: Two of NASA's four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical issues in recent weeks.

The missions affected by the outages—hopefully temporary—are NASA's Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001, and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history.

The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover's communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate.
dc25bdc997384eed: CARTAGENA: Gunmen held 25 people hostage in a supermarket in the Colombian tourist city of Cartagena on Tuesday, prompting a major security operation that saw snipers deployed and nearby streets sealed off.
The attackers appeared to have tried to rob an armored vehicle before fleeing into the supermarket, taking about 30 people hostage, authorities said.
Five hostages have since been released, all elderly women, according to Colombian president Abelardo de la Espriella.
The standoff unfolded in Cartagena, a Caribbean port known for its picturesque colonial old town, beach resorts and cruise-ship tourism.
Authorities briefly suspended arriving flights as security forces responded, before later restoring operations.
De la Espriella said special forces had been deployed to the scene. City authorities said the navy and army were also involved in the response.
"This is going to turn out well for the hostages" said De la Espriella. "I'm not so sure it's going to turn out so well for the criminals."
"We are there dealing with the situation" De la Espriella added, ruling out the involvement of armed guerrilla or paramilitary groups.
"It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping -- no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people."
Images broadcast by Colombian media and shared widely on social media showed masked gunmen armed with rifles standing beside hostages who appeared to be kneeling on the floor inside the store.
Police snipers took up positions on nearby buildings overlooking the supermarket.
Several other officers crouched, weapons drawn at the entrance to the Exito supermarket, as the siege stretched into the afternoon.
Scores of people gathered behind police cordons to watch the crisis unfold.
Onlookers lined nearby roads and sidewalks, many filming on mobile phones as traffic was diverted around the shopping center.
Supermarket employees were among those feared taken captive. "My son is there," Jacob Perez, father of one of the workers, told AFP.
"He didn't leave work and he's not answering his phone. I think they took it from him," he said.
Local media reported the gunmen were demanding nearly US$2 million, two armored vehicles and safe passage to the city of Barranquilla, 130km to the northeast on Colombia's Caribbean coast.
AFP could not independently verify those reports.
The hostage crisis comes amid a worsening security situation across parts of Colombia.
Late Monday, authorities blamed a dissident FARC faction for a car bomb attack in the city of Villavicencio that wounded 25 people and caused extensive damage.
The right-wing De la Espriella has championed a hardline campaign against criminal groups, but violence has continued to rise in several parts of the country in recent months.
35d4b177014e5ac9: WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump on Tuesday bestowed the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's top civilian honour, on Rudy Giuliani, a close ally and former mayor of New York City.

Giuliani, who led America's largest city from 1994 to 2001, is perhaps best known for cracking down on New York's organised crime, including the notorious mafia, and for handling the aftermath of the Sept 11, 2001, attacks.

However, the former prosecutor and ex-personal attorney for Trump fell from grace after spreading misinformation about the 2020 election. He was ordered in 2023 to pay US$148 million in damages for defamation related to his election fraud claims.
"Doing the right thing for others has been my guiding light," Giuliani, 82, said in a post on X from the medal ceremony in the White House's Oval Office.
While working for Trump, Giuliani was one of the main figures behind the attempt to overturn the results of the 2020 election, which was won by Democrat Joe Biden.
He was disbarred from practising law in New York and Washington as a result of his actions, and indicted on charges related to the 2020 election in Arizona.
But Trump issued a federal pardon to Giuliani last year upon his return to office.
"Mayor Rudy Giuliani is a dedicated public servant whose decisive leadership has left a lasting impact on New York City and our nation," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said in a statement.
10a99156b6480f7e: LONDON: West Ham were unable to stop their wretched run as boss Scott Parker was left waiting for his first victory after a 1-0 defeat at Portsmouth on Tuesday.
The Hammers were widely expected to win promotion back to the Premier League after last season's relegation.
But instead they are languishing in 12th place in the Championship following Odin Bailey's winner at Fratton Park.

Former Fulham, Burnley and Bournemouth manager Parker has lost two and drawn two since replacing Nuno Espirito Santo, with the east Londoners without victory in six and 11 points off the top of the table.
West Ham failed to scored for the first time this season, despite hitting the woodwork twice as Bailey's first-half strike was enough for Portsmouth to rise to 10th.
Will Lankshear was back among the goals as Middlesbrough cemented their position at the top of the table with a 2-1 win over Swansea.
Lankshear had missed the final two games prior to the international break because of a hamstring injury, and was only afforded a late substitute appearance in Saturday's win over Bristol City.

Having been restored to the starting line-up at the Riverside Stadium, Lankshear -- the Championship's leading scorer -- claimed his 14th league goal this season to reestablish Middlesbrough's lead in the second half.
Joseph Opoku's driven finish for Swansea had cancelled out Myles Peart-Harris's early opener.
Second-placed Wolves are one point behind Middlesbrough after beating Derby 3-0.
Norwich's impressive run came to an end as QPR held them to a 1-1 draw at Carrow Road.
The Canaries had won their previous five Championship fixtures but had to come from behind this time after Harvey Vale had fired the visitors in front just before the break.
Philippe Clement's side were quickly back on level terms in the second half through a well-taken Anthony Musaba effort.
Sydie Peck equalised in the 90th minute as Sheffield United came from behind to secure a 1-1 draw with Southampton at Bramall Lane.
Lewis Dobbin had given the visitors an early lead but the Blades stepped up a gear after the break and finally found a way past Saints goalkeeper Daniel Peretz through Peck.
The equaliser saw the Blades move within a point of the top eight and remain two behind their sixth-placed opponents.

18ed3c03caa6a48b: WASHINGTON: A cybersecurity breach at the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) exposed some unclassified information, US media reported on Tuesday.
The New York Times said the recently discovered intrusions targeted an open-source intelligence analysis system — a computer network that sifts through public, unclassified material for insights.
The newspaper, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, said classified material was not jeopardised.
The Times quoted an ODNI official as saying there had been no disruptions to critical capabilities. It said the CIA declined to comment.

The report comes several days after the Agriculture Department and FBI were reportedly targeted in cyberattacks, amid mounting concerns over the security of US computer systems following a wave of major technical outages.
Asked about the reported FBI breach on Saturday, President Donald Trump said he had only recently learnt of it.
"I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he told Fox News.
The outages in recent weeks have disrupted travel, communications and e-commerce for countless users across the United States, even affecting a top-secret network at the National Security Agency.
White House cybersecurity chief Sean Cairncross was fired last week as criticism mounted over the spate of issues.

THE Education Ministry is planning to introduce dedicated classes for autistic pupils next year.
Education director-general Datuk Dr Mohd Azam Ahmad said teaching pupils with autism required a specialised approach.
He said ministry data showed a steady rise in the number of pupils with autism, prompting plans to set up special education classrooms and recruit more teachers.
Education (School Operations Sector) deputy director-general Datuk Zainal Abas said enrolment of pupils with special education needs had increased annually, partly due to greater parental awareness.
"The ministry has been working on a special education planning framework since last year, including the construction of additional classrooms," he said.
Pupils with special education needs currently have two pathways — enrolling in special education schools or the Special Education Integration Programme (PPKI) in mainstream schools.
Ideally, each PPKI classroom in mainstream schools should cater to seven pupils, supported by a special education teacher and teaching assistant.
Zainal said dedicated classes for autistic pupils would provide a better learning environment.
These pupils are currently taught alongside pupils with Down Syndrome and other learning difficulties.
The 2026 Preschool Curriculum will also introduce two additional learning areas for pupils with special education needs — bringing the total to eight — to better prepare them for Year One.
Meanwhile, Azam said the country's first Special Education Sports School in Bandar Enstek, Negri Sembilan, was expected to take in its first batch of Form One students next year.
He said all students should have equal access to quality education and opportunities to develop their potential.
8a191ebdd5cbbf50: BRUSSELS: The EU on Tuesday threatened Bulgaria with a fine over its failure to keep public spending under control, less than a year after it joined the euro area.
Bulgaria's deficit -- the annual shortfall of revenue to spending -- is set to reach 5% this year, and projected to fall to 4% in 2027.
Under EU rules, the public deficit is meant to be no more than 3% of GDP, and debt must not be above 60% of GDP.

EU economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis said Bulgaria faced a penalty of up to 0.02% of its economic output. The commission in its opinion said Bulgaria had not taken "effective action" to correct its excessive deficit.
Bulgaria became the 21st member of the single currency area in January 2026.
If imposed, it would be the first such fine as the European Commission has never punished member states over breaking spending rules -- despite multiple breaches.
The commission came close to slapping fines but backed away in 2016 from punishing Spain and Portugal for running high deficits.
The EU has told France and Belgium to bring their debt and deficit down.
France, the EU's second-biggest economy, has a deficit much higher than EU rules allow and is already in the commission's public spending sin bin.

But Brussels said France's 2027 budgetary plan was on the right path, although the commission added its "assessment is surrounded by considerable uncertainty in view of the ongoing parliamentary discussions on the budget".
French prime minister Sebastien Lecornu is struggling to pass a deficit-cutting budget for 2027 in a parliament where President Emmanuel Macron's centrists no longer hold a majority.
44f6d57a797b432e: According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters, Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for users worldwide.

Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft's target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. "Needless to say, we aren't here yet," Henderson wrote.

The memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company's post-incident report, dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident.
e5971634b407fdde: MADRID: Jude Bellingham scored a sensational goal to help Real Madrid come from behind to thrash PSV 5-1 in the Champions League on Tuesday, continuing their 100% start.

Kylian Mbappe netted a brace with Federico Valverde and Vinicius Junior also on target for Los Blancos, who fought back strongly in the second half after Ivan Perisic sent the visitors ahead from the penalty spot.
Madrid climbed provisionally top of the league phase standings with their fifth victory from five European matches, and 10th consecutive triumph across all competitions.
PSV put up an impressive fight in the first half but Jose Mourinho's side blew them away with a dynamic showing in the second, inspired by England midfielder Bellingham.
The former Birmingham and Borussia Dortmund star watched the first half from the bench, with Mourinho explaining he had a minor fitness issue.
However, with Madrid trailing to Perisic's penalty, Mourinho called on Bellingham at the interval and the 23-year-old inspired a memorable second half display at the Santiago Bernabeu.
"The second half we played was incredible... that's how we have to come out from the first minute," Valverde told Movistar.
"I think when Jude came on, he gave us that calm. When it came to building up play, we could move the ball much better."
Ruben van Bommel drilled wide early on for Dutch champions PSV, while Vinicius crashed a shot off the bar at the other end.
PSV took the lead when Aurelien Tchouameni trod on Sven Mijnans's foot and Perisic rifled in the resulting penalty.
Mourinho made a triple change at half-time, including bringing on Bellingham, and Madrid were transformed.
Bellingham gem

KUALA LUMPUR: RHB Banking Group recorded more than 1.2 billion e-payment transactions on Payments Network Malaysia Sdn Bhd's (PayNet) national payments network between July 2025 and June 2026.
This was a 37 per cent increase year-on-year, from 886 million transactions in the corresponding period a year earlier.
The growth was the highest among Malaysian banks.
Of the total, 536.8 million transactions were payments made by RHB customers, while 676.7 million were payments received by individuals and businesses into RHB accounts.
The increase reflects a shift among customers and merchants towards faster, more convenient payment methods.
These transactions include retail purchases, bill payments, online transactions and business collections.
RHB attributed the growth to greater adoption of digital payment methods by customers and businesses.
The group was named the winner of the E-Payments Excellence Award (Bank) at PayNet's Malaysian E-Payments Excellence Awards (MEEA) 2026, marking its second consecutive year of recognition.
RHB Group managing director and group chief executive officer Datuk Mohd Rashid Mohamad said digital payments were fast becoming the preferred way for customers to manage their transactions.
He said customers expected transactions to be quick, simple and reliable, whether they were paying for a meal, making an online purchase, settling bills or collecting business payments.
"As these expectations continue to evolve, our focus is on making it easier for customers and businesses to transact while ensuring they can do so with confidence.
"Being recognised for the second consecutive year reflects the role digital payments now play in everyday life.
"It also encourages us to keep raising our service standards as we work towards becoming the Best Service Bank," he said.
The group said it was the first bank in Malaysia to enable merchants to accept DuitNow Pay for online and recurring payments through RHB Pay, its unified payment gateway.
The enhancement gives businesses greater flexibility in collecting funds while offering customers a seamless experience across different transaction types.
RHB Pay will progressively support additional payment options, including Direct Debit, DuitNow QR and e-wallets.
The group said the recognition reinforced its commitment to expanding digital payment services for individuals and businesses.

38e71ca7d096a306: JERUSALEM: Israel's Yashar party, led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, said on Tuesday it had agreed to sign a coalition pact with a right-wing opposition party as it seeks to form a government following last month's election.
Yashar said Eisenkot had met Avigdor Lieberman, head of the Israel Our Home party, earlier on Tuesday and they agreed on a deal afterwards — the first such alliance since the election.

Israel's parliament was sworn in on November 10 without a new government, after the Oct 27 election stripped Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of his majority but left others with no clear path to power.
President Isaac Herzog has tasked Eisenkot with forming a government, while Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister.
Netanyahu's right-wing Likud alliance with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties outperformed election expectations but still lost its majority. It now holds 53 of the Knesset's 120 seats.

Eisenkot's centre-right Yashar party and its patchwork coalition partners — including Lieberman — hold just 48 seats. But they have potential allies in parties representing Israel's Arab minority, which hold 19 seats and are aligned with Eisenkot in their vehement opposition to Netanyahu.

The agreement between Eisenkot, whose party won 21 parliamentary seats, and Lieberman, whose party won seven, was something of a surprise, since Lieberman had been vocal in his opposition to forming a government with support from Arab parties, as well as to a unity government with Netanyahu.
Lieberman has also said his main goal is to oust Netanyahu from power.

Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government under a 28-day mandate, but he could ask for a 14-day extension. If he fails, Netanyahu would get a shot. If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.
Talks are also ongoing between Eisenkot, some of his "change bloc" partners and Likud on forming a unity government.

The left-wing Democrats party, which won eight parliamentary seats, separately said it was suspending talks with Eisenkot because of progress in his discussions with Netanyahu's Likud on a possible unity government and "given the deadlock in negotiations to form a 'change government'".
Yair Golan, head of the Democrats, has said he prefers a government without Netanyahu but with Arab parties.
d1c5829c565a71d1: LONDON: Arsenal striker Viktor Gyokeres showed why he is such a polarising figure with a thunderous goal and a crucial miss in Tuesday's 1-1 draw against Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League.
Gunners boss Mikel Arteta had urged Gyokeres to seize his opportunity after selecting the Sweden striker instead of Kai Havertz for the league phase tie at the Emirates Stadium.
Initially, Gyokeres looked like doing just that with his first goal at the Emirates Stadium this season, and only his third for the Gunners in all competitions.
But the 28-year-old has been much-maligned for his erratic displays since arriving from Sporting Lisbon in 2025.
And he gave more ammunition to his critics when he missed a golden opportunity to seal the points with a woeful header in the closing stages.
Dortmund had equalised through Maximilian Beier by then and Arteta was left to rue his decision to put his faith in Gyokeres.

In a showdown between the current leaders of the Premier League and the Bundesliga, Arsenal were too profligate in attack and error-prone at the back to say they deserved all three points.

Arteta will hope for a much more ruthless display in a significant Premier League showdown with spluttering title rivals Manchester City in north London on Sunday.

Gyokeres wasted his chance to finish as Arsenal's hero for once when he sent a close-range diving header woefully wide from Martin Odegaard's cross.
Arsenal's luck was out after Odegaard's delivery twice hit the post and appeared to strike Serhou Guirassy's hand before it was finally scrambled clear.
Rice was equally unfortunate with a first-time drive that cannoned back off the near post to leave Arsenal frustrated.

THE United Kingdom and 13 other countries on Monday "acknowledged" the top United Nations court's ruling that Myanmar perpetrated genocide against its Rohingya minority as London announced new sanctions.

The foreign ministers of Australia, Belgium, Canada, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, Luxembourg, New Zealand, Portugal, Spain, the Gambia and the UK said Myanmar had "violated its obligations under the Genocide Convention".

"We underscore that the court's judgment is binding upon Myanmar and call on Myanmar to comply fully with its obligations under international law, including the court's decision," they said in a joint statement.
The UK separately said it "formally recognises" genocide against the Rohingya and announced sanctions on five senior military figures.
"The horrific violence and persecution inflicted on the Rohingya cannot go unanswered," said Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.

The sanctions included asset freezes and travel bans, said a Foreign Office statement, adding that London "also intends to introduce legislation targeting the export and supply of aviation fuel to Myanmar".

"The UK is providing an additional £5m in new funding to support Rohingya and other communities with essential lifesaving and life-affirming services to 350,000 people who need it most in Rakhine State, where humanitarian need is most acute," the statement added.
It said a further £3 million would "go towards strengthening accountability and justice for survivors of human rights abuses across Myanmar".
In a historic verdict on Nov 19, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 crackdown in the western Rakhine State.
The ruling was the first time in the ICJ's 80-year history that it has determined that a state committed genocide.
Myanmar's government called the ruling unfair and a "great disappointment".
Shortly after the verdict, Britain announced it would expel Myanmar's defence attache. — AFP

070fd7356168d41d: WASHINGTON: Jensen Huang apologised to Nvidia staff and said he was in therapy on Tuesday, as a stock rally triggered by his shock return as CEO faltered amid persistent doubts over the investigations he faces and the fate of the AI investment boom.

"I made some terrible mistakes," Huang told an hour-long all-hands meeting at the company's Santa Clara, California, headquarters, The New York Times reported after reviewing a livestream of the event.
He told staff it was "not acceptable" that he had broken a code of conduct he helped write, and dismissed suggestions that he had returned because US President Donald Trump had pressured the board.
But Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had been in contact with directors about Huang's return. "I spoke to them, let me put it that way," Trump said. "And I convinced them."
After surging more than 30 per cent on Monday, Nvidia shares fell about six per cent by the close of trading on Tuesday.
"The optimism faded quickly" for Nvidia, wrote Fawad Razaqzada of Forex.com, with "questions over corporate governance and board oversight still lingering".
So far, Monday's surge was a "one day wonder... We are not seeing an upside follow through today at all," said Ken Mahoney, president and CEO of Mahoney Asset Management.
TRUMP PRESSURE
Huang resigned on Nov 12 over extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, a departure that sent shares in Nvidia and companies closely linked to the AI buildout tumbling.
Trump was reportedly persuaded to back the return of the Taiwan-born CEO after top tech investors told him the US economy and Wall Street depended on it.
Nvidia said on Monday that it had reinstated Huang as chief executive after receiving information from the US government that he did not pose a national security risk.
Trump is also an investor in Nvidia, owning as many as 370,000 shares in the company as of Sept 30, according to filings.
Shares linked to the AI boom have fallen steeply in recent weeks amid fears that the AI bubble, inflated since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, was finally bursting.

In downward-trending markets, quick rebounds are common but "tend to get negated and that has been the sequence since early October", Mahoney said, adding that "sellers have absolute control of the market here".
Nvidia is central to the AI investment story — its powerful processors are the key tools used to train and run AI models believed to be at the heart of a technological revolution.
The massive spending on its AI chips and software, housed in sprawling data centres, catapulted the company into the ranks of the world's most valuable firms.

Huang used that success to turn Nvidia into a kind of central bank for other AI companies and start-ups, doling out loans and financial guarantees to firms that would otherwise struggle to borrow from traditional lenders.
'GOOD CORPORATE CITIZEN'
Investors are also weighing a barrage of legal challenges facing Huang and Nvidia.

The board that let Huang go and then rehired him is still overseeing an internal investigation into concerns that he may have been the target of a Chinese espionage campaign, even though Trump says he has been cleared.

The Justice Department is separately investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that allegedly bought Nvidia processors and routed them to Chinese customers in violation of US export restrictions.
The Securities and Exchange Commission has also reportedly opened a probe into Nvidia's accounting practices and potentially misleading communications to shareholders.
"Nvidia is a good corporate citizen. That shouldn't be groundbreaking," US Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters at an unrelated press conference in Washington on Tuesday.

"If Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation, or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people," he added.
Huang will nevertheless face lawmakers at a closed-door hearing before three House committees on December 1 and a livestreamed Senate committee hearing on Dec 3.

Lawmakers from both parties have expressed anger over the circumstances of Huang's return, and the scrutiny is likely to intensify in January, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress.

BEHIND a polite "I'm okay" often lies a quiet emotional strain. A new five-episode vertical mini-series, titled 'I'm Not Okay, Cikgu!', puts that hidden struggle centre stage on social media.

Developed and produced by Folklore Studio with full backing from Yayasan Hasanah, it stars Mira Filzah, Waheeda Wassini, Mia Sara Shauki, Zul Zamir, Jun Vinh Teoh, Meer Nash and Syafiqah A. Pohan, helping audiences spot early warning signs in peers.
Yayasan Hasanah trustee and managing director Siti Kamariah Ahmad Subki noted that relatable digital storytelling reaches younger viewers through tangible action.
"Being young does not mean the problems faced are small. What you feel still matters and there is no need to pretend that everything is fine all the time," Siti Kamariah said.
"We hope this series can help young people recognise when a friend is struggling beneath the surface."

She stressed adults' duty of care: "As adults, we also have a responsibility. We need to listen and give them space to express their feelings, rather than belittling what they go through or rushing to give advice," she said.

af1f41b5a5e1d76b: BERLIN: Germany's consumer protection association said Tuesday it would take legal action against Meta and the makers of Ray-Ban over data privacy concerns linked to AI-powered smart glasses.

The vzbv argued that potential buyers of the glasses were not sufficiently informed that their use could be in breach of the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
"Products must be designed in such a way that people can use them in compliance with data protection rules and the rights of third parties remain protected," said Pop.

5ab2e4de5c120b6e: BEREHOVE: Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky and Hungary's Peter Magyar held talks in west Ukraine Tuesday, with both hailing a new era in ties after years of tension between the neighbours under Budapest's previous Kremlin-friendly ruler Viktor Orban.

Magyar, a pro-EU conservative who took office in May and ended the long Orban era in the country, crossed into Ukraine to meet Zelensky in the war-torn country's westernmost region Transcarpathia -- which is also home to a Hungarian ethnic minority.
The Hungarian prime minister met Zelensky in the city of Uzhgorod, where they laid wreaths in a local cemetery and held talks, before holding a media briefing in the border town of Berehove.
"This is an important moment and it is .. very sensitive," Zelensky said in a press conference alongside Magyar, calling their conversation "positive."

"It is in the interests of all neighbours to maintain good relations with one another... I am very grateful that you have been able to achieve this; let us begin to build trust –- better late than never," Magyar said.
The pair played a symbolic volleyball match in a school in Transcarpathia.
Under nationalist Orban, Kyiv's ties with Hungary -- a neighbouring EU and NATO country -- were essentially frozen, with the former prime minister travelling to Moscow during Russia's invasion.
Relations improved significantly after Kyiv recently passed legislation addressing Budapest's longstanding concerns over the rights of Ukraine's Hungarian minority.
Following the vote, Hungary agreed to allow the European Union to open new sections of EU membership negotiations with Ukraine.
Magyar said he met with local ethnic Hungarians who welcomed the change in tone.

"They’re very pleased that the two countries have finally started to move closer to one another, that we’ve finally put a stop to this completely unnecessary and inexplicable political escalation," he said.
He said the pair discussed "symbolic" projects, such as the reconstruction of Hungarian high school in Berehove, which turns 125 next year.
Entering another winter, Moscow's full-scale offensive against Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions.
'Friendship with Putin leads to nowhere'
Zelensky said Ukraine was now counting on the support of post-Orban Hungary, including in its aspirations to join the EU.
In order to end the war, "solidarity with Ukraine is essential, whilst friendship with Putin leads to nowhere", Zelensky said in an apparent jibe to Orban.
He also said he had an "absolutely honest" conversation with Magyar on Kyiv's EU aspirations, who has expressed skepticism on Ukraine joining the EU quickly.
"I said quite frankly today, Prime Minister, that for us this is an irreversible path," Zelensky said, adding that Ukraine will not go "back to Russia" and that this was "the choice of our people".
Ukrainians had in 2014 held a pro-EU revolution that overthrew a Moscow-backed leader.
Magyar had earlier condemned Russia's invasion, highlighting his break from Orban's stance.
"I would like you to know that the Hungarian people deeply condemn this appalling Russian aggression," he said.
Energy, transport
Zelensky also said the pair had discussed energy and the prospect of bringing Hungarian diesel into Ukraine -- for Budapest to help Kyiv with its exports during wartime.
"There is a shortage of electricity and so on, and our people are defending themselves, our communities are defending themselves... We are counting on Hungary’s support as well," Zelensky said.
Magyar said he was bringing humanitarian aid worth around $2.9 million, including medicine and energy equipment.
Ukraine and Hungary share a short border, with Transcarpathia forming the westernmost part of the country and Uzhgorod lying on the border with nearby Slovakia.

1479a2d5f1158c80: Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.

It's too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.

The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There's not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, "It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field."

58c64dd3bfb5f2ac: In 2017, Apple removed the home button from its iPhones. Users lost a convenient, tangible control — part of a larger shift to digital buttons, knobs, and sliders we also see in cars (like with radio presets and air conditioning) and kitchens (see smart fridges). We can’t leave physical controls behind entirely, though. They tend to be more convenient and efficient — think of how you can use a physical gaming controller without looking at it — and, at times, more precise, like when you use a dial to get the volume just right. But tangible controls are typically preprogrammed to do a specific thing, minimizing their usefulness. A new system called “TangiMap,” co-developed by an MIT graduate student and researcher at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), helps bring tangible control back to your software. The system personalizes the physical controls on everyday devices by mapping digital widgets onto tangible inputs, turning things like editing photos, animation, performing music, and creating 3D models into more dynamic and tactile experiences. Just as a DJ’s pads switch between triggering cues, loops, and samples, TangiMap gives a device’s controls entirely new roles. But how, exactly? TangiMap relies on an AI agent, or semi-autonomous programs that “think” and complete well-defined tasks, to find and act on context about the software you’re using, your tendencies, and the device used to control that program. To gather the required context, the agent can draw on sources such as the program’s API (the rules that let programs talk to each other), an MCP server (a standard that connects AI agents to apps), or a screenshot interpreted by a vision-language model. Then, the agent uses a large language model to put all the info it's gathered into a file before mapping specific digital functions to physical controls. “TangiMap builds on our broader vision of reprogramming common objects to be more dynamic,” says Yunyi Zhu ’20, MEng ’21, a doctoral student in the MIT Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and a CSAIL researcher whose advisor is MIT Associate Professor Stefanie Mueller. “Here, AI agents help us adapt physical controls to whatever we’re working on. We want to bring back physical controls so we can interact with our devices eyes-free, the way you adjust a car’s volume without looking away from the road. Physical controls also let you adjust several settings at once, like tweaking brightness and contrast together when editing an image, which is hard to do on a screen.” The system helped the researchers turn a standard mixer into a photo-editing controller. That way, they could adjust color in Adobe Lightroom, with a complementary visualization of those controls displayed on their screen. The team did the same with sound-mixing software, so that performers can adjust their music in real-time with their own inputs to knobs and faders.  The researchers also reprogrammed a simpler mixer to work with the 3D modeling program Blender. Their interface included an area where users can type in a prompt, and once the model was generated, users could adjust features like shininess on a mixer using physical controls. Within Adobe’s Character Animator software, TangiMap connected specific expressions and movements to buttons on a control pad so users could animate (or “puppeteer”) a cartoon character live. Zhu and co-author Chang Xiao, an assistant professor at Boston University, presented their tool at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology earlier this month. Zhu and Xiao created a custom user interface (UI) for each application. While that adds another layer of personalization to the creative process, the team is hoping to create a more streamlined system that helps the designer to generate the UI for their device by taking a picture. The researchers are also considering the physical aspects of user interactions. They want to use more ergonomic devices and also ensure that TangiMap accounts for where users position their hands when doing different tasks. For example, users typically hold a mixer differently when they’re using it to make music than, say, when playing a video game. You may want controls mapped closer or further apart, depending on what you’re doing. Zhu is hoping to do a user study to get more feedback about TangiMap, and whether this kind of “smart DJing” could indeed improve those experiences. But the dynamic reprogramming she ultimately envisions is even more ambitious. “The same way our phones and computers generalize to a range of tasks, we want other objects to be more intelligent,” she says. “I would like to build physical items that use an AI agent as a brain to decide what to reprogram into. They could understand what to transform into, given a specific situation.” A chemical jar, for instance, could tell you if it’s sealed correctly when asked, and when you want to see what it’s typically used for, the container would instead display that information. While that kind of versatility and interactivity is a ways off, more powerful agents and more intricate fabrication pipelines could bring everyday objects to life. Their work was supported, in part, by Google’s Gemini Academic Program Award.

e41a71b86838ecc4: Extraordinarily harsh droughts and heavy flooding have become more common around the globe this year due to an unusually strong El Niño. AP Photo/Charlie RiedelThe extreme weather fueled by an unusually intense El Niño has caused flooding in low-lying Florida communities, hammered the California coast and upended hurricane patterns – just to name a few examples. But it also poses a growing challenge for companies that need timely climate data to manage supply chains. This information is disappearing due to federal budget cuts, leaving businesses less prepared to handle the impact of extreme weather. To be sure, forecasters saw the 2026 El Niño coming. The Climate Prediction Center at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, has been forecasting a very strong El Niño since the spring, and its October update put the odds at 83% that this El Niño will become the strongest since record-keeping began in 1950, likely lasting into early 2027. That kind of warning is valuable. It gives companies months to stock up, reroute shipments and line up backup suppliers before storms arrive or droughts set in. But bit by bit, other valuable sources of climate data are getting cut. That includes a federal database on disasters, which adds up costs weeks after the event, that NOAA stopped updating in May 2025. The Trump administration has also cut or undercut federal climate analyses, as well as staff and funding for daily forecasting, which has left large parts of the country without coverage during extreme events – a risky prospect for businesses. As a scholar of business operations and sustainability, I believe these cuts could have cascading effects on companies and supply chains by leaving them more vulnerable to future weather disasters. Eventually, these disruptions will hit consumers as well through higher prices. Gaps in climate science grow In North America, El Niño weather patterns are linked to severe storms in the Pacific, as well as floods, fires and droughts. The economic hit can be substantial, from transportation delays to massive crop failures. Strong El Niño events have historically cost the global economy trillions of dollars. This El Niño arrives as the pace of natural disasters picks up. While the U.S. averaged fewer than five “billion-dollar” disasters a year in the 1980s, that number now stands above 20 a year – a huge leap, even accounting for inflation. And the 2023 and 2024 totals were the highest on record. While the scope of weather damage gets worse and worse, critical data is missing. That includes NOAA’s decision to retire its “Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters” database, ending updates after 2024. For more than four decades, it tracked the cost of U.S. weather disasters after the fact – and businesses and researchers alike have relied on it to build prediction models. For example, scientists use these historical records to put odds on future losses or to forecast economic activity. Some of my own research also relies on historically accurate climate and weather data. Unfortunately, the gap in climate science may be widening. In 2025 the federal government shut down Climate.gov, which served as a central repository for weather and climate data, while its El Niño blog has been frozen since June 2025. The National Climate Assessments, the U.S. government’s preeminent reports on climate science, were taken offline, while the National Weather Service cited staff shortages as it cut back weather balloon launches at multiple sites, which feed forecast models. Fortunately, some of these data-gathering efforts have migrated elsewhere. The scientists behind the El Niño blog have moved to a nonprofit, while another nonprofit is carrying on the efforts behind the billion-dollar disaster database. El Nino’s effects, especially strong in 2026, have disrupted crops and supply chains around the world, including a delayed monsoon season in India. Ashish Vaishnav/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images What this means for supply chains The Trump administration has justified these cuts by citing high administrative costs and potential errors in the prediction models. But that still leaves companies, which lean on public weather data more than most shoppers realize, scrambling. In many industries, including retail, food processing and agriculture, the payoff from acting early to safeguard supply chains can be large. Real-time and near-real-time data is used in supply chains for enhancing crop yields, finding the best routes for transport, inventory planning, and ensuring worker safety during weather emergencies. For example, Walmart invests heavily in technology and specialists to monitor weather-related disruptions and build resilient supply chains. Another example is insurance companies, which use weather data for designing commercial insurance policies and processing claims. Risk Management Solutions Inc., a leading catastrophe risk-modeling company owned by Moody’s Corp., regularly use NOAA’s hurricane datasets to inform its advanced risk models. When public climate data disappears, companies still need timely information to run their supply chains, so some will pay for alternative data. This typically comes from paid private services and subscriptions. Startups such as WindBorne Systems, Sofar Ocean, Tomorrow.io, Black Swift Technologies and Saildrone offer private weather balloon data and advanced climate prediction services. While privatization can fill some gaps, it’s usually only the large retailers and insurers who can afford these forecasts. Smaller suppliers, local farmers and independent truckers further up the supply chain often can’t. And that’s exactly where many disruptions begin. What it means for consumers Shoppers feel these disruptions when shortages feed into higher prices, often months later. In 2024, for example, extreme weather in the Americas, including Florida, pushed U.S. orange juice prices to an all-time high that fall. They have have stayed elevated since hurricanes Helene and Milton battered Florida’s groves. Holiday staples are also not spared. A 2021 heat dome in the Pacific Northwest led to major damage to Christmas tree farms, causing their prices to rise an additional 5% to 10% that year. And these effects are often global. Poor rains in West Africa more than doubled cocoa prices in 2024, and that inflation is still feeding into U.S. chocolate prices, which were up 14% in 2026. A historic El Niño, arriving just as federal climate data becomes sparse, makes this winter an ideal, if unfortunate, test of what climate information is really worth. Suvrat Dhanorkar does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

fff3e0c357eca5c4: Arm is swinging the hammer at an enthusiast’s site hosting a bloat-free version of its instruction reference documentation, demanding it be taken offline after several years of availability.

The demand from Arm lawyers to Jon Palmisciano concern Jon’s Arm Reference, a site that provides the same arm Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) info available on Arm’s site, but with what Palmisciano describes as “without a million popups and all of the bloat” that Arm provides on its own.

According to Palmisciano, his copy of the Arm ISA was culled from machine-readable XML files and stripped of the bloat. He built his version in 2022 with new CSS on top of it, and the addition of a quick search feature that, according to his comments on Hacker News, isn’t available in the official version.

“The aim has always been to make it the most comfortable and bullshit-free browsing experience for people who need these docs daily,” Palmisciano wrote in HN. Based on the responses the site seems to have plenty of fans.

That doesn’t matter to Arm, though: As far as the lawyers are concerned, Palmisciano’s site is a copyright violation due to its use of Arm trademarks and inclusion of copyrighted reference material for the Armv9-A and Armv9-A architecture.

Arm doesn’t care if Palmisciano’s project is well intentioned or for the benefit of the many software developers that write code for its chipsets, either: They want it offline by December 4 – 10 days from the publication of this story – or else.
As for what is going to happen, it seems like Jon’s Arm Reference will likely cease to exist in a little over a week – at least in its current form.

“Ideally I'd love to just get permission from Arm to keep the site up, but I'm pretty pessimistic about that,” Palmisciano told us. That said, Palmisciano has “already seen a few archives and mirrors already.” The HN thread discussing the takedown order includes links to several versions, and Palmisciano has another trick up his sleeve that he’s considering playing: Open-sourcing the software he used to build his ISA page.

“I'd also consider open-sourcing my tooling so that people can (for their own private use) turn the original XML downloads from Arm into an identical site they can host locally,” Palmisciano told us. He said that he'll likely tweet about opening the tooling if he does do so. He's also considered directing the URL for Jon's Arm reference to point to the open-source tool, but Arm wants the subdomain it's hosted on removed from his site as well, so that may not happen.
Arm has been in touch to defend itself as well, saying that Arm appreciates the efforts of people like Palmisciano, but that it still has to protect its brand, and documentation.

"We have a responsibility to ensure Arm is the primary source of technical resources and information and to protect the Arm brand," an Arm spokesperson told us. "Striking the right balance between third parties sharing helpful peer-to-peer resources while ensuring copyrighted Arm-related technical content is accurate has been critical to building the thriving ecosystem we have today."

In other words, if you’re an Arm dev worried about losing a valuable resource and having to turn to a website that bombards you with junk just to look up a few simple opcodes and operands you’d better find a backup host before next month.
That said, Arm is willing to work something out with Palmisciano, the company told us.

"We have recently flagged our concerns with regard to the use of Arm copyright content and the Arm brand on this website and shared the Arm trademark guidelines," Arm explained. "Our hope is to open a constructive dialogue, and we've asked that the website owner reach out as we seek to resolve this."

As Palmisciano posted on HN, Arm is asking for removal of its trademark and copyrighted documentation. That, Palmisciano said, "seems hard to work around while still keeping the site useful." He also followed up around 8.30 pm GMT on Tuesday to let us know that he has not yet heard directly from Arm. ®

c190f8b3b890d0c3: WASHINGTON: A rally sparked by Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia's chief executive faded on Tuesday, with the company's shares falling as doubts persisted over the probes he faces and the fate of the AI investment boom.
"The optimism faded quickly" for Nvidia, wrote Fawad Razaqzada of Forex.com, with "questions over corporate governance and board oversight still lingering."
After vaulting more than 30 per cent on Monday following Huang's shock comeback as CEO, Nvidia was down about eight per cent Tuesday.
"This could be a 'one day wonder' and so far it is since we are not seeing an upside follow through today at all," said Ken Mahoney, president and CEO of Mahoney Asset Management.
Huang resigned on Nov 12 over extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, a departure that sent shares in Nvidia and companies closely linked to the AI buildout tumbling.

The rescue of the Taiwan-born Huang was orchestrated by US President Donald Trump, who, according to reports, was talked into advocating for the CEO's return after top tech investors told him the US economy and stability on Wall Street depended on it.
Nvidia said Monday that it had reinstated Huang as chief executive after receiving information from the US government that he did not pose a national security risk.
Trump is also an investor in Nvidia, owning as many as 370,000 shares in the company as of Sept 30, according to filings.

The stock market in recent weeks has seen massive falls in shares linked to the AI boom, with fears growing that the AI bubble was finally coming to an end after four years of bullish growth sparked by the launch of ChatGPT in 2022.

In bearish markets, quick rebounds are common but "tend to get negated and that has been the sequence since early October," Mahoney said, adding that "sellers have absolute control of the market here."
Nvidia is central to the AI investment story – its powerful processors are the key tool to train and run the AI models that are believed to be at the heart of a technological revolution.
The massive spending on its AI chips and software, housed in sprawling data centres, catapulted the company into the ranks of the world's most valuable firms.

Huang used that success to turn Nvidia into a kind of central bank for other AI companies and startups, generously doling out loans and financial backstops to firms that would otherwise struggle to find easy financing from traditional lenders.

The departure of the leather jacket-wearing CEO had thrown the AI economy into doubt, and his return seemed to inject confidence back into the AI trade on Monday, before fizzling out again on Tuesday.
- LEGAL BATTLES -
Investors are also weighing a barrage of legal challenges facing Huang and Nvidia.

The board that let Huang go and then rehired him is still overseeing an internal investigation into concerns that he may have been the target of a Chinese espionage campaign, even though Trump says he has been cleared.

The Justice Department is separately investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that allegedly bought Nvidia processors and routed them to Chinese customers in violation of US export restrictions.
The Securities and Exchange Commission has also reportedly opened a probe into Nvidia's accounting practices and potentially misleading communication to shareholders.
The Trump administration has generally avoided going after its allies, so the federal probes may not amount to much, said Columbia University professor Eric Talley.
Huang will nevertheless face lawmakers at a closed-door hearing before three House committees on Dec 1 and a livestreamed Senate committee hearing on Dec 3.

Lawmakers from both parties have expressed anger over the circumstances of Huang's return, and the scrutiny is likely to intensify in January, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress after sweeping this month's midterm elections.
California's attorney general has also opened an investigation into the company's chip exports and shareholder disclosures.

"We all have an opportunity to enforce laws, and I would say a duty, especially if other entities, like the federal government in my humble opinion, are not," California Attorney General Rob Bonta told CNBC.--AFP

80315362768f2ecf: A Romanian hacker, armed with only an open source coding agent, a Chrome browser, and a Mac, tried multiple ways to break into a financial services firm, ultimately found an access key - luckily, it was a decoy - and carried out an entire (almost) attack in under six minutes.

It’s a stark reminder that miscreants don’t need sophisticated malware - as in the Binance heist - or AI pen-testing tools like ARTEX to carry out intrusions into critical networks. Open source coding agents, and specifically OpenCode in this case, also work just fine.

“What surprised me most was how little it took and the toolkit: a free coding agent, the curl that comes with every Mac and an ordinary Chrome, all from one laptop,” Jesta co-founder and CTO Lior Finkelshtein told The Register. “Until now I thought that we had more time until tools like OpenCode are used in offensive operations. This incident shows us that it's already in use in the field, and we will probably see more of that in the future.”

Jesta is a Tel Aviv-based security startup that builds defensive tools to detect and stop autonomous AI attacks. In a report shared exclusively with The Register, Finkelshtein documented an attempted intrusion targeting a major financial services company that’s also a Jesta customer - the security shop declined to say which one.

Jesta’s investigation into the incident determined that someone in Bucharest downloaded a free AI coding agent called OpenCode and pointed it at the financial services customer on November 16 at 4:24:57 a.m. ET.
'Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking'

OpenCode is an open source coding agent that lets users connect to more than 200 model providers or local models, including Anthropic’s Claude models, OpenAI’s GPTs, Google’s Gemini, DeepSeek, and Z.ai’s GLM. Jesta doesn’t know which model the attacker used, as there was nothing in the traffic that named the model. OpenCode's web fetch tool, however, did name itself, so Jesta knows the attacker used this coding agent - not a scanner - to do the dirty work.

“Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking,” Finkelshtein said in a Tuesday report about the agent-led attack. But, he added, nothing in the coding agent “stops you from pointing it at someone else's website either. When you do, the agent goes through the site the same way it goes through code. It reads, tries something, reads the result and tries the next thing, for as long as you let it run.”
That’s what it did in this operation, which took less than six minutes and cost the human operator nothing.

The first call came from a Chrome browser on a Mac, requesting the front page of one of the financial firm’s systems. The site refused it, and six seconds later, the same IPv6 address in Bucharest, on an ordinary DIGI Romania business line, tried again. It used the same Chrome version, but said it was an Android Pixel 10 phone (it wasn’t) to see if the site would let a phone in (it didn’t).

After failing to gain access through the front page, the agent asked the system for its API definition, which was also refused. Five seconds later, it tried a different address - this one was a decoy set up by Jesta - and it answered the agent, providing the readable file defining how the API works.

The agent read the document, and 13 seconds later followed a link it contained. At 4:26:01 a.m. ET, Jesta’s defenses marked the website visitor as an AI agent, opened a case, and from here on out, everything the agent accessed was contained inside a fake environment designed to trick intruders. This included a phony key, which the attacker then used to attempt to break into the company’s systems.

“It worked like a developer,” Finkelshtein said about the coding agent. “It read the API docs and did what they said. It found a key and used it. It checked whether the lock was real, then made up a key of its own and tried that. None of the threat feeds the customer has knew the address, so a blocklist would never have stopped it. The bar for doing this is now installing an app. Think about how many people can do that.”
'No blocklist would have helped'

In addition to OpenCode, the attacker used only Chrome 157, both in desktop and mobile modes, and curl/8.7.1, a command-line tool that has shipped with every Mac since macOS 15. The agent passed information between the three tools. It included the planted key in a command-line request and then tested three scenarios – using the decoy key, no key, and a fabricated key – to determine whether what it found in the API documentation was legit.

It also tried multiple URLs using the browser. While it ultimately identified a valid endpoint, it attempted to read from one that accepts only data submissions, so its request was blocked again. Five minutes and 44 seconds after the first request, it gave up, and the logs haven’t detected any activity from this same intruder since then.
The security shop and its customer disclosed the activity to law enforcement and told us it’s “being handled.”
While the attacker wasn’t able to steal anything in this attempt, security teams still need to take note, according to Finkelshtein.

“No blocklist would have helped” detect the malicious traffic, he explained. “Most security tools still decide by asking whether an address is known to be bad, and for this one the answer was no. If that key had been real, it would have been in.”

Instead of blocklists, Finkelshtein suggests paying attention to what the visitor does. In this case, several of its actions gave it away - including following a link that only existed inside an API doc, using a desktop browser and a fake phone, then curl, all from the same address within minutes, and trying multiple keys - including one with a made up name and then no key - within seconds.

“Open source lets anyone build software without a big team,” Finkelshtein wrote in the Tuesday blog. “AI is doing the same for hacking. The skill is in the model, the model is a setting, and the person giving the instructions doesn't need to know how any of it works.” ®

22995c289ab600a9: By nine votes to six, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people in connection with its 2017 “clearance operations” in Rakhine State. The ruling is an alarm bell for all states accused of genocide. The year 2017 was not the first Rohingya exodus from Myanmar: in 1978 and again in 1991-92, hundreds of thousands of Rohingya poured into Bangladesh to escape state persecution. Many returned, and were forced to flee again when new violence erupted. Today, more than 1.2 million Rohingya are in refugee camps in Bangladesh without any concrete prospect to return to Myanmar. Most Rohingya want to return, but not without conditions that would ensure their safety. The most crucial condition is the guarantee of citizenship rights. Since Myanmar stripped the Rohingya of their citizenship in 1982, they have been living under apartheid-like conditions. Among many discriminatory policies imposed on Rohingya life, the Rohingya faced restrictions on movement, education and health care while families were restricted to a two-child limit. Returning to Myanmar just to face the same conditions of life is not an option for many Rohingya. The repatriation conundrum It’s unlikely, however, that Myanmar will agree to grant citizenship to the Rohingya. Since the 2021 coup d'état that ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi and her National League for Democracy, the military has had sole control of the government. Gen. Min Aung Hlaing is seen at the IX Moscow conference on international security in Moscow in June 2021. (AP Photo/Alexander Zemlianichenko) Earlier this year, Min Aung Hlaing, the architect of the Rohingya genocide who had been commander-in-chief of the Myanmar Forces since 2011, stepped down from his role and was subsequently elected president by a military-dominated parliament. This makes the prospect of a safe and dignified repatriation of the Rohingya to Myanmar a near impossibility. The Myanmar military and government aren’t the only entities complicating the return of the Rohingya. Since late 2023, vast swaths of Rakhine state, where most Rohingya resided until 2017, have been under control of the Arakan army. The army is the largest and most powerful non-state armed group in the country and it is vying for the independence of the Arakan region, where Rakhine is located. The Arakan army is openly hostile to the Rohingya, and those residing in the territory it controls are facing many of the same restrictions that were previously imposed by the state. The enforcement deficit The ICJ established Myanmar’s responsibility for the genocide, and consequently ordered it to provide reparations and compensation, with details still to be decided. But, in practice, there is little the court can do to compel Myanmar to take accountability and pursue justice if it refuses to do so. The ICJ has no independent enforcement mechanism; it only relies on states’ willingness to obey international law. Only the United Nations Security Council could decide to take coercive action against Myanmar, but China and Russia, which both hold veto power, are likely to oppose it. The two states have provided Min Aung Hlaing’s regime with political, diplomatic and military support over the years. Each also has its own issues with international human rights law, namely Russia’s war in Ukraine and China’s treatment of the Uyghurs. How the ruling might help the Rohingya The ICJ ruling has brought much-needed attention to the plight of the Rohingya. Renewed interest in the Rohingya crisis is expected to draw donations that could help alleviate some of the more pressing needs. Funding for the refugee camps has dwindled in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic and the dismantlement of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID). Currently, the Rohingya in Bangladesh only receive US$7-$12 per person per month in food assistance. Read more: Thousands are feared dead in Myanmar’s quake. Trump’s USAID cuts will cause even more unnecessary deaths Combined with the lack of income-generating opportunities, the cuts to food rations are frequently identified by refugees as the most severe challenge they face in the camps. More attention could also result in stronger political pressure, not just on Myanmar but also on its regional partners. Malaysia, for example, began deporting refugees back to Myanmar in September 2026. Since the government continues to deny access to international agencies for the refugees, including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, it could not be verified whether these returns were voluntary, as Malaysia claimed. It’s unlikely the Rohingya, who make up the majority of Myanmar refugees in Malaysia, are returning of their own free will. International pressure could force Malaysia to stop the deportations and avoid causing further harm to its already vulnerable Rohingya refugee community. Not ‘illegal immigrants’ Finally, the most immediate benefit of the ruling is that, for the first time, there is a formal recognition of the Rohingya as a distinct people. The ruling directly contradicts Myanmar’s assertions that the Rohingya are “illegal immigrants from Bangladesh” who have no legitimate claim to rights and land in Rakhine. The ICJ ruling clearly affirms that the atrocities the Rohingya have suffered are indeed genocide, and while it doesn’t guarantee justice for the Rohingya, it’s a necessary precondition that opens the path to restorative justice. San Beauchemin is a member of the International Association of Genocide Scholars.
