e2ba0e13f0a1a55f: In a Grade 2 classroom in Rautahat, in Nepal’s southern plains, teacher Renuka Dahal holds up a picture card of a mango. She gives the Nepali word, then asks her students what they call it at home. They respond in Tharu and Maithili, the languages many of them speak with their families. “I ask my students to teach me words in their language,” she told UNICEF in 2025. “It makes them feel that I care about who they are.” And that small exchange marks a real change. For Canadians interested in Indigenous language revitalization, and for teachers welcoming newcomer students, Nepal’s experience shows what it takes to move language rights off paper and into the classroom. For generations, many children in Nepal started school in a language they didn’t understand. Yet research shows that beginning school in a familiar language can strengthen learning and make it easier to acquire additional languages, including Nepali and English. Nepal has written that lesson into its 2015 Constitution, which guarantees communities the right to education in their mother tongue. A country of 124 mother tongues Nepal is one of the most linguistically diverse countries in the world, though the state has not always acknowledged it. The 2021 census recorded 124 mother tongues. Fifty years earlier, in 1971, when the Panchayat regime was promoting Nepali above all other languages, the census counted just 17 languages. Today, Nepali is the first language of just under 45 per cent of the population. I have worked in Nepal since 1991, first as a volunteer schoolteacher and later as a linguist and anthropologist. I have spent decades researching the country’s linguistic diversity. The census numbers reflect a shift I have witnessed on the ground, in communities. In 2021, for the first time, the census asked people about their ancestral language as well as their mother tongue. Nearly three million more people name Nepali as their mother tongue than they name it as their ancestral language, a sign that many families have shifted to Nepali. For other languages, the gap goes the other way. Some 300,000 more people name Nepal Bhasa, the language of the Newar community, as their ancestral language than name it as their mother tongue. Nepali is also spreading as a second language: 46 per cent of the population now speaks it that way, up from 33 per cent in 2011. Whatever pressures Nepal’s other languages face, Nepali is certainly not a language at risk. Rights on paper On paper, Nepal’s laws side with children. The government’s School Education Sector Plan 2022-32 commits to scaling up early-grade teaching in children’s mother tongues. In practice, implementation has been sluggish and uneven. As comparative education scholar Uma Pradhan has shown, policy has long treated mother tongues as a bridge to Nepali, a stepping stone to be left behind, with the state offering little support. In a 2026 study from Tanahun, one grandparent spoke about a granddaughter in Grade 2 who was being taught only in Nepali and English: “She [does not have the] opportunity to study in [her ancestral] language; so, there is a gap.” Grade 1 students at Shree Sahara Bal Primary School in Pokhara, Nepal, in June 2013. (Photo by Jim Holmes for AusAID), CC BY The evidence for local languages A 2024 study commissioned by UNICEF Nepal examined language use in 30 schools across all seven provinces. Its conclusion was unequivocal. When children learn in their mother tongue or a familiar language, they take a more active part in lessons and do better in assessments and exams. Many schools have rushed to switch to English-language teaching, often for financial reasons and with little teacher training. Yet students taught in Nepali outscored their English-taught peers in Nepali, in science and even in English, according to the study’s analysis of school assessment results, which was limited in scale. In Dailekh, in western Nepal, principal Sher Bahadur Rana told UNICEF that teachers once corrected children who used their own “language or dialect.” After training in multilingual teaching, he said, “we learned that children learn faster and feel more confident when we teach them in the language they speak and understand best.” Obstacles to implementation A recent review by education researchers Pariksha Onta and Amado Padilla, covering 111 studies and policy documents, points to a “persistent disconnect between constitutional commitments, classroom practice and targeted funding.” Where mother tongues are taught at all, they are usually a subject rather than the language children learn in. Textbooks in children’s mother tongues remain scarce, and most of those that do exist are translations of Nepali materials with little locally relevant content. Far too few teachers who speak local languages are recruited or trained. Parents, meanwhile, are caught in the middle. Many see English-language schools as a marker of quality and employability. And funding is lacking: in 2026–27, education and sports together received around 10.3 per cent of Nepal’s national budget, well below the international benchmark of allocating at least 15 per cent to education. Onta and Padilla’s review also highlights what works. In some Kathmandu Valley schools, children learn in Nepal Bhasa for their first three grades before Nepali and English are phased in. A strong foundation in the mother tongue supports learning in the other languages, which means families don’t have to choose between them. From paper to practice As I argued previously with colleagues Lava Deo Awasthi and Yogendra Prasad Yadava, rights “do not implement themselves.” Children should begin school in the language they understand best, with Nepali and English introduced gradually, building on that foundation. Making this work requires sustained funding, teachers trained to teach in children’s languages, and materials that reflect their lives and communities. Some municipalities have introduced local-language education programs, while Nepal’s Curriculum Development Centre has developed curricula for elementary education in more than 20 mother tongues. Language policy can sound technical, but at heart it is about whether a child’s first experience of school is a welcoming one. In Renuka Dahal’s classroom in Rautahat, where children now teach their teacher, the message is simple: their languages belong in school, and so do they. 8706ebb14650cba2: THE first foreign astronaut on a Chinese space mission said on Tuesday that he will be carrying 'the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis' when he blasts off from the Gobi Desert this week.
Beijing has poured billions into the Chinese space programme, whose prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts, typically rotated every six months.

The Shenzhou-24 mission is set to lift off at 8.18 am (0018 GMT) on Wednesday from the Jiuquan launch centre in northwest China, China Manned Space Agency spokesman Zhang Jingbo told a news conference.

Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a Pakistan Air Force pilot and payload specialist, will be the first foreign astronaut to fly on a Chinese space mission and also the first non-Chinese to board the Tiangong space station.
"I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis," Ali told a separate news conference held later on Tuesday to introduce the crew.
"To every child who is watching while I'm in orbit, just look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams," he said in English, following other remarks in Urdu and Mandarin.
Ali will join a short orbital flight expected to last around five days before returning with the Shenzhou-23 spaceship, which docked at the Tiangong space station in May.

Pakistan's space agency said Ali would conduct experiments in orbit, including cultivating microalgae as a potential food and oxygen source for future space missions, and testing the effects of spaceflight on quinoa seeds.
Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif hailed the mission as a testament to the "exceptional trust, mutual respect and enduring brotherhood" between the two countries.
"Pakistan-China friendship is surpassing the heights of the Himalayas, in its journey to outer space," he said.
Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a regular briefing that 'China and Pakistan are all-weather strategic cooperative partners.'
Pakistan's Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, who is in China for the launch, said the mission underscored the trust and 'iron brotherhood' between the two countries.
China was excluded from the International Space Station in 2011 when the United States banned NASA from collaborating with Beijing.
This prompted the Asian giant to invest heavily in its own space activities, landing a probe on the far side of the Moon in 2019 and a rover on Mars in 2021.
China successfully landed a reusable rocket for the first time in July, according to its space agency, marking a major step in its space ambitions and in reducing launch costs.
China is aiming to land astronauts on the Moon before 2030, a race in which the United States is also competing with its Artemis programme.
The crew currently aboard the Tiangong space station is headed by 40-year-old Zhu Yangzhu, Lai Ka-ying and Zhang Zhiyuan, also 40.
Lai is Hong Kong's first astronaut and the only woman currently aboard.
After the new, all-male crew reaches the Tiangong, Pakistan's Ali will return to Earth alongside Lai and Zhang.
Zhu will remain on board to complete China's first full-year stay in space – a key test of endurance critical for future lunar and potentially deep-space ambitions.
Zhu will be accompanied for the next six-month Tiangong rotation by 51-year-old space veteran Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi, in his late thirties and making his first voyage to space.
Ali is not the first Pakistani in space, with Monaco-based polar adventurer Namira Salim having flown on Virgin Galactic's Galactic 04 mission in October 2023.

c47be6da5020cf67: NINE months into the biggest energy shock in modern history, the oil market's recovery is surprisingly swift, but plentiful crude supplies are masking a stubborn diesel shortage that could yet upend fuel markets.
Benchmark Brent crude has dropped by more than 20 per cent since the start of the month to just over US$90 a barrel.
Recovering Middle East exports and fading fears of a major escalation in the United States-Iran war have driven the decline.
The retreat comes after high fuel prices pummelled US President Donald Trump's Republican Party in this month's midterm elections.
Crucially, petrol and diesel prices have also retreated from their peaks, offering consumers some relief and promising to ease inflationary pressures on governments.
In Europe, a major diesel importer, futures prices have fallen by a quarter from their September peak to around US$160 a barrel, but they remain nearly twice their level at the start of the year.

In the US, the world's largest refiner and oil consumer, retail diesel prices have slipped below US$6 to a two-month low, while petrol was down below US$4 for the first time since August, according to GasBuddy.
Any lasting recovery hinges on easing Middle East tensions, however, and that is far from assured.
Iran has stepped up attacks on tankers around the Strait of Hormuz and struck facilities in Bahrain and Kuwait, while Yemen's Houthi militia continues to target Saudi Arabia.

As a result, oil flows through Hormuz slowed to around 9.5 million barrels per day (bpd) in the 10 days through Nov 19, from an average of 12.2 million bpd last month, which was the highest level since the war began in late February, according to shipping analytics firm Kpler.

The Middle East disruption has resulted in the loss of nearly three billion barrels of oil, more than any previous crisis, forcing consumers to draw heavily on inventories, which have fallen by a cumulative 462 million barrels since the start of the war, according to the International Energy Agency. Recovering Middle East exports have begun to close that gap.
Commercial US crude stockpiles have risen by around two per cent since the start of this month after hitting their lowest point since 2018 in September.
China also appeared to add to its vast crude inventories last month.
Crude, in other words, is no longer the market's biggest headache.

Fuel markets remain considerably tighter. The tightness, though, is tilted heavily towards diesel following the loss of refining capacity in the Middle East and months of Ukrainian attacks on Russian infrastructure.
Last year, the Middle East and Russia together accounted for more than two million bpd, or nearly 30 per cent, of the 7.4 million bpd of diesel shipped by sea.
Global seaborne diesel exports have averaged just 6.2 million bpd so far this year despite sharply higher US shipments, explaining why diesel remains scarce.
Petrol tells a very different story. The market has been far less exposed to the loss of Middle Eastern and Russian supplies, allowing inventories to recover much faster.
US petrol margins of around US$20 a barrel are back below their pre-war levels.
European diesel refining margins have similarly retreated from around US$90 a barrel in September to US$60, but they remain roughly triple their 2025 average.
Falling product prices have also sharply reduced US refining profitability. The benchmark US refining crack spread has dropped from a record US$72 a barrel in September to around US$41 now.
That leaves refiners caught in an unusual bind: running hard to capture strong diesel margins, they are simultaneously pumping more petrol into a market that is already recovering quickly.

For now, diesel's extraordinary profitability should comfortably compensate refiners for weaker petrol returns. And with global fuel inventories still diminished after nine months of disruption, petrol prices are unlikely to collapse.
However, if petrol supplies build far enough to crush margins, they could eventually overwhelm diesel's profitability and drag overall refining margins toward levels that force plants to cut runs.
For now, that remains a distant prospect. But until all product markets come back into balance, unexpected price anomalies will likely continue popping up.
The writer is from Reuters

adb3a252020b9df1: JIUQUAN: When the Shenzhou-24 space flight takes off on Wednesday for China's Tiangong space station, it will be a moment of pride not just for China, but also for Pakistan.

Zeeshan Ali, a 40-year-old pilot, is set to be the first Pakistani in orbit and the first foreign national to board the space station, as China promotes Tiangong as a hub for international cooperation while the Nasa-led International Space Station faces possible retirement by 2030.

Part of a three-man crew that includes Chinese commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi, Ali will work as a payload specialist and is set to stay at the station for 5 to 10 days, conducting experiments.
The launch of the spacecraft, which will use a Long March-2F rocket, is scheduled for 8.18am from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in northwest China.

To prepare for the flight, Ali trained for seven months in Beijing, during which he underwent intensive Chinese-language classes, learning Chinese songs and reading Chinese poetry. He also practised calligraphy and played table tennis.
"I'm not flying for myself. I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder," Ali told reporters.
Space cooperation between China and Pakistan dates back to the early 1990s.
China has launched Pakistani satellites and a Pakistani-built rover is also set to fly on a Chinese lunar mission around 2028.

Pakistani prime minister Shehbaz Sharif called the flight "a historic first" in a post on X and thanked Chinese president Xi Jinping, saying, "Pakistan-China friendship is surpassing the heights of the Himalayas, in its journey to outer space."
"China has always been very good at using space for soft power outreach," said Victoria Samson, chief director of space security and stability at the US-based Secure World Foundation.

"See how many satellites it builds and launches for other countries, and how it builds telescopes and tracking centres in the Global South — so this is just one more action of that same genre," she said.
A long stay for one Chinese astronaut
While Ali's stay is much shorter than the usual six-month rotation for a Chinese astronaut, it is a big deal for Pakistan.

"It brings prestige, important science and technology know-how, and a level of deeper collaboration and diplomatic goodwill with China," said Blaine Curcio, ​founder of Hong Kong-based Orbital Gateway Consulting.
"By having an international astronaut, China is making it clear that they are open for business," Curcio said.

China's self-built station, named Tiangong or Celestial Palace in Chinese, has been fully operational since late 2022. It can host up to six astronauts during handovers when an arriving three-person crew overlaps with the departing crew.
This time, the handover will be different.

Shenzhou-23 commander Zhu Yangzhu will stay on to support Beijing's study of how the human body copes in space — a crucial step towards a planned crewed mission to the moon and a potential journey to Mars. The rest of the Shenzhou-23 crew will depart Tiangong alongside Ali.
Zhu, who will stay for a year, will hold the record for the longest single stay in orbit by a Chinese astronaut by the time he leaves.

China's goal of human presence on the moon by 2030 remains unchanged following the delay to its Chang'e-7 lunar mission, which failed to meet launch conditions this year amid adverse weather linked to a tropical storm.

That compares with the US target of 2028 to return humans to the moon amid a tense race for a moon base buildup, a stepping stone to eventual human exploration of Mars. China plans to establish a research base on the moon by 2035 with Russia.
Washington has warned that Beijing could seek to dominate access to resource-rich areas of the moon. Beijing rejects such allegations, saying it advocates peaceful use of outer space.
Flying to the moon was also on Ali's mind.
"I hope for the next chapter of China-Pakistan space cooperation to grow from one astronaut, one flight to multiple joint flights, to (the) moon, Mars and beyond," he said.
9add114a88a6efb3: Homo erectus was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought. A handful of teeth from two caves in southern China's Guangxi Province just filled in a significant gap in the fossil record of a region that's vital to the story of how our genus, Homo, took over the world.

The chemical makeup of the teeth's enamel suggests that, over the course of their lives, these Homo erectus moved across surprisingly large distances and made their living in dense tropical rainforests—an environment we'd previously assumed that only our species had ever gained a real foothold in. And one of the teeth offers a strong clue that Homo erectus probably shared this vast landscape with the Denisovans.
A handful of teeth with a lot to say

Baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China. University of Copenhagen paleoanthropologist Frido Welker and his colleagues unearthed a total of nine hominin teeth from among the more than 18,000 bones and fragments from non-hominin animals found there. Macquarie University paleoanthropologist Kira Westaway and her colleagues analyzed proteins and chemical isotopes from the enamel of five of these teeth.

fe2d72767e674eb6: Microsoft has brought its HorizonDB PostgreSQL service into public preview in Fabric, aiming to bring transactional and analytical workloads closer together.
The corporation says applications can submit queries through a single PostgreSQL endpoint, with transactional and analytical work handled by the appropriate engines.

Analysts said the move follows similar efforts by Databricks and Snowflake to combine operational databases with analytics. But tighter integration with Microsoft's stack could make applications harder to move elsewhere.

Fabric HorizonDB joins SQL database and Cosmos DB in Microsoft's Fabric database portfolio. "By bringing operational databases, analytics, and AI together on a unified, governed platform, developers can build intelligent applications with less data movement and complexity. Fabric HorizonDB will also serve as the PostgreSQL backend for Fabric apps," Microsoft said.

Microsoft first unveiled Azure HorizonDB in preview in November 2025 and made it generally available last week. It competes with other cloud database services and distributed systems such as CockroachDB and YugabyteDB, both of which support PostgreSQL's wire protocol.
At the time, it said HorizonDB would offer "massive read scale without the need to replicate the database between instances."

Speaking to The Register last week, Shireesh Thota, veep of Azure databases and Fabric applications, said that bringing the system into Fabric – its platform for data lakes, data warehouses, and analytics launched in 2023 – would connect operational data in HorizonDB with analytical data in OneLake, Fabric's unified data lake.

"Once the data hits the OneLake storage, you can have analytical engines that take advantage of it. In HorizonDB, the PostgreSQL query engine can talk to the distributed query engine that we use in our Fabric data warehouse. We're fusing these query engines, thereby enabling the developers to submit a query that has pieces of the query that can work on OLTP and pieces of the query that can work on OLAP," he said.

"The application need not worry about two endpoints, or about consistency of data and all that complexity. They can just talk to HorizonDB as a Fabric endpoint, and they can submit all these queries. We are basically operationalizing in OneLake."

Operational data remains in HorizonDB's database storage, while mirroring maintains an analytical copy in OneLake, introduced in 2023, which replicates a snapshot of the external database to OneLake in Delta Parquet tables and keeps the replica synced in "near real time."

Thota said the process would not affect the transactional system. "Our core goal is to never impact OLTP workload while we are doing this, and we succeed [by] reading off the log as an additional replica to do this mirroring," he said.

But the overall plan of putting serverless PostgreSQL OLTP in an analytics platform, bringing it close to OLAP systems, is one some vendors are already executing to meet the demands of new AI agent-led workloads.

Adam Ronthal, research veep in Gartner's Data and Analytics Group, said: "The addition of Microsoft Fabric HorizonDB follows the 2025 acquisitions of PostgreSQL vendors by Databricks – Neon – and Snowflake – Crunchy. It delivers a high-performance, serverless operational RDBMS that is tightly coupled with Microsoft's lakehouse offering and well-suited to the ephemeral demands of AI agents.

"Competing directly with AWS Aurora and Google Cloud's AlloyDB, HorizonDB acts as a foundational serving layer for the next generation of AI- and analytics-infused applications. For organizations aligned with Azure and Fabric, it provides an industry-standard PostgreSQL foundation for AI development."

Andrew Snodgrass, research vice president of analyst company Directions on Microsoft, said the announcement of HorizonDB in Fabric was a "surprise," although "a watered-down version" compared to the version of the serverless database that became generally available on Azure last week. "It joins (document database) CosmosDB in Fabric and SQL database (based on the SQL Server engine) in Fabric. It highlights that Microsoft is still focused on making Fabric the data hub of their universe."

HorizonDB – both in Azure and Fabric – is a PostgreSQL service which Microsoft says has 100 percent compatibility with the open source system that has enjoyed a meteoric rise over the last decade. The support for PostgreSQL has led some to question the software giant's commitment to its own proprietary OLTP system, SQL Server.

Thota pointed out that the SQL database, based on the SQL Server engine, is already available in Fabric. Microsoft is also evaluating similar integration for that service, although he gave no timetable. "We are just beginning this journey, and most of the innovation is neutral to PostgreSQL and SQL. Some of it would be particular to how the individual query engine fuses with the analytical query engine. PostgreSQL does it slightly differently than SQL, but the idea is that most of the work is neutral. We are evaluating that work as well. I don't have timelines for that, but it is certainly in our thinking," he said.

Nonetheless, Holger Mueller, principal analyst at Constellation Research, said it was good to see Microsoft go all in on support of open source. "In general, it is an acknowledgement that they cannot win the battle for the SQL database with SQL Server – as it is as proprietary as the leader Oracle – and now they bank on the openness of PostgreSQL as another approach," he said.

However, using HorizonDB integrated into the Fabric/Azure stack may create so many dependencies with Microsoft's technology that lock-in to the vendor will remain a risk. "The primary concerns of open source – scale and support – have been eliminated by Microsoft's commitment and by now track record... the challenges are the embeddings of HorizonDB into the bigger Microsoft stack – which will make portability hard again. But every vendor wants and provides stickiness – clothed in ease of use and lower TCO," Mueller said. ®
b18b9599bd3c5d9f: BEIJING: Chen Jining, the top Chinese Communist Party leader in Shanghai, is under investigation for "serious violations of discipline and law", state media reported Tuesday, using a common euphemism for corruption.

The probe against Politburo member Chen comes less than a month after the ruling party promised tighter discipline, and signals that president Xi Jinping's sweeping 14-year anti-corruption campaign is still expanding.

Xi has purged dozens of top officials and overseen a clear-out of the military's top brass in recent months as he prepares for a key party congress next year, where the 73-year-old president will oversee a leadership reshuffle and almost certainly secure a fourth term as party leader.
Chen is the latest top official to be probed by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, the party's anti-corruption body, state broadcaster CCTV said, without providing further details.
Corruption charges typically follow such investigations in China, suggesting Chen's political career is effectively over.
The 62-year-old is the fourth member of the Politburo - an elite Communist Party decision-making body currently with 21 members - to face investigation during its current term, which began in 2022.
Chen's removal "proves one thing: that no one is safe in today's Chinese politics", said Wen-Ti Sung of the Australian National University
"Xi said at the fifth plenum that anti-corruption is 'always on the road'. Chen just became exhibit A," Sung told AFP.
The fifth plenum of the party's Central Committee, led by Xi, was held in late October and adopted a decision on reducing corruption, state news agency Xinhua said at the time.
Headed for the top

Jonathan Czin, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, said that "it's really remarkable to dismiss a fourth Politburo member. Even after the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown, the Party only dismissed two Politburo members".
"Chen's case is especially striking because he is still young enough to serve another term," he added.
Chen has been in post in Shanghai, one of the country's most prosperous cities and a commercial and financial hub, since 2022.
He was seen as a candidate for eventual elevation to the party's top leadership.
The last Shanghai party chief to be investigated for discipline breaches was Chen Liangyu - no relation to Chen Jining - who was removed from office in 2006.
Chen Liangyu was replaced by Xi in 2007.
Before moving to Shanghai, Chen Jining served as mayor of Beijing, China's capital, from 2017 to 2022.
He also had stints as minister of environmental protection and president of China's elite Tsinghua University, where he studied environmental engineering as a student in the 1980s.
He met with a delegation from the Swiss pharmaceutical company Roche in Shanghai last Wednesday, according to local media.
Shanghai leaders have previously gone on to the Politburo Standing Committee, the party's highest decision-making body.
China's current premier, Li Qiang, was formerly Shanghai party chief, while his predecessor in the city, Han Zheng, is China's vice-president.

68944b822386a4dc: LAUSANNE, Switzerland, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Senegal were reinstated as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations winners on Tuesday after the Court of Arbitration for Sport upheld their appeal against being stripped of the title, ruling that the referee's decision to resume the match was covered by the "field of play" doctrine.
The CAS panel set aside the Confederation of African Football's Appeal Board decision that had forfeited Senegal's 1-0 extra-time win and awarded Morocco a 3-0 result.
The panel found that "the referee did not commit any error of law", CAS secretary general Matthieu Reeb said.
The result of the Jan 18 final in Rabat is confirmed as 1-0 for Senegal.
"Again and Always African Champions," the Senegalese football federation posted on Instagram.
Senegal walked off for 14 minutes after a penalty was awarded against them late in regulation time.
Players returned to the pitch before the match resumed, Morocco missed the spot kick, and Pape Gueye scored the winner in extra time.
CAS said the referee's decision to resume play fell within his sole authority, and that the effects of that decision were limited to the pitch.
Articles 82 and 84 of the AFCON regulations, which Morocco relied on, apply only when a referee calls off a match permanently, the panel said, so they did not apply here.
The panel acknowledged the referee decided under extreme tension but said that did not justify calling his decision "arbitrary".
The panel also noted that the Senegal federation, coach Pape Thiaw and certain players had already been sanctioned by CAF in separate disciplinary proceedings.

The panel was chaired by French sports law expert Gerald Simon, with assistance from Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli and Ulrich Haas, a Hamburg-based attorney and professor of law at the University of Zurich.
CAS said the full grounds were issued to the parties on Tuesday and that the award will be published in due course unless confidentiality is requested.
Morocco's federation had argued that the referee's decision fell outside the field of play doctrine and that the walk-off breached Articles 82 and 84.

a1954c7a4413f404: Enterprise networks are under severe strain. As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on the network. Now, agentic AI is adding to the load. Tasks conducted by AI agents generate an estimated 450% more network traffic than the same tasks done by human workers.

As AI inference shifts from hyperscale training clouds—the huge centralized data centers where raw AI models ingest vast datasets and learn—to real-time, latency-sensitive applications, the need for on-premises or near-premises infrastructure grows. As a result, the gap between enterprise networks that are ready to support AI and those that are not is widening. As few as half of enterprises believe their current networks can handle AI’s bandwidth and latency demands, according to a recent study.
This report explores how treating network modernization as an on-going strategy rather than a one-off project can help organizations adapt in the face of disruption and uncertainty.
Key findings from the report include:

AI may force companies to shift from a cloud-first approach to routing workloads. Training AI requires server-to-server data center architectures, while inference calls for low-latency connectivity close to users. Enterprises may need to fundamentally reconsider their network architecture to meet these requirements.

AI inference is pushing infrastructure back on premises. Inference typically requires real-time processing and is sensitive to latency, making hosting such capabilities on distant hyperscale clouds neither economical nor practical. Inconsistent latency can lead to AI model failures, driving up queue wait times, saturating GPUs loads, and causing bottlenecks in data flows. Large enterprises may need on-premises or near-premises inference, which reverses years of cloud-first consolidation and forces new approaches to data center architecture, connectivity, and physical infrastructure.

AI workloads are stressing physical network capacity in unexpected ways. The traffic increase from agentic AI, combined with inference moving on-premises, is exposing bandwidth bottlenecks in legacy underlay infrastructure.

Network modernization is an ongoing project that requires a holistic approach, allowing companies to adapt with ease. A combination of strong architectural governance, reusable design templates, and retained internal expertise supports organizations in adapting to disruptive events without rebuilding their infrastructure from scratch each time. Such events could include mergers and acquisitions, changing vendors, or technology upgrades.

NaaS and AI-driven observability can improve efficiency and reduce complexity in network operations. Network-as-a-service (NaaS) and AI-driven observability can offer companies benefits like faster, more flexible provisioning and lower costs.

Data sovereignty and sovereign AI will create infrastructure challenges for global enterprises. Regulators worldwide are passing laws requiring data and AI processing to remain within national borders. This conflicts with how multinational companies currently operate, requiring the build-out of sovereign-capable infrastructure for each geography, which will require significant new investment and complicate operations.

This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.
3287e5d71f39010a: Jensen Huang was barely back in charge of Nvidia when Uncle Sam slapped Megaspeed –­ the Singaporean cloud provider at the center of the scandal that cost him his job ­­– on its trade blacklist.

The US Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has added Megaspeed and a number of affiliated businesses to its Entity List, restricting their access to American technology amid an ongoing investigation into the suspected diversion of advanced GPUs to China.

The final rule [PDF], filed Monday afternoon and scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on Wednesday, names seven businesses across Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand, including Megaspeed's owner, Swiftdata, and Malaysian subsidiary Speedmatrix.
Also in Washington's crosshairs is Apex Enterprise Solutions, a Singapore-based subsidiary of Chinese cloud computing giant Alibaba.

BIS said the businesses posed a significant risk of diverting advanced computing hardware to recipients or applications not authorized by the US government. Anyone looking to supply the seven companies with goods subject to US export controls will need a license, with applications subject to a "presumption of denial."
Despite the timing of Monday's announcement, the US government's interest in Megaspeed predates the revelations about Jensen Huang's private life by some considerable margin.

In a joint statement issued last week, the Departments of Justice and Commerce confirmed that the latter had opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 after spotting suspicious activity while monitoring potential violations of semiconductor export controls.

Investigators requested records from Nvidia relating to both direct and indirect sales to Megaspeed in May 2025, and the GPU giant put the Singaporean outfit on its internal "no sell" list the following month. US investigators, accompanied by Singaporean law enforcement officials, subsequently visited Megaspeed's premises and interviewed its then-CEO, Alice Huang.
The Justice Department has since taken the lead on the criminal investigation.

Alice Huang, who is not related to the Nvidia boss, is a businesswoman with whom Jensen was said to be having an affair – he admitted to extramarital infidelity earlier this month, although he never name-checked the Megaspeed exec. According to reports, US intelligence officials suspected she was working on behalf of Chinese intelligence, though Beijing has rejected the espionage allegations.
Megaspeed maintains that its business is lawful and says Alice Huang formally left the company in August last year. It has also enlisted outside lawyers to conduct an internal investigation.

Nvidia's own Huang lasted all of 11 days in corporate exile. The chipmaker's board unanimously voted to reinstate its co-founder as president and CEO on Monday, less than a week after board chairman Harvey Jones indicated that bringing him back wasn't on the cards.

The U-turn followed a lobbying campaign by some of Silicon Valley's biggest names, including Elon Musk, and some rather more consequential intervention from the White House. President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had personally persuaded Nvidia's directors to give Huang his job back.
Nvidia's board said it had received assurances from senior US government officials regarding the national security implications of Huang's return.

There are still plenty of people in Washington who have questions for Huang, however. The Nvidia boss is due to sit down with three congressional committees on December 1, with the chipmaker's general counsel, Tim Teter, scheduled to face lawmakers the following day.
Nvidia has also established a board-level committee to oversee national security and export control compliance, putting its trade compliance personnel under the supervision of three directors.
Nvidia shareholders may be delighted to have Jensen back, but the returning CEO has barely a week to prepare for his congressional grilling over the affair that helped bring about his departure. ®
ac1174b96a1a1dc5: BEIJING: Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO restores one of the most influential advocates for technology ties between the US and China, but he returns to a more restrictive business environment, with political pressure mounting on both sides.

Few American executives enjoy Huang's popularity in China. During a visit to Beijing in July last year, the Taiwan-born billionaire posed for selfies with fans and signed leather jackets.

China's state-backed Global Times newspaper cautioned in an editorial on Tuesday against interpreting Huang's return as a sign Washington would ease chip restrictions, stressing the need for China to strengthen semiconductor self-reliance.
Narrowing room for manoeuvre
Huang was only gone for 11 days, after resigning on Nov 12 following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged spy for Beijing, Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang.
However, Huang returns to a far more restrictive business environment.

On Monday, Washington added Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed, which Alice Huang formerly led and controlled, and a Singapore subsidiary of Chinese technology group Alibaba to its trade blacklist.
The move followed a commerce department rule issued last week that requires US export licences for advanced chip shipments to Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer vowed on Monday to investigate Huang, other Nvidia executives and the Trump administration when Democrats take control of Congress in January.
Huang faces an early test of his political influence on Dec 3, when he is due to testify before the Senate Banking Committee at a hearing on US export controls.

There have been changes at Nvidia too. The company said last week it had stopped shipping previously licensed AI chips to China, after generating US$2.4 billion in sales of such products in its latest quarter.
The company also established a committee of independent directors to oversee export-control compliance and national security risks.

Alfredo Montufar-Helu, Beijing-based managing director at Ankura Consulting, said Huang's popularity among ordinary Chinese people and access to both countries' leadership made his return positive for bilateral relations.
"However, an incoming Congress critical of Trump's trade truce with Beijing was likely to push for tighter chip restrictions," he said.
"That heightened scrutiny will complicate business for US tech firms in China and ultimately constrain the bridging role Huang can play," he added.

b0b919e462e4cf0b: Anthropic has introduced Claude Ship to review, fix, and approve pull requests (PRs), offering more AI automation to help teams handle the output of AI coding tools.

Claude Ship combines the generally available Code Review service with two new agents in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. It is available to Claude Team and Enterprise customers using GitHub repositories.
Anthropic said: "On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too." Its stated goal is to "ship code as fast as teams write it."

One consequence of the AI coding revolution is the sheer amount of agent output, which requires review and approval before going live. Claude Ship is one way to address that by automating more of the workflow. PR Steward works through failing continuous integration (CI) checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback. Claude Approvals can actually approve a PR, something that might rattle the nerves of some engineers.

Claude Approvals applies an approval policy, written by the team as a file in the repository. "Claude can approve routine changes on its own if the policy allows it, or can require deeper human sign-off for certain scenarios," Anthropic said.

The company advised caution: "For most customers, we recommend enabling this first in observe-only mode to build confidence before configuring branch protection to require Claude Approvals' green light."

While developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests (depending on their permissions and the repository's branch rules) with a /ship command in Claude Code, administrators can set up the rules on a repository-by-repository basis. "Claude Approvals starts when a connected repository has a policy file on its default branch, and an admin can turn it off," Anthropic said.
"Teams set the pace. They can start with one repository, choose a review level and when reviews run, set a monthly spend limit, and run their approval policy in observe mode until they trust it."
The extra automation also brings extra charges. Usage is token-based, and even observe-only approval policies can incur costs if they invoke classifiers or Code Review.
Anthropic also includes the familiar disclaimer: "Claude Ship uses AI and may miss bugs, security vulnerabilities, or other issues."

The Register spoke to an engineer who works for a company that uses Claude. They were a little cynical about the whole thing, saying: "It just seems like a glorification of what I already use Claude on – git merge or git rebase.

"Our golden rule so far with Git is to limit Claude to read operations there; this layer of separation still lets devs stay in control and allows them a judgment of the AI changes – what to keep, tweak, or commit.
"If that's offloaded to Claude and it has Git history-rewrite access, the devs will lose that overview and judgment opportunity."
How much authority Claude receives depends on the organization's configuration. Approval is not the same as merging, and existing branch protections and required checks still apply.
Anthropic's answer to a growing queue of AI-generated changes is more AI. Teams still have to decide which decisions they're prepared to delegate. ®

The telecoms regulator says the move is to "ensure reciprocity and fair dealing" in the rules governing satellite operators. The main aim appears to be hitting back at European efforts to build up the region's own space communications industries.

According to the FCC, the US has so far welcomed satellite systems licensed abroad on a level playing field, but that regulators elsewhere have begun holding US systems to different rules than they apply to their own domestic suppliers.

"This has operated to the disadvantage of American satellite providers that are or may be burdened with regulatory and spectrum limitations that their competitors in foreign nations simply do not face," said FCC chairman Brendan Carr.

The FCC has singled out the EU's Digital Networks Act, which proposes harmonized connectivity rules across the bloc. A separate proposal would overhaul authorization for mobile satellite services (MSS) in the 2 GHz band after existing rights expire in May 2027.

Earlier this year, the FCC laid out some of its concerns, saying that EU-wide authorization of satellite spectrum would replace the national licensing by member states "with which US satellite operators have become accustomed," and could require wholesale relicensing of any US systems operating in Europe.

"The FCC voting on foreign satellite companies is consistent with the Digital Networks Act, but is more of a response to the EU's decisions on how it plans to allocate the EU-wide 2 GHz spectrum," CCS Insight analyst Joe Gardiner told The Register.
"The EU outlined in its proposal that, for two-thirds of the spectrum, only operators based in the EU with EU ownership and aligned with the EU's strategic goals will be considered for the spectrum.

"This has locked out companies like SpaceX and Amazon Leo from attaining access to spectrum that is highly valuable for satellite direct-to-device services. The US government is looking to retaliate, to support the US constellations that would have attempted to win this EU-wide spectrum."
Following an initial consultation in March, the FCC will vote in December on opening a rulemaking to reconsider how foreign-licensed satellite operators gain access to the US market.
"It is time for this regulatory asymmetry to end," Carr said, adding that the FCC now proposes to mirror any regulations that foreign nations apply to American satellite providers.

"If there are limits or restrictions on American providers operating abroad, then the notice proposes to apply those or similar regulatory restraints to satellite providers from those countries that are operating here."

Britain is outside the EU, but does not escape the FCC's ire. The agency previously claimed the UK Space Agency allocates a significant portion of its budget, circa 75 percent in 2023/24, to European Space Agency (ESA) procurements, which US companies are not allowed to bid for as America is not a member of ESA.

British satellite operators could therefore face restrictions on access to the US market if the FCC adopts reciprocal measures. The UK's space industry generated £18.6 billion in income in 2022/23, according to the UK Space Agency. ®

Google Wants To Make a 24/7 AI TV Channel. You’ll Be the Main Character

Google has filed for a patent that would use the information it knows about you to create an AI-generated TV channel full of personalized “shows” starring you and featuring customized advertisements. The patent is the latest signal of the AI video endgame: endless highly specific, customized content that is automatically generated based on the wealth of data companies and advertisers collect about you.

Tech companies regularly file for patents that they don’t end up actually putting into real products, but this one, called “creating a channel of video experiences tailored to a user,” describes a system that many AI companies have been clearly trying to build. It imagines something called “My Channel,” which would be filled with AI content generated based on demographic data, their video watch history (presumably from YouTube), and other information it knows about the user. It would then make “the user as the protagonist for the whole video.” The patent was first noticed by Patentlyze, a news site that tracks tech company patents, who shared it with 404 Media.

“You are a customized video generating model. Generate a customized video for a user where the user will play the protagonist,” a hypothetical LLM prompt in the patent reads. “The generated customized video includes characteristics based on the . The generated customized video follows the style and format of the of the user. The generated customized video sticks to the of the user but the narrative for the generated customized video is customized. The and parameters are ordered from more preferred to less preferred.”

It suggests that the channel would be connected to an “advertising server,” and that advertisements would be inserted into the customized AI content: “an advertising stitcher included in the advertising server generates an updated customized media content item by inserting at least one advertisement into the customized media content item,” it says.

The patent imagines, for example, “a crime/comedy caper,” “a fun romantic comedy,” “a sci-fi adventure,” and “an action/thriller experience” with a viewer named “John” as the protagonist. Another prompt included in the patent suggests that someone who had recently watched cricket highlights of a “Player 1” might then be served a similar video “that incorporates elements of the Cricket World Cup and Player 1’s recent performance. Perhaps [user_name] could be cheering for India in the stands or interacting with Player 1 in some way.”

The notable thing about this patent is that it is barely an evolution of what is already happening on social media and what is beginning to happen on streaming free TV channels on services like Samsung TV Plus and TCLtv+.

The people generating AI slop on social media are making incredibly specific content because they know that social media algorithms will be highly effective at filtering people there. Meta is already allowing advertisers to use AI to generate many slightly different versions of an advertisement; its targeting AI then automatically shows them to users who are most likely to react to a specific version of an ad. As I’ve previously reported, TCL has been experimenting with AI-generated content on its streaming free TV channels, and, even without AI-generated content, free streaming TV channels have gotten incredibly specific. It is now possible, for example, to watch reruns of individual shows 24/7/365.

AI boosters have long been saying the future of entertainment is allowing anyone to generate their own TV shows, or to generate “new” episodes of existing properties. An always-on, autogenerating, customized AI TV channel isn’t far off from that idea.

As I’ve previously argued, the future that tech companies envision is one in which we are somehow even more siloed than we are now. They imagine a world in which everyone lives in their own reality and watches their own, customized content, which is a world in which big, unifying pieces of media are harder to make and are few and far between. The Google patent comes on the heels of a Microsoft patent that describes a system that alters spoken words (and the person’s lips) in live video, thereby distorting reality.

The University has said it’s not sure how much water the data center will use but that it could be as much as 650,000 gallons a day. It also said it’s “evaluating several cooling techniques to identify the most efficient approach,” a process that “includes continued evaluation of reclaimed wastewater for cooling, which would significantly reduce demand on municipal potable water supply systems.”

Los Alamos National Labs (LANL), America’s nuclear weapons scientists, have partnered with the U of M to construct a massive $1.2 billion 290,000 square-foot data center in Ypsilanti, Township, Michigan. Residents of the Township are angry about the “research computing center” and worry about how much water it’ll use, what it’ll do to electricity bills, and its connection to nuclear weapons.

In April, the Township’s utilities authority approved a moratorium on delivering water to data center projects while it studied how they might impact the community’s water supply. In response, U of M sent a letter to the Township utility board threatening legal action.

Concerned Township residents have spent the past year strategizing with community leaders about how to delay or stop construction. The Township’s anger caught U of M off guard and it attempted to address community concerns in several public meetings. It hasn’t gone well.

The pamphlet attempted to contextualize the data center’s place in America’s nuclear weapons research. “It would not involve nuclear weapons manufacturing, physical weapons testing, or the storage of hazardous nuclear materials,” the pamphlet said. But it would help “improve cybersecurity practices to safely manage existing nuclear material out of state.” In January, LANL confirmed its portion of the data center would be used for nuclear weapons research.
U of M did not return 404 Media’s request for comment.

On November 19, the board of regents approved the next phase of development for the data center in a vote of 7-1. 83bd348ce196a997: CHRISTOÚPOLI: As the sun sets in the semi-rural community of Spata near Athens, a group of pupils stretch on the sports pitch of Pierce College, one of Greece's top international schools.
The quiet setting will be very different in a few months' time, when a large data centre will start going up opposite the school grounds.
Two more data centres are already under construction in the broader area, putting the whole district on edge.
"We are not against technological development. What we ask is that it be done in harmony with our lives and property.
Not in an anarchic way just because (data centres) are in vogue," Spata local Yiorgos Minardos told AFP in a meeting with other residents.

Minardos's home in the small nearby community of Christoupoli is less than 200m from another, €150-million (US$165-million) data centre under construction on behalf of Greece's Public Power Corporation (PPC), the main electricity provider, and Dubai real estate developer Damac.
Once covered in olive groves and vineyards, the broader Spata area, some 20km east of the capital, has already seen rapid development since the Athens airport relocated there in 2001.
Data centre drive
A raft of data centres nationwide is being energetically promoted by the conservative government of prime minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis.
It says it wants to develop Greece into a major data and infrastructure hub for the southeastern Mediterranean and the wider region.

"We are working with dedication to ensure that Greece is equipped with the necessary infrastructure to consistently rank among the leading and pioneering countries in the economic transformations already taking place," the prime minister said last year.
Residents counter that state and regional officials have allowed the construction of industrial-scale facilities near their homes that are incompatible with the area's commercial zoning regulations.
Nearly 40 residents challenged the data centre permits in a 2025 complaint at the Council of State, Greece's top administrative court. The case is to be heard in February.
'Critical' data hub
PPC has said that its 12.5MW data centre "is poised to become a critical hub connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa, reinforcing Greece's position as a leader in IT capacity in Southeastern Europe".
Originally slated for completion this year, it is still a concrete husk.
A larger project built for Microsoft a few hundred metres away, 19.2MW in capacity, is designed to "minimise energy consumption", according to its construction company Renco.
However, confirming residents' concerns, Renco's construction partner Terna called the Microsoft centre an "industrial-type facility".
The third centre near Pierce College, jointly developed by the investment firm Pimco, will have a capacity of up to 80MW.
Budgeted at €300 million, it is slated for completion in 2028, as is the Microsoft facility, worth some €100 million.
The government in March presented a study by consultancy PwC pointing to investor interest in developing data centre capacity of over 1 GW, more than 20 times the current level.
There are more than 35 investment requests, the study said, mostly in the greater Athens area.
AI power demand

In a question to parliament in October, former socialist prime minister George Papandreou warned the technology "can exert significant pressure on electrical grids, increase the cost of the required infrastructure, and pass part of that cost on to consumers".
The International Energy Agency has said data centre electricity demand in Europe is projected to increase by 70% by 2030.
Meta, Google, Microsoft and Amazon are all investing heavily to meet growing demand for their AI products and services.
However, resistance to data centres is growing in Europe and elsewhere.
In the US, local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 such projects in the first quarter of 2026, according to the monitor Data Center Watch.
They require lots of fresh water to help cool servers, raising fears of localised shortages.

"Large providers use evaporative cooling systems that require water on roughly 15% of the days in a year," said Elissavet Feloni, an assistant professor at the University of West Attica's school of engineering.
That demand "coincides exactly with heatwave days ... precisely when (water) reservoirs are under maximum stress".
Heatwave concerns

Christoupoli residents said they were incensed when the company building one of the data centres told them to "simply shut their windows and put on air-conditioning" to cushion the noise of the cooling machinery.
They also fear the facilities will heat up the land around them, in an area already prone to heatwaves.
"When it's quiet at night, we can hear the lions and apes" at the zoo, said local homeowner Ioannis Alatinis.
"Given the jungle this place is going to turn into, it's kind of fitting," Alatinis said.

Masters in Business Transcript: David Eichhorn, CEO and Head of Investment Strategies, NISA Investment Advisors
[00:00:02] ANNOUNCER: Bloomberg Audio Studios, podcasts, radio, news.

[00:00:07] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Strap yourself in for another banger. I sit down with the head of NISA Investment Advisors. They run a half a trillion dollars or so in institutional assets. [00:01:09] DAVID EICHHORN: Barry, I’m delighted to be here. Love the show, and excited to chat today.

[00:01:13] BARRY RITHOLTZ: I’m delighted to have you. What you guys do is really fascinating and so unusual. We’re going to delve into that. [00:02:04] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Right. First one in your family to go to college?

But the math really was the superpower that I think supercharged the finance degree, frankly.

So I met Phil Dybvig, who I love to describe now as Nobel Laureate Phil Dybvig, at Washington University. Because of the math degree, he took a shine to me, for lack of a better term. And it’s one of those—in the land of the blind, the one-eyed man is king. I had some programming background. I knew relatively sophisticated math for what was in the finance department, and he really helped get me my first job at JP Morgan. And I’m eternally grateful for Phil, and he remains a great friend to this day.

[00:03:07] BARRY RITHOLTZ: You spent your first three years after college at JP Morgan, again working on the institutional side, helping clients develop investment policies, strategic asset allocations, and perhaps most importantly, asset-liability management strategies. [00:04:57] BARRY RITHOLTZ: And so I think the average layperson hears “liability” and they’re thinking car accident. Explain, especially from a pension fund manager’s perspective, what do future liabilities mean in plain English?

[00:06:53] DAVID EICHHORN: Okay. I say way too much, so who knows. What did I say?

0fc51390fa9c3aee: About half a million Californians were affected by the state's hike in minimum wage for fast-food workers. AP Photo/Jae C. HongEven before the 2026 midterm elections delivered a clear message about cost-of-living concerns, many states had been raising their minimum wage on their own as one way to increase workers’ purchasing power. And some have taken a more targeted approach, setting wage floors for specific industries. As the example of California shows, however, these initiatives can produce mixed results. In April 2024, California began requiring fast-food chains with at least 60 locations nationwide to pay a minimum wage of US$20 an hour, $4 above the statewide minimum at the time. The governor’s office estimated that more than 500,000 workers would be covered by this mandate. As a researcher of health and labor markets, I joined with economists David Neumark, Gary Wagner and Vitor Melo to run a study measuring the impact on California’s fast-food industry – specifically, whether restaurants employed fewer workers because of the ensuing higher labor costs. We found that the answer depends on which establishments you look at. For the state as a whole, the law didn’t affect employment in any statistically detectable way, we concluded. But smaller chains did take a hit, with employment falling by roughly 20%, while the number of locations dropped by about 10%. New openings fell by 17%-20%, and closures rose by 9%-21%. This employment decline comes almost entirely from fast-food chains ceasing to operate in California, rather than from staffing cuts at the locations that remain. The impact of minimum wage hikes holds importance far beyond the fast-food sector. Their proponents point to the fact that the federal minimum wage of $7.25 an hour has stayed unchanged since 2009 and argue that states and municipalities need to take action on their own. Los Angeles is phasing in a $30 wage for hotel and airport workers, while California’s healthcare workers just received another scheduled increase. Vermont lawmakers have proposed a $20 fast-food wage of their own. In addition, a total of 16 states will raise their minimum wages across the board on Jan. 1, 2027. With the federal minimum wage unchanged since 2009, many states and municipalities have raised the wage floor on their own, including for specific sectors. AP Photo/Andrew Harnik Smaller chains see an impact The question of whether and how minimum wages affect employment still provokes a vigorous debate among economists. In California’s case, some researchers have found that lifting the minimum wage caused small declines in employment compared with other states; others contend that the effect on jobs is essentially zero. More broadly, some researchers have found that minimum wage hikes cost jobs. But the time horizon matters, and effects tend to get larger in the long run. Our study didn’t try to settle that disagreement. Instead, we wanted to find out how employers did adjust, and whether large and small chains responded differently. What happens when higher minimum wages raise one sector’s costs and prices while its closest substitutes – such as sit-down restaurants – keep paying the lower statewide minimum wage? We relied on a database that recorded every business location in the country by name, along with the number of employed workers, each year. That let us directly identify the chains that were subject to California’s law, count each chains’ national footprint to apply the 60-location rule, and track outcomes from 2019 through 2025: total employment, employment at locations that stayed open, the number of locations, and openings and closures. We also compared California with other states and separately compared each chain’s California restaurants with the same chain’s restaurants elsewhere. Finally, we divided the covered chains into two groups: The 20 largest, which account for about 60% of covered jobs, and the 261 smaller ones. For the state as a whole, we found that employment at covered restaurants was basically unchanged, and employment at restaurants that stayed open didn’t change. Among the 20 largest chains, there was no detectable effect at all for any of the measures we tracked over this period. But the smaller chains tell a different story, recording substantial declines in employment, locations and openings, while closures rose. How to reconcile the flat statewide numbers with the sharp effects on smaller chains? The largest chains employ most of the workers affected by the new minimum wage rule, so the statewide total is dominated by them. And the reduced entry and higher exit among smaller chains may have eased competitive pressure on the largest ones. A final point: The biggest chains tend to be the most automated, relying more on equipment such as self-serve kiosks that can reduce the number of workers needed. That may help explain the muted employment response among these larger businesses. Taking the longer view First, we caution that the absence of a clear short-run effect on total employment doesn’t prove that the policy won’t cause bigger job losses over time as companies adapt to the new law. We also can’t answer what happened to the workers at the most affected restaurants or what happened to prices at those establishments, although other research suggests they rose by 3% to 4%. That said, the law was implemented barely 2½ years ago, and some of the larger effects that economists might expect – such as the closure of labor-intensive restaurants or fewer openings – are already apparent among smaller chains. Second, it’s important to remember that California’s fast-food minimum wage applies only to chains with 60 or more locations. So the smaller chains in that range likely lack the scale, automation and pricing power of the national brands and are most sensitive to the new wage floor. Indeed, the law appears to have shifted California’s fast-food market toward its largest chains, a pattern that other researchers documented in a similar study that looked at Germany’s national minimum wage. For the cities and states now weighing wage floors of their own, the California evidence isn’t a slam dunk either way. It shows that the costs, broadly speaking, fall first on the smaller chains covered by the law – but whether it meaningfully impacts the largest chains is unclear. Liam Sigaud is affiliated with the Paragon Health Institute, a not-for-profit health policy research organization.

387667a188a01814: Bringing a classic MacOS Finder to Linux is all very well, but there's no shortage of Linux desktops… however, bringing one to 9front is even more unexpected – and even more useful.

9/UX is a new project by Jeff "Progrium" Lindsay, who was one of the people behind Docker, Webhooks, and more. When you follow that link, and you should, pay close attention to what looks like a screenshot at the top. It is not an image. It's a real live executing instance of the OS, running inside your web browser, running on top of hyper9. (That is worth reading too – it's an impressive project in its own right.)
As its GitHub repository describes, 9/UX is a "Macintosh-inspired graphical environment for 9front."

"9/UX brings the classic Mac and A/UX desktop experience (a spatial desktop, a global menu bar, consistent controls and dialogs, icons, and resource-driven presentation) to 9front, built the Plan 9 way: rio and libdraw draw the screen, 9P exposes every application's UI state and commands as files, namespaces define the working environment, the plumber opens documents, and ndb holds human-editable metadata."

Lindsay introduced 9/UX earlier this month in a short X thread, saying he "made my own kind of A/UX but on Plan 9." In its creator's own words, "it's slop", but this is kind of interesting, original, creative bot-assisted coding that we enjoy looking at. At the end of last week, he returned to explain more:
"9/UX isn’t just a pretty Mac-style UI on Plan 9. It's filesystem inspectable. Shell scriptable. Even the Mac resource file format can be used through the filesystem."

Regular readers may have noticed that The Reg FOSS desk is fascinated by Plan 9 and its FOSS continuation 9front. We've written and presented at length about this remarkable OS, and tried to explain its FOSS continuation 9front several times. But even with the best will we can muster, its unique GUI is not an especially friendly or easy one. Its idiosyncratic UI was inspired by the late great Niklaus Wirth's unbelievably tiny Oberon OS, which we have written about before. It's cryptic, and that's being generous.

The research and development effort that led to Unix didn't stop when Unix 7th Edition escaped from the Bell Labs in 1981 and mutated into Unix System III. The industry enthusiastically adopted System III and later System V. A decade after 7th Edition Unix, Linux became a GPL version of something very like that traditional Unix, closely followed by the BSDs – and between them, they have very effectively distracted most of the FOSS world ever since. Even so, Research Unix lived on, saw 8th, 9th, and 10th editions, and then was replaced by Plan 9. In 1996, many of Plan 9's limitations were overcome by Inferno – whose revival as InferNode we covered this week.

We always vaguely thought that if 9front were to receive an improved GUI that was slightly more compliant with later GUI design standards, it might be with a version of the Inferno UI… But apparently not. A new, easier, and yet still simple, clean and attractive desktop for 9front is here, and it looks like classic MacOS from the era of Apple's 68030 Unix A/UX.

We do not think the chances are high that the 9front community will adopt this with enthusiasm. Even so, there is an AI programming manual for agents, and we've seen some interesting looking LLM-assisted 9front apps of late. Several can be found in the agent9 distribution, which includes LLM-assisted ports of C++, Python, and Rust, plus a version of DOSbox, and even a package manager called pac9.®

6e10ac0a9bdd763d: SYDNEY, Nov 24 —Warmer overnight temperatures are linked to poorer memory in middle-aged and older people, according to an Australian study, reported Xinhua.

The study, led by the University of Newcastle and QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute in Australia, analysed data from 1,873 Australians aged 42 to 75 and found that warmer nights were consistently associated with lower performance on a test of associative memory, according to a statement released by the university on Tuesday.

Associative memory involves learning, storing and recalling the relationships between unrelated items, such as remembering where keys are or linking a face to a name. It can be among the earliest cognitive functions to decline in Alzheimer’s disease, although lapses in associative memory are also a normal part of aging, researchers said.

The study highlighted links between climate, aging and brain health, underscoring the need for further research into how rising temperatures could affect brain health as people age, said Anna Behler from the University of Newcastle, lead author of the study published in Environment International.

Participants completed 12 online cognitive tests assessing memory, language, attention, reasoning and problem-solving skills. Of the 12 tests, only associative memory showed a significant relationship with overnight temperatures.
Co-author Renate Thienel from the University of Newcastle said heat-related sleep disruption could be one possible explanation, as sleep plays an important role in memory consolidation.

Further research is needed to determine whether the effects are temporary or whether repeated exposure to warmer nights could have longer-term consequences for brain health and potentially dementia risk, the researchers said. — Bernama-Xinhua
7d9f2fc63e652e8d: TANJONG MALIM, Nov 24 — Just a year ago, Grace Ezra Bunad, a young Bidayuh woman from the rural district of Lundu in Sarawak, considered abandoning her dream of going to university after facing financial hardship following the loss of her main source of support.

The death of her father, Bunad Jawi, in a road accident when she was 17 dealt a heavy blow to the family in Kampung Seraya Hilir, Lundu. He died shortly before she was due to sit her Sijil Pelajaran Malaysia trial examinations.
The youngest of four children said her mother made a living through small-scale farming, while her siblings worked as food outlet assistants and manual labourers.

“After finishing matriculation in Sarawak, I received an offer to further my studies at Universiti Pendidikan Sultan Idris (UPSI). However, I was worried and nearly lost hope, thinking about the living expenses and the RM1,500 registration fee I had to come up with at short notice.

“Back then, I believed I would have to repay the National Higher Education Fund Corporation (PTPTN) loan in full, and the cost of furthering my studies was beyond what my family could afford,” she told Bernama recently.
Her hopes were revived when UPSI lecturers visited her family home in Sarawak to learn more about her family’s financial circumstances before she enrolled in September last year.

The first in her family to enter higher education, Grace Ezra was among those selected for the SULUNG 4.0 First-Generation Student Development Programme, run by the Ministry of Higher Education (MOHE).

Grace Ezra, who hopes to become a Mathematics teacher, said the SULUNG scholarship helped reduce her financial burden by covering her semester tuition fees, along with laboratory, health, and sports charges.

“I feel even more motivated knowing that I may be eligible to have my PTPTN loan converted into a scholarship if I continue to achieve excellent academic results,” said the undergraduate, who is currently in her third semester.

In addition to assistance from MOHE, Grace Ezra has also received support through several other initiatives, such as RM600 in financial aid from the Sarawak state government each semester, a RM3,000 computer voucher, book vouchers, subsidised flight tickets and the Dapur Siswa MADANI facility at her campus.
She said the SULUNG programme eased her financial difficulties while also offering emotional support through the university’s counselling unit, which tracked her academic progress.

“This support motivates me to do my best and make sure I do not disappoint those who have invested in my education. I believe that through education, I can change my family’s fortunes and provide a better life for my mother and family back home,” she said.
The SULUNG programme aims to help students from B40 families become the first in their households to pursue undergraduate studies at a public university, regardless of their chosen field.
UPSI vice-chancellor Prof Datuk Dr Md Amin Md Taff said 206 students had received assistance under the programme since SULUNG 1.0.

“The SULUNG programme plays an important role in creating opportunities for students from low-income households to pursue higher education, especially those who are the first in their families to attend university,” he said.
Md Amin said the support not only eased tuition and study-related costs but also gave students the confidence, motivation, and ongoing support to complete their studies successfully.

bc4f0bfbd49928e0: ISTANBUL، Nov 24 — A British hacker responsible for leaking footage of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) was released from custody Monday despite receiving a seven-year prison sentence for a series of cyberattacks targeting major companies، Anadolu Ajansi reported.

Rockstar Games told a British court in 2023 that the cyberattack cost it approximately US$5 million (RM20.6 million) to recover from in addition to thousands of hours of staff time.
