03f1c8c280b8ac5b: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 24 — “You don’t even have a signature dish.”

That was the complaint Soh Yong Zhi heard from a few diners in the months after Eat and Cook was named American Express One To Watch at Asia’s 50 Best Restaurants 2022; how, they asked, had a restaurant like this won anything?
Soh shrugged it off. “Eat and Cook is not the type of restaurant where we want to repeat a dish,” he told Malay Mail in January 2024.

Today, the restaurant has several, including fresh oysters from the brackish waters of Bagan Pasir, served with a bunga kantan mignonette, and a roasted 28-day-aged local mountain duck, served with satay fashioned out of minced duck leg.
Eat and Cook's famous "deconstructed" asam laksa, the first dish Lee Zhe Xi and Soh ever created, about three months into life in a Bukit Jalil mall, is back too, on the à la carte menu.
“That dish is very meaningful to us, and it traces our journey,” Soh says.
It is one of many things that have changed.
Eat and Cook Villa, at 12, Jalan Delima in Imbi, opens today as the restaurant’s third address and its largest: two dining rooms under one roof.
The Dining Room, an à la carte room built for sharing, seats 60. Service at The Experience, a 10-course tasting menu at RM499, begins on December 4.

The Villa sits in a bungalow with high-rises on every side. The roof is brown and built to look like an attap roof, each of its seven thousand tiles carved by hand. Some run long, and some short, Lee says, and that is the point. “There is perfection in imperfection.”
Inside, the doors open onto ochre walls and dark wood throughout; the effect is earthy.

The bar comes first, then the wine cellar, which holds about 800 labels. Lee says they have plans for Krug and Dom Pérignon to be poured by the glass, and that each month a large-format rare bottle, a Lafite or a Mouton Rothschild, say, will be served by the glass through a Coravin.
They intend that half pours allow diners to try wines of that rarity at a fraction of the cost, without committing to a full glass.
The rest of the drinks include locally brewed miju, and a house toddy that is bottled on site and keeps up to a year when stored properly.

Past the cellar, the dining room opens under a skylight. To the cellar’s left, a lit corridor lined with jars of cheong and kombucha, still fermenting, leads into The Experience, which seats 20 at the tables and four at the counter.
The name is plain on purpose. “We wanted the new Eat and Cook to feel like a home,” Lee says. “We didn't want to rebrand with a really fancy name.”
Six years ago, Eat and Cook was six seats around a counter in a 100-square-foot unit in a nearly empty mall in Bukit Jalil, run by two chefs who had lost their hotel jobs to the pandemic.
Now there are three restaurants, including Sun and Moon, their hundred-seater all-day dining concept right next door, and Barkar, the open-fire restaurant at G Tower.
The last service for Eat and Cook at its most recent space in Bukit Jalil was on May 31, 2025. Today, almost exactly 18 months later, the Villa opens. “We expected longer,” Lee says.

The projected time was a result of other cost considerations. “RM10 million” is the round figure Lee gives when asked about the cost of the whole space. It's the biggest investment they've made so far.
Before the site was secured, he says, they were planning for two or three years, because “we really wanted to make sure our finances were stable before proceeding with this project.”
That cost invites a very natural reason to run both a tasting menu and an à la carte service.
“The tasting menu is for people to experience something unique,” Lee says.
“But it’s not a sustainable business,” Soh adds, with a chuckle.

“And you need a restaurant that people can keep coming back to,” Lee continues. He puts the case in terms of the market: “Malaysia is still a market that’s price-sensitive; our economy is still all over the place, so a lot of people are pulling the handbrake on spending.”
And in terms of the kitchen: a high-priced restaurant that serves 10 guests a night leaves its team with “no sense of urgency”, he says, and over time “you will lose your manpower”.
So they strike a balance. “Our thinking is that we are willing to have slightly lower revenues to keep our restaurant full,” Lee says.
“This is a restaurant for the people… at a slightly above-entry level.” He is candid about the alternative: “If people only come to Eat and Cook once a year, sei lo. I die already.”
The à la carte menu runs from RM20 for a salted fish bun to RM298 for the Kampung Seafood Noodles, before service charge and tax. The compromise has limits, and he knows where.
The Villa’s Salad is RM79, and it includes 20 vegetables from the herb garden on site to farms up in Perlis. It drew complaints about price from friends and family.

“A lot of them complained that our salad is very expensive, but I don’t mind it, because that’s the hard work our farmers and we have put in,” Lee says. “Getting baby okra and baby chayote comes at a price; we’re just trying to accurately reflect its value.”
Explaining that value to diners, he says, is “the hardest thing to do in the world", and it falls to the front of house, whether presented verbally, table by table or on “a little card”.
Almost every fine dining restaurant now talks about fermentation, and some that aren’t quite “fine dining” do too.
Lee’s answer to the obvious objection starts with salted fish. “In Malaysia, we have a lot of salted fish. That’s a form of fermentation,” he says.

One of the starters on the menu is a bun with fish garum (fermented fish sauce) folded into the dough, then glazed with salted fish when it's baked. It's then topped with bonito flakes made from yellowfin tuna caught in Sabah.
“We want to connect traditional Malaysian ways of food preservation and take them to the future.”
The idea took shape on the road. In Perlis and Kedah, the team learned how people in the north make belacan: not dry, a little wet, red instead of dark, and untoasted.

“What if we take these nostalgic Malaysian ways of making food and adapt them for something modern?” Lee asks. At the Villa, that means no bought vinegar: they ferment kombucha for longer into vinegar, with chillies, papaya and rambutan.
It means garums from anything, not only anchovies; trimmings of squid from Barkar are fermented with koji until they taste like prawn or crab.

And it means a nod to his grandmother, who made fruit enzymes to wash things around the house. “We’re trying to draw a link between that kind of thing and what we’re doing here at the restaurant,” he says.
A room of crabs, fish, gooseberries and mushrooms fermenting in jars, in a mixture of salt and koji or in plain salt, should announce itself by smell.
The Eat and Cook Lab, on the first floor of the building, does not smell; it is remarkably clean.
The first real whiff comes at the second stage of fermentation, in a temperature-controlled chamber kept at 55 degrees Celsius. It smells like what savoury tastes like.

Inside a huge urn sits soy sauce made in partnership with Mu Artisan Soy Sauce. Fermented with pineapples for three years, a layer of salt crystals have formed at the surface. “I have to say it’s a bit sayang; the salt crystals were much fuller before we moved it here.”

On the à la carte menu, the lab shows up in dishes as different as grilled paku with fish garum ice cream (RM39), Grandma’s popiah with squid garum (RM20 a piece) and the seasonal fish with an acar dressing of chilli kombucha (RM78).
The fermentation program also changes what they can afford to buy.
The yellowfin tuna that becomes the bonito flakes comes from Sabah. “It’s caught in the evening, arrives in KL the same night, and we can receive it here by 2am,” Soh says.
Some weigh 20 to 25kg. “It’s a bit of a gamble, because sometimes they’ll be small, or if they come back with 10 fish, we have to take everything.”

Taking everything is only possible because of what happens next. “We can do a lot with the trimmings; it’s partially why we have such a big fermentation program here: it lets us take more stock than we would normally be able to go through, and it keeps our suppliers and especially the fishermen happy,” Lee says.

On slipper lobster, which, he says, plenty of peers ask him about how he gets consistent supply: “If they catch 25kg today, I will take it all. I can ferment the leftovers.” The fishermen know this, he says, “and we don’t press them on price.”
The same logic applies to produce. “I mean, sometimes we have ‘asshole’ requests too,” he says. For papaya, they ask farmers to leave the fruit on the tree until fully ripe.

“When they ask me, ‘What if it spoils by the time it gets to you?’, we tell them we’ll pay the full amount,” Lee says. “We can still get trimmings from it and turn it into a papaya cheong, or vinegar.” The chilli sauce is sweetened with ripe papaya, not refined sugar.
The fruit shows up on the menu in the Papaya Dessert 2.0 (RM88), where it is listed as tree-ripened, and in the papaya chilli that comes with the prawn cracker (RM29).

The suppliers are the same people they began with, Lee says: they have a guy in Sabah for tiger prawns, flower prawns and tuna; and a guy in Bagan Pasir for amadai, oysters, mussels and giant grouper. “Without them, we can’t cook anything.”

Soh says the farmers were mostly incurious about what happens to their produce, but it has changed in recent times: “I don’t know what you’re doing with these, but you just take lah.” Recently, the team started sending them photographs of the dishes.

Behind the restaurant, the kitchen’s organic waste is composted and turned into fertiliser for a herb garden. Sawtooth coriander, pentas flowers, ulam raja, peppercorns and chillies all grow there, in the middle of the city.
Aidil tends the plants. He is 18, from Kelantan, and started recently; his sister, who works at Barkar, got him the job. “He’s really our guy; he takes care of everything here,” Lee says.
Lee returns to the next generation more often than he does to awards. “If we can produce 10 head chefs from this restaurant, that would make me happier than three stars,” he says.
Both he and Soh are 29, and Gen Z themselves. But he is frank about what the industry’s newest entrants have been taught to expect from YouTube and what the industry has to learn in return.

“We used to be harsher on our team, repeating the lessons we learned from the previous generation,” he says. “But you need a different approach with the new generation. There needs to be more explanation and guidance, not just scolding them.”

Soh, who describes himself as the supportive half of a pair with “completely opposite” characters, is more candid still. “Yes, sometimes we curse,” he says, “but after about 10 minutes we have to sayang balik and explain to them.”

What Lee wants to pass on, he says, is not technique so much as a feeling from the small town where he grew up. “I can ask for something from a shop, and they know that my parents will pay for me the next day,” he says.
“I feel like this kind of community feeling has disappeared, and this is what we should try to bring to the future with the next generation.”
He doesn’t plan to be in the kitchen forever. “I want to quit eventually; I want to have my own time,” Lee says. “I see myself working in my own little restaurant, and I only open it when I’m happy.”

Asked what comes after the Villa, Lee does not name another restaurant. “A farm and fishery,” he says. “We want to enter the supply chain.” The team has started already, he says, with the oyster and grouper hatchery it works with.
The motive is what he has watched happen to farmers over the past six or seven years. “The real farmers, the hardworking farmers, don’t get the recognition they deserve, and funding, too,” Lee says.

“I try to talk to people, but nothing happens. The real farmers work so hard and burn through their money for it.” If everything goes well and stays stable, he says, “the next part of our vision is to go to the source.”

The other looming question hanging over any restaurant that returns after a long gap: awards. Eat and Cook sat out 18 months while others gained recognition in their absence with awards such as Asia’s 50 Best. Will they go for it now?

“I don’t mind doing it,” Lee says. “A lot of people just see it for the awards, but when we’ve been there, it’s not about the awards for us. It’s about the connections and community we can learn from.”
The benefits, he argues, go well past the trophy: “We get to understand the perspectives of these chefs from other countries: their cuisine, the market there.”

He does not pretend the circuit is above criticism. “A lot of people judge and say, ‘Oh, 50 Best is just a game, blah blah blah.’ It may be, but for us, we see it differently.” Years ago, after meeting at an award show, Lee arranged for the team to learn from Chef Jun Lee of two-Michelin-starred Soigne about “the standards required in a place like Seoul”, travelling there and cooking food for diners. That is, Lee says, “much more than just bringing a signature dish to cook at someone else’s restaurant.”
“I think that’s the biggest benefit we get — an expensive one, yes, but a benefit for sure.”
Eat and Cook Villa
12, Jalan Delima, Imbi, Kuala Lumpur.
Open Tuesday to Sunday, 5.30pm — 11pm.

22de5291eb6fe1a4: NEW DELHI, Nov 24 — Bangladesh’s fugitive former prime minister Sheikh Hasina said today she wants to return to the country on December 16, with Dhaka warning she could only come home in handcuffs.

Hasina, 79, has vowed repeatedly to return from India in December, despite being sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown during the 2024 uprising that ousted her.

She has insisted on going back to Bangladesh despite Dhaka authorities saying she would be hanged if she returned, and that she had no further legal recourse after missing the deadline to appeal against her conviction.
”She has... indicated that her return will be on Bangladesh’s Victory Day on December 16,” Hasina’s spokesman Syed Mozammel Ali told AFP on Tuesday.
Victory Day is a national holiday marking the 1971 surrender of Pakistani forces, which paved the way for Bangladesh’s independence.
Hasina’s father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, then became Bangladesh’s founding president.
Hasina fled to India as crowds stormed her palace in August 2024, with the ousted leader now asking Dhaka to arrange an aeroplane to bring her home, Ali said.

”She now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka,” he said, adding that it was “the responsibility of the government to make possible her return to Bangladesh on Victory Day on December 16”.
Dhaka has sought her extradition from India, which says the request is under legal review.
”Sheikh Hasina’s desire to return to the country on December 16, and the reality of the situation are not the same,” Humaiun Kobir, Dhaka’s junior foreign minister, told reporters on Tuesday.
”If she were to return, she can only come as a prisoner in handcuffs,” he said.
Hasina’s lawyers had applied for a Bangladeshi passport and national identity card through the country’s high commission in New Delhi, she said.
Many Bangladeshis want to see Hasina hanged, while others fear her return could galvanise her supporters and trigger a fresh confrontation between rival camps.
Kobir accused Hasina’s loyalists from her Awami League party—whose activities have been banned—of being behind a spate of petrol bomb attacks.
”The attacks have failed to intimidate people,” he said.

At least four people have been killed in political violence since mid-November, including three party activists and a bus worker who died when his vehicle was torched, according to Bangladeshi media reports.
Hundreds of additional paramilitary Border Guard Bangladesh forces have been deployed nationwide, government statements said. — AFP
60e8aadceb71593e: From Ann Teoh
Today marks exactly 10 years since Amri Che Mat went missing.
A Suhakam public inquiry unanimously concluded in 2019 that Amri was a victim of enforced disappearance – specifically by state agents, namely the police's Special Branch.
It was past 11pm on Nov 24, 2016, a Thursday, when Amri drove out of his house at Padang Behor in Kangar, Perlis, to have supper with a friend.
Just minutes later, less than a kilometre from his house, his Toyota Fortuner was boxed in by three four-wheel-drives. Screeching sounds, glass breaking, and that was it. It took less than a minute.
Providence would have it that the incident was witnessed by a passing motorcyclist and a restaurant owner across the road from where it happened.

Amri’s Fortuner was found abandoned at a construction site in Bukit Chabang, Kedah, a few hours later. His wife, Norhayati Ariffin, did not realise Amri hadn't come home until the next morning when she received a call about the abandoned car.
Before Amri took a nap at 7.30pm, he had asked his wife to wake him up at 10.30pm. That was the last time Norhayati saw her husband.
This sounds like a bad conspiracy novel, but reality is stranger than fiction.

DNA swabs were taken from the Fortuner when the car was found, but were sent to the chemistry department only five months later. Amri’s family also did not get the police support they wanted. Instead of trying to locate Amri, Norhayati was queried about her husband’s involvement in Shia activities.
Shia Islam is prohibited in Malaysia and Amri was watched by religious authorities and the police, but was never arrested or charged. Instead, he disappeared.
How do we know Amri was being watched? Would he have disappeared at a different time if he didn’t go out that fateful night? It's quite possible judging by the circumstances.
A car workshop owner across Amri’s house later testified that unknown cars, with engines running, took turns parking outside Amri's house day and night for three days before he went missing.
One of those cars was a gold-coloured Toyota Vios with a Penang number plate, which was also spotted when Pastor Raymond Koh was abducted 81 days later.

The Vios belonged to an operative of the Special Branch in Kuala Lumpur. He was identified as Saiful Bahari Abdul Aziz, but the police always had an excuse for why the key witness could not be present to testify.
Koh was abducted the same way on Feb 13, 2017. His car was also boxed in as men in black rushed out from three black four-wheel-drives. There was also a gold-coloured Vios nearby.

Koh’s abduction was more audacious than Amri’s; it happened in broad daylight on a Monday morning in SS4, Petaling Jaya. Amri’s case only had eyewitness accounts but Koh's case included video evidence.
Besides witness Roeshan Celestine Gomez, a chambering student who happened to be driving behind Koh's car, the pastor's abduction was caught on the CCTV cameras of two houses nearby.

Strangely, the police didn’t rush to get the CCTV recordings. It was Koh’s family who looked for them once they knew about Roeshan’s police report. After the CCTV recordings were spread through the media, the case couldn't be hidden any longer.

With two Malaysians abducted this way – and Joshua Helmi and Ruth Sitepu also missing since end-November 2016 – and a growing suspicion they were abducted, a group of civil society groups sent a memo to Suhakam seeking action.

Suhakam then carried out public inquiries on both Koh and Amri’s disappearances. Amri’s case took Suhakam 10 months to complete starting from January 2018, with 27 days of hearings and 24 witnesses summoned.

Suhakam's final reports said evidence pointed to Amri and Koh being forcibly abducted by the Special Branch. It also stated that in both cases, the police failed to investigate the disappearances properly.

The Cabinet then set up a special task force in 2019 to look into the matter. Its report in 2020 stated that it was “highly probable that Amri’s disappearance was caused by rogue police officers acting alone or in a group with unidentified individuals from religious groups".

Three years after Amri disappeared, Norhayati, who became a single mother to their four daughters, sued the police and government for malfeasance and failure to investigate his abduction properly, among others.

The civil suit filed on Nov 18, 2019, took six years, partly because the government initially refused to release the special task force's report. By the time the High Court made its decision, nine years had passed since Amri disappeared.

On Nov 5, 2025, the High Court awarded Norhayati general and exemplary damages totalling RM3 million, and another RM14,457.52 mainly for the children’s education expenses. The court also ordered a re-investigation into Amri’s disappearance.

Justice Su Tiang Joo said the police breached their own SOPs, citing severe delays in handling DNA evidence, failure to investigate the Vios owner, and failure to investigate CCTV recordings, among others. The police also made almost no effort to keep the family updated.

Su said Norhayati’s mental anguish, pain and suffering included having to dissolve her marriage under fasakh – as advised by the Perlis religious affairs department – “to bring succour to the needs of the four daughters".

Norhayati was unable to get welfare aid as a single mother if she remained married to Amri. Secondly, the divorce dispensed of the need for Amri to be a wali for one of their daughters who was getting married.
Perhaps it was to be expected that the attorney-general would appeal the High Court decision. With that, the award was stayed while Norhayati and her daughters continue to wait.
Today, we want to remember Amri.
Whatever wrongs he allegedly committed, Amri deserves a fair chance at defending himself in a court of law.
That’s the basic minimum of a modern democratic society proclaiming the supremacy of the constitution and rule of law as two of its five Rukun Negara tenets.

Abducting Amri was cowardly and dastardly because the government has the machinery, laws, institutions and manpower resources to frame a legal case against him and prosecute him, if he indeed did wrong.
The police chose a shortcut instead, and the executive arm of the government allowed that shortcut. This was a betrayal of the rakyat's trust.
Today, we remember Amri Che Mat, a Malaysian, a father of four girls (now grown women), and surely, a friend to many through his NGO, Perlis Hope.
Ann Teoh is an FMT reader.

9c8bf06abbbe421e: Complaints include marriage disputes, unfair trial, unlawful land grabs, corruption, torture, and more
Originally published on Global Voices
An old man in the Talas province addressing Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov during a public meeting. Photo from the Presidential Administration's website. Fair Use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In October and November 2026, Kyrgyzstan’s president, Sadyr Japarov, held public meetings with the population in all seven provinces of the country. What were meant to be formal events turned into quests for justice by people driven to desperation.
The meetings revealed the ineffectiveness of the existing justice mechanisms and showed how people saw the president as the only guarantor of justice.

The effectiveness of Kyrgyzstan’s law enforcement and judicial bodies was people’s most common justice-related complaint. During a meeting with residents of the southwestern Batken province on October 11, a woman complained to the president about her former husband, who accused her of forging their marriage certificate and framed her for crimes she did not commit to avoid the division of assets after their divorce.

She also said her former brother-in-law provided false testimony to back up his brother’s accusations. She now lives in an apartment with their three children in constant fear that her former husband may kick them out because he allegedly bribed police and courts.

This trivial legal dispute reached the point where the woman had to beg the president to ensure a just investigation and ruling. Japarov condemned her former husband and said that he should have left everything to her and their kids after the divorce.
Here is an Instagram reel with his response to the case.
View this post on Instagram

On October 26, Japarov met with residents of the Kazarman district in the southern Jalalabad province, where Shirimbek Abrahmanov told the president about his father, who was imprisoned for allegedly offering a bribe of KGS 2,000 (USD 23) to a police officer during a traffic stop. The district court acquitted him of the charges.
However, the local prosecutor’s office appealed the decision in the provincial court, which found Abdrahmanov’s father guilty and sentenced him to two years in prison.
Here is an Instagram reel with the complaint and Japarov’s response.
View this post on Instagram
Japarov could not hide his anger when he heard the story, especially after finding out the provincial court took seven months to issue a verdict. In reply, he confronted local authorities and said:

Are the traffic police officer and the prosecutor in cahoots? Does that mean they’ve ganged up on him? If it were a large bribe, that would be one thing. But to have someone imprisoned over two thousand soms — that’s a disgrace.
The man was released from custody shortly after Japarov’s intervention and subsequent pardon.
Similar complaints resurfaced multiple times during presidential meetings in other provinces, highlighting systemic problems plaguing the judicial and law-enforcement systems.
The message is clear: people have lost all hope of finding justice at the hands of local police and courts.

Surprisingly, following his meetings with the public, Japarov concluded that the level of distrust towards courts has decreased, but admitted that problems in the judicial system remain and must be solved quickly.

On the one hand, the lack of justice and the dysfunction within the courts and police bodies, which are plagued by corruption and bureaucracy, are real pressing issues affecting millions of people across Kyrgyzstan. However, the current political regime led by Japarov, who came to power in October 2020, has made little tangible progress.
In 2026, Kyrgyzstan was ranked 99th out of 144 states in the Rule of Law Index compiled by the World Justice Project. For comparison, in 2020, it was ranked 87th.

On the other hand, people’s desperate appeals for justice helped Japarov sustain his man-of-the-people image. By listening to people’s requests and swiftly resolving their issues, the president can reinforce his popularity. In turn, this leads to the maintenance of the personalistic regime built around Japarov since his arrival to power.
Written by Nurbek Bekmurzaev

637817716fa5fe63: Troy Hunt, the founder of data breach reporting site Have I Been Pwned (HIBP), has revealed how organizations respond when he informs them they’ve leaked data – if they respond at all.

Hunt gave Anthropic’s Claude access to an email inbox containing over eight years of his email correspondence and then asked the AI to write a post summarising them, a method he said “was the best way to highlight the behaviors I keep seeing across many breaches and subsequent disclosure efforts.”

Writing in person, Hunt described those behaviors as “standoffish behavior, deliberate delays, heavy involvement from lawyers, and a constant theme: prioritizing corporate interests over those of their customers.”

Once Claude takes over writing duties, it opens with the observation that Hunt sent his standard notification email to 73 organizations between March 2018 and November 2026 and also used website contact forms.
Claude/Hunt focuses on the breach notifications that don’t go well, for example when first contact “often goes nowhere” because “many organisations have no obvious way to report a security incident.”

Some organizations Hunt contacted logged his notifications as customer support requests. “In one case, Troy received three automated surveys asking him to rate the support he'd received,” Claude wrote, before observing “A message that an organization’s customer data is being traded among criminals ended up in the same queue as a question about a late delivery.”

Once someone at victim organization gets the message, a common response is to say they can find no evidence of the breach. Others try to play down the incident, saying it was only a website defacement or that Hunt is re-reporting a previous breach the victim has already disclosed.
If an organization accepts Hunt is probably onto something, it typically says it needs to investigate the matter.

Claude’s take on Hunt’s mails suggests he responds by pointing out that this is an irresponsible approach, because while the investigation takes place, “people whose data has been taken don't know they need to change a password or watch for phishing.”
Next, victims send in the lawyers who ask if their employer or client is legally required to reveal the breach.

Hunt typically replies by saying it is up to the victim to decide if the incident meets the threshold that triggers mandatory disclosure requirements under local laws, but that he intends to notify HIBP users regardless.
Victims don’t like hearing that and respond in three ways:
Calling to discuss disclosure, rather than committing to it;
Asking to see the wording HIBP will use in its disclosure, a request that sees Hunt refer the victim to the HIBP site for examples of the thousand-plus breach reports already on the site;
Arguing that disclosure, not the breach, is the real harm.

Hunt/Claude suggests that each argument victims use to avoid disclosure “sounds reasonable on its own,” but argues “Together, they mean the people most affected by the breach are the last to hear about it.”
The post also reports on some better interactions, such as a small booking platform that was initially skeptical about Hunt’s report, then admitted he was right and acted swiftly to inform customers.

A European travel app hardened its systems, rotated its keys, and published a disclosure. “Troy held off loading the data so he could link to their statement, and thanked them for their transparency,” according to the Claude-generated text.
The bot’s analysis also offers examples of when breach notifications go well.

“Someone with authority over security answered quickly,” Claude concluded. “They treated Troy's data as help rather than as a threat. They told their customers what they knew, even when they didn't know everything yet, and updated the details later. None of them needed lawyers to manage the conversation.”

Hunt appears to have asked Claude to offer its opinion of his email trove. “I don't think the main obstacle to disclosure is technical, or even legal,” the post states. “It's about incentives. For the organization, every day without a public statement is a day without bad headlines.”
Hunt also said he won’t make a habit of having AI write his content, but said Claude “absolutely nails it!” Unlike many of the orgs Hunt contacted. ®

0a9a89060a20b8ad: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang outside the White House with US President Donald Trump and other AI executives in September 2026. Kevin Dietsch/Getty ImagesJust 11 days after resigning as chip maker Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang has been rehired by the company he co-founded, vowing “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around”. The company’s board said its unexpected, unanimous decision came after “input from senior levels of the United States government”. US President Donald Trump went even further, declaring in an interview that he “convinced them” to bring Huang back. The company had bluntly ruled out Huang’s return just days ago. But why would a US president meddle so openly in the world’s second-most valuable company? And why does the leader of Nvidia matter beyond the US – including the speed at which data centres are built worldwide? A trillion-dollar turnaround Nvidia’s stocks plunged after Huang announced his resignation on November 12, following reports of extramarital affairs, one with a woman identified by US intelligence as being in touch with China’s top spy agency and another with an Nvidia employee. Both raised concerns about Huang’s judgement as CEO. Allegations of previously publicly belittling staff – including a senior executive who temporarily succeeded him as CEO – have also been reported by the Wall Street Journal and New York Times. Nvidia’s stock closed at US$174 a share on November 11, the day before Huang quit. Within eight days, the share price had fallen to about US$126, knocking as much as US$1.2 trillion off its market value – and dragging down the wider US share market. On the day of Huang’s return, the company’s shares surged 31% to US$165, pushing its market valuation back up by nearly US$1 trillion. What’s behind Trump’s ‘extraordinary’ intervention? The relationship between the US government, Nvidia and other tech companies has become really entangled. Even so, it’s extraordinary for a president to have called one of the world’s most valuable companies and told its board to reinstate the CEO. It’s hard to imagine any president other than Trump doing that. As an economist, I think in terms of incentives. On Nvidia, I believe Trump had four main incentives to weigh in. First, there’s the obvious economic impact of Nvidia’s falling share price on the wider US stock market. Asked if last week’s AI selloff was a factor in his push to reinstate Huang as CEO, Trump said: “Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term.” Trump added “I made the deal” and that his intervention was “very important” to Huang’s return. Then there’s a political incentive. There’s been growing talk in the media in recent months about the “AI bubble” bursting. The wobbles in AI stocks became especially noticeable when Nvidia lost about one-third of its market capitalisation after Huang’s resignation. All of those losses threaten the perception that markets do well under Trump – a claim he’s long made. While Trump’s intervention in Nvidia is extraordinary by historical standards, it’s not the first time his administration has significantly intervened in the market. Under Trump, the US government last year took a 10% stake in Intel. It has also bought 10–15% stakes in other tech-related companies, especially miners of critical minerals needed for AI. The success of AI and tech-related mining companies has become inextricably tied to this administration. Then there’s a personal incentive. The Financial Times reported the surge in Nvidia’s share price on Monday could have made Trump between US$1.3 million and US$15 million. That’s based on his most recent financial disclosures, which show Trump may have owned as many as 370,000 shares at September 30. Finally, there’s Trump’s personal relationship with Huang. It’s been reported he takes Huang’s advice on all things AI to a significant extent, both in private and in public. For instance, Huang recently took a phone call from Trump while on stage. Huang has been one of the few AI industry leaders who hardly mentions potential downsides of AI. Trump has shunned mentions of AI doomsday scenarios or the need for greater safety. Why does this matter globally? Under Huang, Nvidia has become the central bank of AI: fuelling the AI boom, both with its advanced chips and its funding of tech firms that need those chips. Nvidia is a cash-rich company, with enormous profit margins. Many well-known tech companies that buy Nvidia chips, such as Anthropic and OpenAI, are still comparatively cash poor. They have huge spending commitments and need someone to fund them. The companies then use the money Nvidia provides as an investor to buy Nvidia chips. The better they do, the more chips they buy – and the better Nvidia does. Nvidia has also been a crucial investor in data centres, providing US$228 billion in guarantees, leases and investments for data centre providers. Read more: Who’s paying whom? The circular money machine behind the AI boom (or bubble) But what happens if investors lose confidence in AI? Nvidia’s “circular financing” arrangements mean it’s extremely exposed to the AI industry overall, both on the data centre side and among the AI companies. After Huang resigned, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, was appointed as interim CEO. Kress – who’s staying on as CFO – has reportedly been an important counterweight to Huang on risky financing deals. According to several media outlets, Kress renegotiated a proposal for Nvidia to provide US$250 billion in guarantees for an OpenAI data centre in Ohio, instead cutting that commitment in half. However, Kress is not universally opposed to circular financing. In August she publicly defended Nvidia’s approach, saying “we know some will call this circular financing. We see it differently”. Why does that history matter? Because if Kress or someone other than Huang had been CEO, investment in AI might have slowed. That would have real-world impacts well beyond the US, including how quickly data centres expand worldwide. Huang has been the world’s best known salesman of AI. Now that he’s back as CEO, his incentives – like Trump’s – are the same as before his resignation. Hype up AI’s future, shut down criticism of it and keep the circular finance flowing. Marta Khomyn receives funding from the Australian Research Council. She has some Nvidia shares via her superannuation and ETFs, but no direct ownership of Nvidia shares.

048f15b5fe3e2ca2: Cisco and OpenAI have released an open-source tool called Shirudo to implement compensating controls in Linux, potentially improving security for users who can’t quickly patch newly discovered software flaws.

Shirudo relies on eBPF, the technology that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel. eBPF programs are effectively kernel plug-ins but don’t get unrestricted access to system resources.
Developers have mostly used eBPF to create network functions that enable things like the open source Kubernetes observability and security tool Cilium, a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project.
Cisco and OpenAI think eBPF can help organizations cope with the flood of 100,000-plus software flaws reported this year, many after the debut of AI-powered bug finders.

The increased volume of flaws, and patches to fix them, is a problem for many organizations which already struggle to test fixes or find change windows in which to implement them. That problem has seen greater interest in “compensating controls” – changes to applications or infrastructure that harden them against flaws or malware, without requiring a patch.
With Shirudo, Cisco and OpenAI are suggesting two things:
The privileges eBPF programs enjoy make them a fine way to implement compensating controls for Linux;
Agents should scan your infrastructure for vulnerabilities, then use tools like OpenAI’s Codex to write compensating controls as eBPF programs at machine speed.

“Shirudo” is apparently the Japanese word for “shield,” so Cisco and OpenAI have called the eBPF programs the tool creates “shields.” The two companies envision humans checking every shield Shirudo creates before putting it into production.

Shirudo is open source and available here. The two companies say they’ve already demonstrated it could mitigate the recently discovered flaws in Java without requiring downtime for an Elasticsearch implementation.

Cisco and OpenAI are not alone in advocating for compensating controls. Third-party software maintenance outfits like Rimini Street have used them for years to protect software when their clients no longer have the right to access patches. VMware has introduced “virtual patching.” Palo Alto Networks and Rapid 7 also like this approach, and offer automation to develop controls.
Where Cisco and OpenAI differ is their decision to make Shirudo open source, and their ambition that other players adapt and advance it.

That offer is not entirely altruistic, as if Shirudo takes off it could create more demand for Codex. Cisco’s angle comes from the fact it owns Isovalent, an early champion of eBPF and the creator of both Cilium and the Tetragon sub-project on which Shirudo is based. Switchzilla is using eBPF in other products, so normalizing its use through an open source project can’t hurt. ®
97bbc033a9e9fa11: A president’s absence and a president’s disqualification are two different things. Malaysia Athletics must establish what its constitution requires when an incumbent becomes ineligible to hold office.
World Athletics has disqualified Karim Ibrahim. He has not appealed against the decision, and the international governing body has not lifted the sanction.

Article 13.2.8 of Malaysia Athletics’ endorsed constitution sets out the consequence. It makes a person ineligible to be nominated, elected, appointed or hold office if he has been disqualified, removed or suspended by Malaysia Athletics, the Olympic Council of Malaysia, the Asian Athletics Association, World Athletics or another local or international sports authority or organisation.
That ineligibility continues until the relevant authority releases the person from the sanction or he succeeds in an appeal.
Karim’s disqualification therefore makes him ineligible to hold office under this provision. Malaysia Athletics must formally record it and address the consequences for the presidency.
The issue now is not the existence of the sanction, but how the association applies its own constitution to the leadership position it has affected.
The deputy president’s authority needs a clear basis
Malaysia Athletics deputy president Wan Hisham Wan Salleh now regards himself as the acting president. But the constitution must provide a sound basis for that position.

Article 12.2.2 allows the deputy president to chair Malaysia Athletics meetings when the president is absent. It also allows him to assume the president’s rights and duties at those meetings, as designated by the president.
The clause deals with the president’s absence. It does not expressly state that the deputy president automatically becomes acting president when the incumbent is disqualified from holding office.
Nor does it spell out how the deputy president should assume the full responsibilities of the presidency in those circumstances.
That difference cannot be brushed aside.

A president who is away or unable to attend a meeting may still hold office. Disqualification raises a different issue: the incumbent is no longer eligible to occupy the position under Article 13.2.8.
Wan Hisham’s claim to be acting president therefore needs more than an assumption that the deputy president naturally takes over.
The council must identify the constitutional provision, decision or other valid authority that supports his position.

Article 12.2.2 may provide for the deputy president to perform certain duties during the president’s absence. But the wording supplied does not, by itself, establish an automatic succession process after disqualification.
It also does not expressly give the deputy president a mandate to serve as acting president until the next election.
This is where the executive council must do its work. Article 18.1 gives it sole authority to interpret the association’s constitution and by-laws.
It must examine the relevant provisions together, determine what they require and record its decision.

That interpretive power does not allow the council to create a succession rule that the constitution does not contain. It must apply the written provisions, not stretch them to fit an administrative arrangement.
The council should examine Article 12.2.2 alongside Article 13.2.8 and any other clauses dealing with vacancies, removal from office, an acting president or fresh elections.
If another provision sets out the succession process, the council must follow it. If the constitution leaves the position unclear, it should obtain legal advice before deciding how to proceed.
Wan Hisham has said he will brief the executive council at its Nov 29 meeting. He has declined to answer legal and constitutional questions while awaiting legal advice.
The meeting offers the council a timely opportunity to consider the disqualification, clarify the authority under which the association is operating and decide the next steps.
It should leave no doubt about who holds the presidency, what powers that person may exercise and which constitutional provisions support the arrangement.
Other decisions need scrutiny, not sweeping conclusions
The council must also consider whether Karim’s disqualification affects decisions and appointments made during his time in office.
It should not assume that every decision made under his leadership is now invalid. Equally, it should not treat every appointment as beyond question.
Each case requires a review of the relevant eligibility rules, appointment process and circumstances.

The same care applies to the annual general meeting and the election of office-bearers. Karim’s disqualification does not, by itself, invalidate the entire meeting or the positions of everyone elected.
Any challenge must rest on the relevant constitutional provisions and the facts surrounding the election.
Members may also ask whether they can table a motion of no confidence in the current leadership.
The constitution’s provisions on notice, meetings, voting and removal must determine whether they can do so and what effect such a motion would have.
A vote of no confidence does not necessarily remove an office-bearer unless the rules provide for it.
The council should answer these questions by referring to the constitution, not through informal assurances or political agreement.
Members need to know which rules apply and how the association intends to enforce them.
Malaysia Athletics cannot afford further uncertainty over who has authority to lead it and where that authority comes from.
The association must record Karim’s disqualification, establish the status of the presidency and identify the proper process for filling the position.
It must also clarify the deputy president’s powers while that process unfolds.

If the constitution requires an election, the association should follow the prescribed procedure. If it provides another route, the council should explain and apply it. Either way, members must be able to trace the decision to a clear constitutional provision.

This is not a contest between Karim and Wan Hisham, or an opportunity for one faction to gain an advantage over another. It is a test of whether Malaysia Athletics can govern by rules rather than assumptions.
The executive council has the authority to interpret the constitution. It also has a duty to apply it fairly, consistently and transparently.
A constitution cannot be stretched to suit the people who happen to hold office. It exists to govern them, especially when leadership is in dispute. The Nov 29 meeting should make that clear.

d72fc07dea2532a0: Hari itu Ahmad Maslan berpantun di Dewan Rakyat. Selain terkenal dengan resipi nasi gorengnya, Timbalan menteri kerja raya itu memang gemar berpantun. Tapi, bukan tentang kenapa dan apa sebab beliau berpantun yang ingin saya ceritakan. Tolak ke tepi bab politik, saya rasa ada sesuatu yang wajar kita hargai daripada kegemaran beliau itu. Bagi saya pantun perlu diangkat sebagai pusaka negara dan mesti diajar dengan serius di sekolah ketika kita mencari formula lain dalam usaha menggalakkan pelajar berfikir secara kritis dan kreatif.

Pantun mampu mengasah kemahiran tersebut. Hari ini tak ramai orang mampu berpantun secara spontan. Kalau diberikan pen dan kertas serta masa setengah jam, mungkin ramai yang boleh menghasilkan pantun empat kerat. Itupun pantun yang asal boleh sajalah! Bukan pantun yang betul-betul bermutu tinggi. Tetapi bagaimana jika kita perlu melakukannya dalam masa beberapa saat atau membalas pantun secara spontan? Saya percaya kita memang gagal. Di situlah menariknya pantun sebagai penajam akal.

Kita selalu membicarakan pantun sebagai warisan kesusasteraan Melayu. Tetapi jarang sekali kita membicarakannya dari sudut keupayaan kognitif manusia. Bagi saya, pantun bukan sekadar permainan bahasa, tetapi juga suatu bentuk latihan ketangkasan berfikir. Bayangkan apa yang berlaku dalam kepala seseorang ketika mencipta pantun secara spontan. Kita perlu memikirkan perkara yang hendak disampaikan, mencari perkataan yang sesuai, menyusun ayat, memadankan rima serta membina pembayang. Semua itu dilakukan hampir serentak. Belum lagi kalau pantun itu perlu dijawab apabila ada yang menjualnya.

Otak perlu bekerja untuk memahami maksud yang disampaikan oleh orang lain, merumuskan jawapan dan menterjemahkan jawapan itu dalam bentuk puisi yang mempunyai peraturan tertentu. Ini bukan mudah. Cuma, selama ini kita lihat pantun seolah-olah dipermainkan dan dijadikan bahan lawak sahaja dalam rancangan hiburan atau persembahan komedi. Kita kena serius sekali-sekala.

Dalam bidang pendidikan, kita sering bercakap tentang pemikiran kritis. Kita mahu anak-anak kita mempunyai kemampuan menganalisis, mentafsir, membuat perkaitan dan menyelesaikan masalah secara kreatif. Menariknya, sebahagian daripada kemahiran berfikir itu sudah lama dilatih oleh nenek moyang kita melalui suatu kegiatan yang hari ini sering kita anggap sekadar hiburan.

Bukanlah bermaksud syarat hendak berpantun mestilah mempunyai pemikiran kritis yang tinggi. Tetapi proses mencipta pantun itu sendiri memerlukan beberapa kemahiran mental yang amat berguna dalam membentuk pemikiran seseorang. Pantun juga ada tingkatannya. Ada pantun yang mudah, sekadar memadankan bunyi di hujung baris. Ada pula pantun yang pembayangnya mempunyai hubungan makna dengan maksud yang hendak disampaikan. Lebih tinggi lagi apabila pencipta pantun menggunakan perlambangan alam untuk menyampaikan falsafah kehidupan. Contohnya pantun ini:-
Yang kurik itu kundi, Yang merah itu saga; Yang baik itu budi, Yang indah itu bahasa.

Betapa ekonomisnya penggunaan bahasa dalam menyampaikan suatu pemikiran. Tak perlu panjang berjela, empat baris sahaja sudah cukup untuk membicarakan nilai kemanusiaan. Orang Melayu dahulu memerhatikan alam. Mereka melihat tumbuh-tumbuhan, haiwan, sungai, laut dan perubahan cuaca. Daripada pemerhatian itu, mereka membina perlambangan dan menghubungkannya dengan kehidupan manusia. Ini bukan sekadar persoalan penguasaan bahasa. Ini juga persoalan keupayaan membuat perkaitan antara dua perkara yang pada zahirnya kelihatan tidak mempunyai hubungan. Kemampuan membuat perkaitan inilah yang dimaksudkan sebagai salah satu ciri pemikiran kreatif.

Menteri pendidikan patut beri perhatian yang serius akan kemahiran yang sudah lama kita miliki ini. Pantun bukan sekadar diajar sebagai salah satu bentuk puisi tradisional dalam mata pelajaran bahasa Melayu semata-mata tetapi dijadikan kegiatan yang melatih anak-anak berfikir secara spontan. Adakan sesi jual beli pantun di dalam kelas. Seorang pelajar mengemukakan persoalan dalam bentuk pantun dan seorang lagi menjawabnya juga dalam bentuk pantun. Biarkan mereka belajar sambil berseronok walaupun pada permulaannya mungkin mutu pantun masih rendah. Lama-kelamaan sudah tentu pelajar akan jadi mahir serta tangkas seperti pantun lama ini:
Limau purut lebat di pangkal, Batang mengkudu condong uratnya; Hujan ribut dapat ditangkal, Hati yang rindu apa ubatnya?

Perhatikan kehalusannya. Jika anak-anak kita mampu mencipta pantun sebegini bermakna mereka telah memahami falsafah hubungan perasaan manusia dengan fenomena alam. Hujan ribut yang dahsyat sekalipun masih dianggap mampu ditangkal, tetapi kerinduan yang tidak kelihatan itu belum tentu mampu diubati.

Bayangkan juga jika seorang guru sains meminta anak muridnya menerangkan sesuatu konsep sains melalui pantun. Sudahlah perlu memahami konsep itu, mereka perlu pula memikirkan cara menyampaikannya dalam empat baris. Tentulah ada yang secara sinis mempersoalkan mengapa perlu menyusahkan diri sedangkan penerangan biasa lebih mudah. Inilah yang saya maksudkan sejak awal lagi ia bertujuan untuk mencabar kemampuan minda. Contoh lucunya ialah mamat-mamat sado yang mengangkat besi di gimnasium pun boleh kita tanyakan soalan yang sama. Mengapa bersusah payah mengangkat besi berat sebab lepas itu letak semula besi tersebut di tempat asalnya. Tapi kita segera faham yang dia sedang melatih ototnya, manakala orang yang berpantun pula sedang melatih akalnya.

Dalam zaman kecerdasan buatan hari ini, kita boleh meminta komputer menghasilkan puluhan pantun dalam beberapa saat. Tetapi tujuan mengajar anak-anak berpantun bukanlah semata-mata untuk mendapatkan pantun yang indah. Yang lebih penting ialah proses mental yang dilalui untuk menghasilkan pantun tersebut. Kita tidak mahu sekadar melahirkan generasi yang tahu mendapatkan jawapan. Kita juga mahu melahirkan generasi yang tahu bagaimana hendak berfikir untuk mendapatkan jawapan. Bertuahnya kita ialah kita sudah ada kaedah yang praktikal dalam hal ini tetapi kita kesampingkannya. Orang tua kita dulu apabila berpantun macam, GhatGpt. Prompt saja terus keluar jawapan.

Satu lagi keistimewaan pantun ialah kemampuannya menyampaikan teguran secara halus. Orang boleh berselisih pendapat, menyindir, menegur, malah berbahas tanpa semestinya menggunakan bahasa yang kasar. Dalam zaman manusia begitu mudah memaki hamun di media sosial, alangkah menariknya jika mereka perlu berpantun dahulu sebelum mahu bergaduh. Sekurang-kurangnya ada tapisan sedikit sebelum menghina orang. Kedengaran mungkin lucu, tapi kita lihatlah hari ini berapa ramai mengalami kemurungan akibat dimaki hamun di media sosial. Berbanding beberapa Ahli Parlimen yang gemar menjerit dan bertempik sehingga penyokong sendiri pun naik malu.

Nenek moyang kita bukan sahaja mewariskan keindahan berbahasa, malah suatu kaedah untuk melatih ketangkasan akal.

Kalau kita sendiri kurang menghargai keistimewaan pantun, tahukah kita bahawa hampir dua abad dahulu sasterawan Perancis sudah tertarik dengannya? af2379ca2419bb97: The leaders of the great model houses, Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman, desperately want the world to believe AI is the skeleton key which will unlock the secrets of the universe.
But if the AI can’t explain what it’s “proven,” are we actually any closer to understanding anything, or have we simply built another black box?

That question is top of mind among mathematicians and computer scientists this week after Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge claimed to have solved a mathematical conjecture so elusive it's gone unproven for more than 150 years. The fact that this note came out one day after Anthropic's record-setting IPO is a coincidence, we're sure.

In a four-page post to his website, the researcher described how with the help of Claude, he believes he has proven the Riemann Hypothesis, one of seven Millennium problems so complex and so important that the Clay Mathematics Institute has offered a $1 million prize to anyone who is successful in solving them.

The Riemann Hypothesis, conjectured by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, contends that all nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function – those with a real part between zero and one – have a real part equal to 1/2.

Confused? Don’t worry. We’ve linked to an explainer that goes into more detail here. What's important is that, if the Riemann Hypothesis is right, mathematicians can place tighter bounds on the difference between the actual distribution of prime numbers and mathematical estimates of that distribution.

Researchers have previously attempted to disprove the conjecture through computational brute force, and therein have shown the hypothesis holds to at least 10 trillion zeros. There’s reason to believe that the Riemann Hypothesis is accurate, but the possibility remains that over a sufficiently long series the pattern might diverge. And so, more than 150 years after Riemann published his hypothesis, it has remained just that.
Alpöge’s proof, if it can even be called that, is now the subject of great debate.

The four pages in which Alpöge remarks on the discoveries he and Claude made aren’t exactly a proof, but rather 14 tarballs worth of Lean code totaling roughly 240 MB. Lean is an open source programming language commonly used to help validate mathematical proofs.

The Clay Mathematics Institute, which oversees the seven Millennium Problems, has promoted the Riemann Hypothesis from “unsolved” to “active” status, but it is not yet considered solved. For Clay to consider the problem solved and award the prize, the proposed solution must be published in a qualifying outlet, remain available for scrutiny for at least two years, and receive broad acceptance from the mathematics community.
As it stands, Alpöge describes the 250,000 pages of text generated by the model for its written proof as a “massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop.’”

Not long after Alpöge's remarks and Lean code were published, Stanford mathematician Ravi Vakil released a nearly 1,000-page draft proof by Alessandro Maria Masullo, who earned his PhD at Stanford in 2020. Masullo has reportedly spent more than a decade pursuing the problem.

Frameworks like Lean make mathematics a prime candidate for AI-assisted discovery for many of the same reasons that the technology has proven so successful in software development: code either compiles and runs or it doesn’t.

Code can also be audited and could, with great effort, be deciphered. But a proof written in Lean isn't a mathematical proof in the traditional, human-readable sense. Although its logical validity can be checked by a computer, understanding the reasoning behind it can be another matter. Traditional proofs ideally explain their arguments in a way that other mathematicians can follow. Cantor's Diagonal Argument offers a comparatively accessible example.
While the clock hasn’t even started for the Clay Math Institute, the Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib Initiative have already declared the Riemann Hypothesis solved.

“We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” the orgs wrote in a joint statement. “We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct.”
Even if the code ends up being right, if we still don’t know why it’s true, have we really learned anything meaningful?
"At the minute, we don't even know why the theorem is true," Kevin Buzzard, professor of pure mathematics at Imperial College London, said in a recent Al Jazeera interview.
Alpöge’s proof may simply be the product of a black box. To quote the late Arthur C Clarke, “any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.”
The implications of such a technology aren’t lost on researchers. Months ago, several prominent researchers called for greater scrutiny and oversight regarding the application of AI in mathematics.

“Mathematics produces not only a body of results, but also understanding, clarity, and judgment among the communities of mathematicians who have shaped them, often in the context of their own autonomously guided research,” the Leiden Declaration reads. “This expert knowledge is essential, both to effectively use mathematics, and to continue to articulate new and significant research questions.” ®
7936a1d5242e0abf: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 24 — Malaysia must ensure that its newly elevated strategic partnership with France translates into meaningful technology transfer and industrial development, rather than relegating the country to a supplier of raw materials for Europe’s strategic ambitions, said Citizens International executive director Imran Mohd Rasid.

He said closer cooperation with France could help Malaysia diversify its economy and strengthen its industrial capabilities, but cautioned against agreements that could create new forms of economic dependence.

“Malaysia must avoid becoming a mineral supplier for somebody else’s industrial revolution. We should welcome French investment, but Malaysia must not exchange one form of dependency for another,” he said.

His remarks follow French President Emmanuel Macron’s two-day official visit to Malaysia on November 16 and 17, during which both countries elevated bilateral relations to a Strategic Partnership encompassing critical minerals, defence, energy and advanced technologies.

Among the key developments was a rare earth industrial project involving French company Carester and Malaysia’s Malaco Mining Group, which is expected to begin operations in early 2027. The project will involve extraction and processing in Malaysia, with further refining to be carried out in France.

Imran, who is also an international relations expert specialising in Global South affairs, said the arrangement could benefit Malaysia if it enabled the country to move beyond supplying raw materials and develop its own high-value industries.
“If France wants access to our rare earths, it should also help Malaysia acquire the technology, knowledge and industrial capabilities to become a producer of higher-value products,” he said.

He stressed that Malaysia should sweek substantive technology transfer, greater participation by local companies in separation, refining and downstream manufacturing, and opportunities for Malaysian workers and suppliers to undertake higher-value activities.
He also cautioned against environmental risks associated with rare earth extraction and processing, particularly waste management and pollution.

The Malaysian government has maintained its moratorium on raw rare earth exports, which took effect on Jan 1, 2024, while allowing limited and conditional exports for research, development and processing purposes.

Deputy Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Minister Syed Ibrahim Syed Noh told the Dewan Rakyat on Thursday that cooperation with France would focus on technological expertise and developing the entire rare earth value chain, from mining and processing to high-value products.

Imran said the timing of Macron’s visit also reflected growing European concerns over strategic vulnerabilities, with the war in Ukraine, energy insecurity and geopolitical tensions exposing Europe’s dependence on external suppliers for critical minerals, energy and technology.
He said Europe’s growing interest in the Global South could give developing countries greater bargaining power.
On the shared emphasis by Malaysia and France on strategic autonomy, Imran said the concept must be understood in the context of their vastly different economic and geopolitical positions.

He said while France viewed strategic autonomy primarily as a means of protecting its international position and reducing vulnerabilities, Malaysia needed to pursue it as a strategy to overcome structural economic dependencies and strengthen its own development capabilities. — Bernama

797d55e6415146b1: Don't mind the recent arrests. The ShinyHunters extortion gang may still be operating, just under the new name of Inception, according to Okta's threat intelligence group.

ShinyHunters is the brash cybercriminal group that, most recently, breached rival gang Clop before hacking the FBI, resulting in at least three arrests of key suspects in September and October. The crims - and their old data leak site - have since gone dark.

“While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion,” Okta threat hunters Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels said on Monday.
Okta tracks this threat cluster as O-UNC-053 - the “O-UNC” prefix stands for an Okta Uncategorized cluster, and it uses this label before formally attributing the activity to a named threat group.

While Okta hasn't formally confirmed O-UNC-053 to be the same crime crew as ShinyHunters, the identity and access management provider’s researchers note that it does use nearly identical social engineering tactics: voice phishing, during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA).

Plus, they note: O-UNC-053 operators change the themes of their phishing domains about every four to six weeks, and they also post claimed victims on ShinyHunters’ data leak site. In November, however, organizations targeted by O-UNC-053 began appearing on a new data leak site branded as Inception and not ShinyHunters.

The first five - Advanced Micro Devices, Cigna Healthcare, Paychex, PepsiCo, and Henry Schein - appeared November 17 on the site, and all were marked “leaked.” Soon after, security maven Dominic Alvieri questioned if Inception was linked to ShinyHunters. “ShinyHunters are not all in jail,” he wrote on social media.
On November 19, AutoZone appeared on the site, with Inception again claiming to have leaked the auto-parts retailer's files. On Saturday, EV technology firm Lucid Group joined the claimed victims.
None of the seven companies have confirmed breaches, and none responded to The Register’s inquiries. We will update this story when we receive more information.
Okta Threat Intelligence “is unable to validate if published data is authentic,” the researchers said in response to our questions.

In the Monday report, the Okta team does note that Inception’s new data leak site listings “included multiple targets for which Okta Threat Intelligence previously observed O-UNC-053 infrastructure registration.”

The infrastructure was registered between six and 19 days before Inception listed the companies on its leak site, and this gap “is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors,” Diallo and Nickels added.

The Com (short for community) is a loosely knit network of online groups whose young members participate in a range of illicit activities including hacking, swatting, digital extortion, real-life shootings, and other physical violence. Many security researchers consider ShinyHunters to be connected to The Com, along with groups such as Scattered Spider and LAPSUS$, with overlapping memberships and shared infrastructure.

“Before and after the change in DLS publication, O-UNC-053 maintained consistent infrastructure and TTPs, leading us to assess that the cluster has very likely changed their brand affiliation,” the Okta researchers wrote. “We cannot currently make a high confidence assessment as to whether O-UNC-053 is operating the DLS themselves or is partnering with another extortion actor.”

Regardless, members of the group formerly known as ShinyHunters and/or O-UNC-053 are still roaming the internet, looking for new victims, and conducting voice phishing attacks to steal data and then extort victims' companies for exorbitant sums of money. Consider yourself warned - and turn on phishing-resistant MFA.®

564fe1ffdb846e90: Amazon has agreed to buy AI optimization technology from an Israeli startup in a bid to speed up its inference operations.

The house of Bezos on Monday announced a deal to purchase proprietary AI acceleration tech from Decart AI, known as the Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), for an undisclosed amount. Amazon also plans to bring Decart’s three founders and their engineering team into the fold.

Decart’s DOS is designed to push AI hardware closer to its maximum performance across different AI models and hardware platforms. The company claims that most AI chips live their lives without reaching their full potential – practically a sin in this age of increased hardware costs and limited availability – and DOS aims to fix that by operating between the model and the chip, optimizing kernels, compilers, and runtimes for the underlying hardware “so every core stays busy.”
DOS is hardware-agnostic, with Decart saying it supports Nvidia GPUs, Google TPUs, and, most critically for our purposes here, AWS Trainium chips.

“More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost,” Peter DeSantis, Amazon SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, and quantum computing, said in the announcement. “That's the pillar Trainium and our AI efforts are built on, and from our earliest work with Decart, we knew they … would help us push it even further.”

Decart doesn’t offer much in the way of details about its proprietary AI-maxxing tech, but claims it can reduce latency, improve throughput, and reduce the costs associated with training and inference runs.

An Amazon spokesperson clarified to The Register that the deal is an asset purchase and not a full company acquisition, with Amazon only acquiring DOS and the tech behind it as well as personnel. As for what may become of Decart after the deal, that’s unclear. Amazon told us to reach out to Decart to learn what may happen to any remaining employees and the company’s other technology, but we didn’t hear back.

Along with offering its optimization stack, Decart has a couple of different AI models: Lucy, a live video model marketed toward advertisers, live streamers, and the like; and Oasis, a world model AI marketed toward companies working on embodied AI applications.

Decart’s non-DOS assets weren’t mentioned in the press release, and per the Amazon spokesperson we talked to, that means they weren’t part of the deal. We can’t imagine that the Decart team is too upset about the potential abandonment of those models, though: While neither company has disclosed a price, Bloomberg claims its sources value the deal at around $7.5 billion.

If Bloomberg's figure is accurate, that would make this deal one of the most expensive in Amazon’s history, right between its $3.9 billion acquisition of One Medical and its $8.5 billion purchase of film studio MGM. ®
f82e2058d3bb9c30: Languages take on thousands of forms. Some are tonal, like Vietnamese, where shifts in pitch convey distinct meanings. English relies on precise word orders, but this matters less for Russian, where words can be swapped without changing the intended message.  Despite so much variety in the linguistic kingdom, an MIT study has found that the human brain may process all sorts of languages in a universal way. Artificial intelligence made this finding possible. In the study published today in Nature Neuroscience, the researchers used multilingual models to predict how the human brain responds to various languages. Those models also helped the researchers detect a shared brain process across people who collectively spoke 21 different languages. “Of course, there are many differences in the ways humans converse with each other. But our team found that there is something fundamentally similar in how the brain communicates,” says Evelina Fedorenko, who is an investigator at MIT’s McGovern Institute for Brain Research, an associate professor of brain and cognitive sciences, and the senior author of the paper. The study is the first to use multilingual models to predict brain responses across many languages. As researchers develop AI language tools to diagnose brain disorders, this work can extend their benefit to speakers of more languages, and may one day even keep endangered ones from vanishing. Parsing the linguistic mind Language allows us to share our thoughts about the outside world and the ones we create in our minds. That power lives within a network of brain regions located in the left hemisphere. “Every language is managed by these same parts of the brain,” explains Andrea Gregor de Varda, the lead author of the new study, a postdoc in the Fedorenko lab, and fellow in the K. Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center. While scientists know that all languages activate the same parts of the brain, de Varda and Fedorenko wanted to know if that meant the brain processes them in the same way. For example, they wondered, does the brain of someone who speaks Korean operate comparably to the brains of a Hindi or Spanish speaker? It’s extremely hard to answer that question if you lack the right tools, de Varda says. And they needed one capable of creating a common code for comparing all sorts of languages — a task that is well-suited to artificial intelligence. Where AI meets the brain Large language models (LLMs) — such as those powering ChatGPT and Claude — interpret language much like the human brain, although they weren’t designed to do so. That surprising similarity is allowing de Varda and others in the field to wield these tools as a piercing lens into the human mind. Such studies often explore LLMs’ ability to learn or make sense of linguistic elements, such as grammar and meaning, to glean insights into how the brain might handle communication. But early LLMs used to work within a single language. The MIT researchers thought another class of models might help expand that scope. “Multilingual language models are LLMs that can process hundreds of languages at once,” explains Fedorenko. Like other AIs of their kind, multilingual models ingest words or phrases and output numbers that scientists can extract. “Those numbers show how the model represents that bit of language,” she says. Now the team could study many languages at once using a single numerical code from the models. But the extent to which the models aligned with the human mind still lurked in the unknowns. De Varda believed he could coax an answer into light through a computational approach. Using machine learning, he merged two data sources: the multilingual models’ code and scans of people’s brains as they performed linguistic tasks. The product was an AI tool known as an encoding model. It takes a multilingual model’s code, say, for a sentence, and predicts how the human brain might light up in response to the same input. Encoding models at the time only existed for a handful of languages including English, French, and Chinese. But de Varda sought to test whether those models could be extended to more — and importantly, understudied ones. Doing so could reveal new aspects in which AI mirrors the human brain, and even detect a shared neural component across speakers of various languages. A mental bridge between languages The Fedorenko lab already had preexisting brain imaging data from speakers of 12 languages: Afrikaans, Dutch, Farsi, French, Lithuanian, Marathi, Norwegian, Romanian, Spanish, Tamil, Turkish, and Vietnamese. They recruited speakers of nine additional ones for their new study — Italian, Portuguese, German, Russian, Polish, Hindi, Arabic, Mandarin, and Korean — and recorded their brain activity while they listened to stories from “Alice in Wonderland” in their native language. By coupling that brain imaging data with outputs from multilingual models, the team created encoding models for those 21 languages. “We found that the encoding models accurately predicted brain responses in all of the languages we studied — even in Marathi and Lithuanian, that, in contrast to English, we only have a limited amount of data on,” says Fedorenko. “The fact that there’s this emergent similarity between models and humans across so many languages is really quite exciting.” Another finding was more interesting still. Even though the researchers trained an encoding model in a single language, it could predict brain activity for a language it had never seen before. For example, an encoding model trained to predict brain responses in French could also predict responses in Vietnamese, without ever being trained in Vietnamese. It was a truly fascinating discovery, de Varda says, because this was only possible if all the speakers’ brains were representing language in a shared way: a neural thread binding human communication. What was that shared component? Dissecting different linguistic features across all the languages suggested that it has something to do with meaning. “That’s the intended power of communication, right? To share meaning; new information or our feelings about the world. So it’s fascinating we see that reflected in this work,” says Fedorenko. In science, this new study gives brain researchers some explanations for long-held curiosities among them. In society, it could steer emerging technologies into a more inclusive direction. Scientists are starting to explore clinical uses of AI language tools, such as those that can detect cognitive decline based on brain activity patterns during language. But most of those studies, and the methods clinicians use today, are in common and well-studied languages like English. By showing how AI and the human brain overlap across many diverse languages, this new research may be a step toward clinical tools that do not leave most speakers out. In another vein, reversing the Fedorenko lab’s approach might help preserve languages on the brink of extinction. “Say you had one single speaker of a language that is dying out. You might imagine a case in which we can train a model in the opposite direction: give it images of that speaker’s brain, and it could translate those into language,” notes Fedorenko. De Varda adds that there are features that clearly differ between languages, too, and that those must be somehow represented in the brain and even LLMs. Defining those differences in future research, he says, might unearth new fragments of knowledge to complete the puzzle of the linguistic mind.
