c642a9ca0e226b9c: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Last week, the University of Michigan’s board of regents approved the construction of a $1.25 billion data center that will power American nuclear weapons research. The regents voted 7 - 1 in a public meeting on November 19 to move forward with the project despite widespread opposition from faculty, staff, and the residents of Ypsilanti Township, Michigan where the data center will operate. A few hours after the vote, the leaders and citizens of the Township gathered to discuss how to stop it.

U of M and Los Alamos National Laboratories (LANL) first announced plans to build what the University then called an “AI research facility” in 2024. U of M now calls the project a “research computing center” and, if all goes to its plan, construction will begin on a 125,000 square foot facility in late 2027. The data center could expand to “no more than 300,000 square feet,” according to a U of M blog post.
<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> During the regent’s meeting, faculty, staff, and members of the community shared their thoughts on the data center’s construction.

“It is widely promoted as the next step in furthering novel research taking place at this University. What is conveniently left out on flyers and pamphlets is that this is only part of the proposition, 10% in fact, the other 90% is being used by Los Alamos — a nuclear weapons developer,” a sophomore studying biochemistry told the board before the vote. “We already have three existing high tech data centers used for research. Why must we push forward with another one that is promoting nuclear warfare?”

An electrician from Ypsilanti Township, a representative of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) union, supported the construction project. “This will create 300 plus jobs for our members, all local, [and] give back to the community,” he said. “IBEW is in favor of the data center, excuse me, ‘high compute research center.’”

People who attended the regent’s meeting to discuss other topics referenced the vote during their presentations. “You voted today to fund a $785 million data center project in Ypsilanti, much to the opposition of the residents of the area, acting against what many residents in the area are calling environmental racism. I think I can speak for many students when I say I am frankly appalled by this decision,” a student who was there to discuss carbon emissions said.

A library worker present to talk about how the University treats its workers invoked the data center. “I’m not sure I can confidently appeal to your sense of compassion around this. The officials and residents of Ypsi Township are saying ‘stop,’ saying ‘no,’ saying ‘this hurts.’ And you and others responsible for this nuclear weapons data center project have shown you don’t care about the basic issue of consent as you plow ahead,” he said.
Ypsilanti Township is at the tip of the spear in the new nuclear arms race.

Despite the opposition in the room, the regents approved the project. “It’s been very controversial [...] For me, this is all about an investment in the community and it’s an investment, in many different ways,” regent Denise Ilitch said just before the vote. “The community will be enhanced — they may not feel it now, some, but I venture to say that there will be much good that will come from this.”

Many in Ypsilanti Township disagree. After the regents voted, the leadership and residents of the Township gathered for a panel discussion about the data center. One of the speakers that night was Jay Coghlan, the executive director of Nuclear Watch of New Mexico, a watchdog group that tracks Los Alamos. “The data center issue here in Ypsilanti is unique in that it is the clearest example of the pending merger of AI and nuclear weapons, which doesn’t bode well,” Coghlan told 404 Media.

Coghlan told 404 Media that he shared the Township’s concerns about how the data center will use water and electricity but said he thinks its construction will have farther reaching consequences. “Our nation is transforming from the military-industrial complex that Eisenhower warned us about to a Silicon Valley-Pentagon-Wall Street complex that closely links economics, economic inequality, increasing militarism, and I dare say the rise of techno-fascism,” he said.

U of M has repeatedly said the data center will mostly be used to power medical breakthroughs and conduct cancer research, something it’s highlighted in flyers and pamphlets it’s mailed to people in the Township. LANL sent a letter to the people of the community in September that promised it wouldn't build nuclear weapons in their backyard.

“I'm going ‘Duh, yeah, you're not going to bring plutonium to Ypsilanti in Michigan,” Coghlan said. “But I expect this data center to have a lot to do with the design of new nuclear weapons. So, in that way, Ypsilanti Township is at the tip of the spear in the new nuclear arms race.”

Coghlan said he finds hope in the opposition to the project. “I’m very impressed by the intensity of opposition that I have witnessed. There seems to be a pretty widespread public awareness of the data center in Ypsilanti, Township.”

During the Township meeting on November 19, after the regents voted, Ypsilanti Township attorney Douglas Winters said he was mad. “What did we learn on November 3rd? Two weeks ago and two days, voters around this country loudly declared that they were sick and tired of government corruption. They were tired of secrecy. They were tired of abuse of power. They were tired of threats to democracy and the disregard of governmental accountability. And, importantly, they also said they were sick and tired of these data centers,” he said. “Somehow that message did not make it to Ann Arbor. That message did not make it to the board of regents.”

Winters and other leaders vowed to keep fighting the data center’s construction. In May, the community’s water authority voted to restrict new construction on infrastructure to data center projects while it conducts a review of their impact on the Township’s water supply. The University called the move “unlawfully discriminatory.” In August, the Township passed a six month moratorium on new electrical infrastructure, a move aimed at delaying the project.
9cbcfc27624697ca: In a 2019 referendum, close to 98% of Bougainvilleans for independence. After more than a century of struggle, Bougainville is moving closer to becoming the world’s newest nation. An autonomous region of Papua New Guinea (PNG) in the northern Solomon Islands chain, Bougainville is taking its next step toward self-determination after a decade-long civil war and a 25-year peace process. In a 2019 referendum, almost 98% of Bougainvilleans voted for independence. Today the parliament of PNG will begin to vote on ratifying that result. A “yes” vote in parliament, if it comes, won’t immediately make Bougainville independent. But it will set the legal machinery moving. Hard questions such as the future of the island’s contentious Panguna mine remain unresolved, but the vote offers a chance to recognise decades of work from the Bougainvillean and PNG sides that have kept the peace process on track. The legacy of colonialism Bougainville was named by French navigator Louis Antoine de Bougainville in the 18th century, and colonialism has shaped its history ever since. In 1899, it was incorporated into German New Guinea, while the neighbouring Solomon Islands became a British protectorate. Colonial control shifted to Australian occupation in 1914, a move legitimised by the League of Nations in 1920. During the second world war, Japanese forces took over, followed by an American-led invasion in 1943. From 1949, Bougainville was again under Australian control as part of PNG. The dismantling of colonial rule began in 1971, and PNG gained independence in 1975. Bougainville’s decolonisation was left unresolved. The crisis years From 1988 to 1998, Bougainville experienced one of the most severe conflicts in the South Pacific. The Panguna mine was a focal point for grievances related to land ownership, environmental damage, a desire for self-determination and the distribution of mining resources. The mine began operating in 1972 in Central Bougainville, and was once one of the world’s one of the world’s largest copper and gold mines. Owned by a subsidiary of the Australian company Rio Tinto, it was a significant source of revenue for the PNG government. In the late 1980s, the environmental impacts of mining and unequal distribution of its revenues led to violent protests by landowners and the closure of the mine. The PNG government responded with force, and the protests developed into an armed rebellion. Conflict ensued, involving the Bougainville Revolutionary Army, the PNG Defence Force and various local factions. Australia provided indirect military support to PNG forces. A years-long PNG-imposed blockade paralysed Bougainville’s government services and economic activity. An estimated 15,000–20,000 lives were lost in the conflict overall. Attempts to end the fighting began with people from local villages, especially women. They used customary and introduced conflict resolution processes, alongside Christian faith, to lay the groundwork for political negotiations. Eventually, peace talks began in 1998, and an agreement was signed in 2001. Two narratives about how peace was achieved There have long been two narratives about Bougainville’s path to peace. One emphasises regional and international diplomacy, which has involved New Zealand‑facilitated talks in 1997–98, unarmed Australian peace monitoring and UN engagement. The second, backed by many Bougainvillean and PNG leaders, stresses a “light intervention” of international support and notes the distinctly Melanesian approach to peacemaking. This process has been inclusive (involving women’s groups, young people, ex-combatants, faith-based organisations and churches) and patient. The Bougainville Peace Agreement In 2001, the Bougainville Peace Agreement established a framework for Bougainville’s political future. The agreement led to the establishment of the autonomous Bougainville government, a weapons-disposal program, free and fair elections, and a referendum on Bougainville’s future political status. The 2019 referendum gave Bougainvilleans a decisive mandate. Then in August of this year, the autonomous Bougainville government and PNG government – with international support – set out a jointly agreed, phased pathway to translate the referendum result into a constitutional transition. Now, the results must be ratified by PNG’s parliament – the final legislative step in the peace agreement process. A “yes” vote will not itself create independence. It will kick off the legal, administrative and institutional actions needed to move towards self‑government and ultimately independence. A “no” or deferred vote will trigger further consultations and protective measures. Panguna, resources and public understanding Even in PNG, not everyone understands the history of the conflict and the nature of the peace process – especially younger people, including parliamentarians. Some have complained Bougainville’s independence would threaten national unity and set a precedent for other provinces. Complex post-conflict issues remain in Bougainville, including unresolved trauma from the years of conflict. This has exacerbated other forms of violence based on gender and accusations of sorcery. Natural resource governance, especially the future of the still-inactive Panguna mine, also remains uncertain. Local communities have led a process that has just seen Rio Tinto agree to pay US$250 million (A$376 million) to begin addressing the long-term environmental and human cost of the mine. Efforts are also being made to diversify an independent Bougainville’s revenue through fishing, farming and the sustainable approach set out in its “green‑blue economy policy”. For many people, Panguna is both an emblem of past dispossession and a potential source of revenue for an independent Bougainville. For others, its reopening would risk reviving conflict. Across the Pacific, community-led peacebuilding efforts aim to prevent conflict alongside providing environmental resilience. While international security pacts are proliferating, practical security on the ground may depend more on addressing colonial legacies, inequality and the impacts of climate change. A way forward Whatever the outcome of the parliamentary vote, the institutions, relationships and habits of joint work built through the peace process give reason for cautious optimism. The people of Bougainville and Papua New Guinea have done the slow work to get to this point. Those of us watching from outside can take this moment to honour the peace process so far and do what is needed to support its future. Tania Miletic was Project Leader of the Bougainville Senior Leadership Professional Development Program 2023-24, an Australian government program, delivered by the University of Melbourne with financial support from the NZ Government.
da45b84cc5fd1d8d: President Donald Trump is among those who pushed to have Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO. Kevin Dietsch/Getty ImagesThe story may sound familiar: The CEO of one of the largest and most powerful tech companies resigns over sexual misconduct allegations. The move causes the company’s stock to drop by more than 10%, wiping out billions in value. It also raises scrutiny of the company’s board of directors and whether it made the right decisions ahead of the crisis. This could easily describe the turmoil facing Nvidia after the Nov. 12, 2026, ouster of its CEO, Jensen Huang, who remarkably returned to his job just 11 days later. But it actually transpired over 15 years ago at Hewlett Packard, under CEO Mark Hurd. Jensen Huang is just the latest in a long line of CEOs who lost their jobs – albeit in his case temporarily – over personal misconduct. And as with HP, scrutiny is shifting from his behavior to his board – and the decisions that led to his exit. Prominent industry leaders are questioning the board’s original decision to oust him. They include Peter Steinberger of OpenAI, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan – not to mention President Donald Trump, who reportedly directed the effort to get Huang reinstated. As a scholar of management who has researched corporate misconduct, I believe the board had made the right call to force him out. After collecting instances of CEO personal misconduct dating back to 1995, I have repeatedly found that doing nothing, as a board, is worse than doing something. CEO personal misconduct isn’t simply a private matter or an isolated leadership failure. I believe it creates reputational and governance risks for directors and can embolden further misconduct when left unaddressed. It may also signal deeper problems within the organization. But it’s still hard for boards to act, particularly when the CEO is also the company’s founder and a central figure in its success. This is likely why the board chose to reinstate Jensen Huang. And why his return sets a terrible precedent. The costs of misconduct One important change over the years is that boards are becoming more sensitive to misconduct matters due to greater scrutiny by the media and public. They’re also more aware of the consequences for their own job that stem from the board’s performance and entanglement in the misconduct. In fact, directors of companies whose CEOs are involved in personal misconduct exit at a significantly higher rate than normal, either because they choose to leave a messy situation or because they’re forced out due to poor performance, my research shows. One of the better known examples is Best Buy founder Richard Schulze, who stepped down as chairman of the board in 2012 after an internal investigation revealed that he knew about former CEO Brian Dunn’s inappropriate personal relationship with a female employee and failed to report it. Former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker attracted much more negative attention after his second DUI arrest compared to his first. Chip Somodevilla/POOL/AFP via Getty Images Directors are also personally penalized for their association with their company’s corporate misconduct. They may lose their board seats or see other companies they’re associated with take a hit. And if they hold executive positions elsewhere, the misconduct may spill over to damage the reputations of those companies as well. In other words, directors have a rational basis to be concerned about their reputations and how a CEO’s personal misconduct may tarnish it. In the case of Nvidia, questions are now being asked about the rigor of board oversight, the lack of CEO succession planning, and whether the board knew anything about the affairs. These questions have now spread to issues of potential national security risks. Another issue is moral hazard: when someone acts recklessly because they know someone else will bear the cost if things go wrong. Assuming individual directors do face penalties for CEO personal misconduct, they have to address the likelihood of incentivizing further misconduct if the CEO is retained, which would further stain their reputation. My research has found that risk to be high. When CEOs are caught engaging in misconduct and the board doesn’t act, it can create a moral-hazard precedent and emboldens the CEO to behave badly again. In fact, when CEOs engage in repeated personal misconduct, the second instance is often even worse than the first. Take former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker, who was the subject of two publicly reported DUI arrests. The second incident, in 2007, attracted considerably more media attention while prompting criticism of the board for allegedly failing to disclose the first incident in 1991. Christopher Kubasik is another example of a second chance gone wrong. He was recently ousted as CEO of defense contractor L3Harris Technologies, more than 14 years after being forced out of Lockheed Martin following allegations of similar personal misconduct involving an inappropriate relationship. In the case of Nvidia, Jensen reportedly lied to company officials about the nature of his intimate relationships for more than a year. From the board’s perspective, if he lied about this, what else has he lied about? And if they let him off the hook, what would he lie about in the future? In reinstating him, the board said it “was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.” Nvidia’s board has come under more scrutiny for its own oversight after it ousted, then reinstated, its CEO, Jensen Huang. Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images A question of culture Broader, often uncomfortable questions about company culture are also at stake. CEO personal misconduct can be a symptom of a larger cultural problem at the company, my research shows. And it’s often associated with other types of corporate misconduct that affect the very operations of a business. In fact, other types of corporate misconduct frequently occur around a similar time frame as the personal misconduct of an executive. Take Dov Charney’s tenure as CEO of American Apparel. During his leadership, the company faced significant accounting problems in 2009-10 that required it to re-audit several years of financial statements. Around the same time, Charney faced multiple allegations of personal misconduct, including sexual harassment, sexual assault, racist remarks and abusive behavior toward employees. It’s in boards’ interest to grasp that personal misconduct can indicate a larger organizational issue – and, as a result, lead to more scrutiny of the board. With Nvidia, for example, there’s now a spotlight on the company’s organizational culture, its financial dealings and its possible role in skirting U.S. sanctions on Chinese chip import restrictions. The board is likely looking at the totality of the issues and not just the personal misconduct. In the runup to Huang’s return to Nvidia, the public debate had largely been centered on what the company might lose without Jensen Huang at the helm. An equally important question, though, is what the company and its board might risk by retaining a CEO whose conduct has raised serious questions about judgment, trust and organizational oversight. The decision to reinstate him suggests that political pressure can interfere with companies’ hiring and firing for misconduct, and that powerful CEOs are above the normal corporate considerations that would lead to dismissal. The Nvidia case might set a precedent, as other CEOs and boards now know the playbook for getting away with misconduct. It’s a board’s duty to protect its organization from managers who go astray, as legendary investor Warren Buffett noted: “It isn’t fundamental dishonesty that causes people to go in a different direction. It’s human nature. There are plenty of people who are really decent people, intelligent people. … But they just don’t come to grips with reality. And boards usually don’t push them to.” This article was updated on Nov. 23, 2026, to reflect Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO. 1ee9f5994a817a2b: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.

Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.

This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll, 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).

But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is, Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer.

You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea.
“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.

The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences.

But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models’ production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “terrible” and “bizarre.” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet.

Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?”

It has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.

Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines. If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place.

Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement.

But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process.
Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

9fe6e27d2189c901: <!--kg-card-end: html--> ARTEX, an open source framework that makes it easy for AI agents to hack companies at superspeed, is causing havoc. People using the tool appear to include Chinese hackers breaking into targets for espionage, and financially-motivated hackers too. Earlier this month, the FBI published a warning to potential targets, and said hackers using ARTEX have targeted government, healthcare, telecommunications, legal, defense, financial services, and semiconductor sectors globally.

ARTEX is written in Go, and all someone needs to do is connect their preferred LLM — from Anthropic, DeepSeek, or whoever — and ARTEX then creates a bunch of agents that are designed to focus on different hacking tasks. There is something qualitatively different about ARTEX when compared to other hacking tools. As the FBI explains, it uses agentic AI to automate much of the hacking process “at machine speed.” This can be reconnaissance — the scoping out of a target to understand their infrastructure — right up to actually hacking a target and stealing their data. An AI agent doesn’t need to sleep, eat, or commute home. ARTEX can complete an entire hack in just a few hours from start to finish, the FBI says. With a tool like ARTEX, a hacker can set up the tool and let it rip. As Google’s threat intelligence arm has noted, hackers are using other similar multi-agent frameworks like CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI too.

Do you know anything else about ARTEX or related breaches? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at joseph@404media.co.

The original author of ARTEX, who goes by Autumn-27 and writes in Chinese, took the tool off of GitHub in October. A message left on their GitHub says, “It has come to my attention that the ARTEX tool has recently been misused by malicious actors to carry out cyberattacks. As the creator of ARTEX, I wish to make the following formal statement.” They go on to say they are not associated with these attacks, that malicious use of the tool runs “entirely counter to my original intent,” and that they are moving ARTEX into a closed-source model and will no longer update it.

362b561c4f5d2c55: The farmer-poet Wendell Berry once described a dystopian world where society is singularly directed toward “the objective” – a relentless drive for industrial extraction that leads to the destruction of nature and communities. The idea captured Berry’s concerns about the industrialization of agriculture and the expansion of natural resource extraction that became prominent across rural America in the latter decades of the 20th century. Over nine decades, Berry watched how agribusinesses’ and farm owners’ pursuit of productive efficiency and maximum profits led to machines and synthetic chemicals replacing human farm labor, and the replacement of diversified farms with monocropping and concentrated animal-feeding operations. Across the U.S., he saw small farms disappear, often consolidated into vast corporate businesses with absent owners. What gets lost in this pursuit of production and profit, he noted, are community, human dignity and flourishing, natural beauty and ecological well-being. People are the heart of rural towns, like Waubeka, Wis. Farm consolidation has shrunk many of America’s rural towns since the mid 1900s. AP Photo/Teresa Crawford As agriculture researchers and rural sociologists, we, like Berry, have seen how the industrialization of agriculture has changed the face of rural America and hollowed out its communities. Once-thriving main streets in rural towns have slowly lost their businesses, with fewer farm-related jobs to keep local residents in the area. Machine dealers and suppliers of farm input such as seeds, fertilizer and pesticides have disappeared. Local grocery stores have been replaced by gas station convenience stores. Schools have shrunk or consolidated with the population decline. Hospitals have closed. This “unsettling of America,” in Berry’s words, shows that the farm economy and the rural economy no longer rise and fall together. Rural communities continue to decline despite farm booms and busts. Losing farming’s rural economy multiplier effect Since the late 1940s, the number of farmers in the U.S. has plummeted by nearly 90%, falling from 5.9 million in 1948 to only 715,000 by 2025. During the same period, the agricultural workforce has shifted from mostly farm owners – about 78% – with a few hired hands in 1948 to one today where most of the work is done by farm laborers, about 68% of the workforce. This means profits from farming mainly flow to a small number of farm owners, while the people doing the farm work are paid much less. The loss of small, owner-operated farms, where a farm family could make a living, is one reason many rural communities have lost population over the past century. In prior eras, farming energized rural communities as money circulated in the rural economy, supporting rural businesses and populations – what is termed a “multiplier effect.” Today, local suppliers and services are harder to find, and farm profits instead flow to owners outside the community. Agriculture today resembles capital-intensive natural resource extraction, like mining, where a small number of very profitable businesses operate most acres in the county. Such farms employ few people at low wages, and profits accrue to distant landlords and investment firms. This shift further reinforces rural decline. The farm economy of the 21st century does little to create additional jobs in rural America. An analysis of 11 counties in Iowa found that every US$1 million of agricultural sales creates 2.4 total farm jobs and 1.6 spin-off jobs in other nonfarm businesses, for a total of four new jobs. By contrast, healthcare creates 10 new jobs and construction creates seven new jobs in all for every $1 million in sales. Both pay good wages, which keeps rural people from leaving and helps rural economies thrive. Both also create more spin-off jobs. In short, agriculture produces profits for the company, whereas healthcare and construction produce good-paying jobs for rural residents. More small farms can help communities thrive In the mid-1940s, the U.S. Senate commissioned two studies on the social impacts of economic concentration and corporate monopolies. In one, Walter Goldschmidt, an anthropologist at the University of California, Berkeley, described two agricultural communities in California, one with a few large farms and the other with numerous smaller farms. He evaluated the social qualities of each and found that the community with more small farms had a higher standard of living and quality of life than the community with a few large farms. The other study, overseen by Columbia sociology professor C. Wright Mills, compared urban manufacturing areas in the Midwest. It found that locations with many small companies had a more robust economic life, with higher socioeconomic well-being, than areas dominated by a few large firms. Many rural sociologists have tested these findings since then. One, a Cornell study led by rural sociologist Thomas Lyson, found a way to counter the effects of farm consolidation. Using U.S. Census of Agriculture and other county-level data, it found that communities with large-scale industrial-style farms that also had politically active populations and a high percentage of people running small, independent businesses tended to have higher levels of social well-being than those without. The effect of economic concentration Looking at the agriculture sector in 2026, it’s clear that policymakers have not listened to the concerns raised by Berry or the rural sociologists. According to the latest Census of Agriculture, America had fewer than 2 million farms in 2022. Fewer than 6% of those farms accounted for over three-quarters of all agricultural production. Farms are getting larger and more specialized. Economist Jim MacDonald documented that half of all cropland in 2017 was on farms with 1,445 acres, more than double the 650 acres in 1987. Half of all dairy farms had more than 1,300 cows in 2017, up from 80 in 1987. Half of all pig farms in 1987 marketed 1,200 pigs or more – the midpoint is currently over 50,000 pigs per year. The number of American farms fell while the size of those farms grew as consolidation became common across the country in the second half of the 20th century. USDA The supply chain is also shrinking, leaving farmers with fewer choices. Today, fewer companies control more of the markets where farmers buy their fertilizers and pesticides or sell their products, which means that farmers have less control over what they can raise or sell. For instance, just two companies accounted for 71.6% of the U.S. corn seed market in 2018-2022, and those same two companies accounted for 65.9% of the soybean seed market, according to USDA researchers. Twenty years earlier, the top two companies in those markets accounted for 47.2% of the corn seed market and 41.8% of the soybean seed market. When four or fewer firms control 40% or more of a market, farmers tend to pay more for seeds, fertilizer and pest control and receive less for their commodities, while consumers continue to face higher prices. Consolidation of land and commodity markets at the farm level often goes unnoticed and sometimes undocumented. University of Iowa economist Silvia Secchi describes how changes in the U.S. Census of Agriculture in 2002 and in 2017 “obfuscates the degree of consolidation” in the farm sector by allowing farms to report up to three or four farm operators. These changes have led to the official count of over 3 million farm operators, even though there are fewer than 2 million farms. By looking at the volume of sales, Secchi found that fewer than half of these 2 million farms produce commodities worth more than $1,000 annually. She contends that this way of counting farmers does a double disservice to small farm operators. First, it lumps disadvantaged farmers into a group that includes retired farmers and farmland owners who might be using their land as a tax write-off. Second, when the overall farm incomes are averaged, the inclusion of these small farmers make the large, high-value farmers appear to need more federal support. How to improve conditions in farm country Restoring the vibrant rural farm economy of the past may be unrealistic, but some policies could at least improve conditions. Devising new – and enforcing existing – antitrust laws to break up oligopolies and monopolies in the materials farms need, such as seeds and fertilizer, as well as in processing and trade could give farmers more choices about what to raise and where to sell it, while protecting consumers from high prices. Irrigated fields stretch for miles in many rural farming regions across the middle of America, including on Colorado’s eastern plains. Jim Wark /Design Pics Editorial/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) Right-to-repair laws could help farmers gain more control over their expensive machinery. Farm subsidies could be directed to smaller farmers who produce food – many of whom were inspired by Berry to become farmers – rather than toward the largest farmers who produce a few commodities at a massive scale. And finally, policymakers can develop rural policies that actually invest in the rural environment and communities, rather than simply subsidizing commodities in ways that primarily benefit the corporate owners of vast areas of farmland. 41496c8a0956b93d: Tech stocks are on a bumpy ride, weighed down by the slump in Nvidia's shares. Liu Yanan/Xinhua via Getty ImagesAfter stock markets, including the tech-heavy NASDAQ, got pummeled on Nov. 20, 2026, many Americans are asking themselves whether the huge bet on artificial intelligence is heading south. While markets rebounded the following Monday, this question still has profound implications for retirement savings, given how much these investment accounts are tied to stocks. Before Monday’s surge, the NASDAQ had plunged about 18% since early October and had lost more than US$4 trillion since Nov. 16. The broad-based S&P 500 also took a beating and had shed all its gains for the year. As a finance professor and certified financial planner, I can’t tell you whether the bubble has truly burst for good. But I can explain how the default model that most 401(k) plans use works, where it protects you, and what you might consider changing. Whether AI stocks recover or not, the steps that protect a retirement account are the same: Know what you own, keep the mix of assets in balance, and hold enough in savings and low-risk funds to cover the years when you’ll need it. Here are some basic facts to guide your planning. Many Americans are saving on autopilot Most 401(k) savers hold a target-date fund, which is named for the year of your “target” retirement and is often chosen as a default option by the employer. To understand how the current stock market volatility affects retirement savings, it’s important to first explain how these funds work. About 55% of U.S. families have a defined contribution retirement account, such as a 401(k) or an individual retirement account. And inside a 401(k), the investing is increasingly done for you. Six in 10 plans administered by the fund giant Vanguard signed workers up automatically in 2025 when they started a new job. And when those plans set a default investment, 98% of savers choose a target-date fund. About 60% of the nearly 5 million savers in those plans held a single target-date fund and nothing else. Taken together, target-date funds now hold $4.8 trillion. Inside each target-date fund is a list of index funds, which are named so because they track a particular market index. Vanguard’s series, the largest, is built mainly from four indices: U.S. stocks, international stocks, U.S. bonds and international bonds. The mix changes the older the saver gets, gradually moving away from high-return, high-risk stocks to safer, lower-yielding bonds. For example, Vanguard’s 2055 fund was just over 91% stocks at the end of September 2026, reflecting the relative youth of those holding it. That share drops to 16% for savers invested in the 2027 fund, who expect to retire imminently. The idea of target-date funds is that you can put your retirement savings on autopilot, with the mix of stocks and bonds getting more conservative the older you get. Brano on Unsplash Tech volatility is forcing new questions That autopilot model is now being tested, starting with Nvidia. In the span of a week, Nvidia went from riding the AI boom to getting mired in crisis. On Nov. 5, after the U.S. midterm elections raised the prospect of new curbs on AI and data centers, Nvidia shares fell more than 9%, while the broad-based S&P 500 index lost 4.4%. Then, on Nov. 12, Nvidia announced that CEO Jensen Huang had resigned. By the end of that week, Nvidia had lost more than $1 trillion in market value within a month. That slide may now be reversed. Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang on Nov. 23, causing its share price to soar. More broadly, it’s too early to say whether the AI bubble is over. Some analysts argue that it’s just losing some air rather than bursting. But amid the turmoil in tech stocks, savers may wonder whether a retirement plan on autopilot should adjust to this fresh volatility. Target-date funds have significant tech exposure Target-date funds are marketed as broadly diversified, often holding thousands of stocks, and financial advisers repeated that point after Huang’s exit. But those stocks aren’t held in equal amounts. Index funds weight companies by market value. So as the value of AI-linked companies soared, their share has grown in the funds most 401(k) savers hold. And that gets to the question of whether there’s a tech bubble riding on overvalued AI companies. By the end of 2025, the 10 largest companies made up nearly 41% of the S&P 500, according to RBC Wealth Management. Yet those 10, almost all of which are in tech and AI, were expected to produce only about 32% of the index’s 2025 earnings. In other words, investors are paying a premium for these shares because they’re expecting great profits later. Bad news can shrink that premium quickly. Savers should also know that a target-date fund dilutes the concentration of AI stocks, but it doesn’t remove them. At the end of September, the 10 largest companies made up 36% of Vanguard’s total U.S. stock fund, with Nvidia at 7%. A 2055 fund keeps about 55% of its money there. So roughly 20 cents of every dollar was riding on 10 companies, and about 4 cents on Nvidia. That means even a small drop in these stocks can have a big impact on your fund, depending on its asset mix. And while diversification hedges against one company’s turmoil, it’s less helpful if there’s a broad repricing of tech stocks. Even in Vanguard’s international fund, the four largest holdings are all tied to chipmaking, led by Taiwan Semiconductor, which makes Nvidia’s chips. Furthermore, diversification doesn’t mean guaranteed protection all the time. In 2008, during the global financial crisis, funds built for people retiring in 2010 lost nearly 24% on average. What to check now if you own a target-date fund In principle, savers don’t need to do anything as long as they choose to stay on autopilot until retirement. Fund managers buy and sell assets to stick to the target mix – a practice known as rebalancing. But rebalancing resets only the broad categories rather than trimming one particular company for growing too large. As Nvidia’s share of the market rose, so did its share of the fund. For people who hold just one target-date fund, I believe the right response to this month’s news is to leave their 401(k) account alone. The fund has been rebalancing all along, and your stake in any one company is modest. When markets are jumpy, savers should review the funds they hold and consider rebalancing toward lower risk if they’re close to retiring. Towfiqu Barbhuiya on Unsplash, CC BY But a saver still needs to check three things. First, consider the year you expect to retire. If you want to move it earlier or later, or want more or less risk, you should choose a fund with a different year. Second, look at what the fund’s share of stocks is today, which is on the fund’s fact sheet. If you’re 60 and your fund is 60% stocks, a 30% fall in stocks would cut your balance by roughly 18%. If that would derail your retirement plans, you can switch to an earlier-dated fund that holds less in stocks and brings less risk. Third, if you have other funds, you should review them. About 1 in 4 target-date investors in Vanguard plans hold other funds. If you add a tech fund or an S&P 500 fund, your account is riskier and more concentrated than the label suggests. What to do if you hold other funds About 31% of savers in Vanguard plans opt out of target-date funds and choose their own investments, perhaps because they find target-date funds too conservative or their fees too costly. For these investors, and for anyone with old 401(k)s and IRAs, there is more to do. Start by looking at the fact sheet for each fund, like this one for Vanguard’s S&P 500 index fund, and compare the top holdings. An S&P 500 index fund, a large-cap growth fund and a technology or Nasdaq-tracking fund look like three investments. But in fact you may own the same handful of companies three times. Next, you should rebalance your holdings according to your plan, not to a prediction. That means returning to the mix of stocks and bonds that you chose in the first place. Trades inside a 401(k) don’t trigger taxes, and many plans offer automatic rebalancing. If yours doesn’t, a simple rule backed by Vanguard research works: review once or twice a year, and rebalance whenever any part of your mix drifts more than about 5 percentage points from your target. Finally, consider broadening the stocks you own. Morningstar Indexes strategist Dan Lefkovitz has pointed to U.S. value stocks, smaller companies and international stocks as areas with less AI exposure. Your plan may offer funds for each. None of these makes you immune to losses, and diversifying can mean trailing the hottest part of the market for years. But the pattern can flip quickly: International stocks gained about 29% in 2025, far ahead of the S&P 500’s 16%. Align your savings to your timeline How much this month’s news matters depends on when you’ll need the money. If you’re decades from retirement, a downturn can work in your favor, because every paycheck contribution buys shares at lower prices. Keep contributing and capture your full employer match. My own research with a colleague has found that accounts on systematic investment plans akin to 401(k)s earned better market-adjusted returns than accounts funded with lump sums. If you’re within 5-10 years of retirement, the bigger danger is what planners call sequence-of-returns risk: A large loss right before or just after you start withdrawing can permanently shrink what your savings can support. A good defense is to hold several years of expected withdrawals in lower-risk assets, such as bonds or money market funds, so you’re never forced to sell stocks after a drop. For retirees, Morningstar’s Christine Benz suggests one to two years of withdrawals in cash and five to eight more in bonds. What not to do The costliest mistake is usually the most tempting: selling everything and waiting for the dust to settle. During the 2008-09 financial crisis, about 117,000 Fidelity 401(k) participants moved entirely out of stocks. Those who stayed out saw their balances grow just 2% by mid-2011, while those who kept some stock exposure saw balances rise 50% on average. Other moves to avoid include stopping your own 401(k) contributions, chasing whatever theme looks safe this month, and pulling money out early, which can mean taxes, penalties and a locked-in loss. Last, don’t hand the decision to a chatbot. It will likely give you sound general guidance, such as diversifying and not panic-selling, and that consensus advice is where AI is reliable. But it is weakest on high-stakes questions that turn on your own situation. cc2adbe7a2fc82f3: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 23 — Oriental Kopi Holdings Bhd is expanding into Cambodia through a franchise agreement, marking its fourth overseas market as the Malaysian café operator seeks to build a regional business supported by recurring royalty income.

The ACE Market-listed group said today its indirect wholly-owned subsidiary, Oriental Coffee International Sdn Bhd, had signed a territory franchise agreement with Indochina Food and Beverage Co Ltd, granting the Cambodian company exclusive rights to develop and operate Oriental Kopi cafés nationwide.
Under the agreement, the first outlet is expected to open in Phnom Penh within 365 days, with expansion into other Cambodian cities to be explored subsequently.

The initial franchise term runs for five years from the opening of the first café and is renewable. Indochina will pay a franchise fee and monthly royalties, although financial terms were not disclosed.

The arrangement allows Oriental Kopi to expand without directly financing or operating the outlets, leaving its local partner responsible for site selection and day-to-day management. Oriental Kopi will supply its branding, recipes, operating systems and staff training while maintaining quality standards.
Cambodia, with a population of about 17 million, offers exposure to a young consumer market and a growing café culture.
The agreement follows Oriental Kopi’s entry into Indonesia and Mauritius in August, through a joint venture with Erajaya Group and a franchise arrangement with Coffee Time Ltd, respectively.
“Cambodia is our fourth overseas market, and the upcoming year will see these markets come on stream,” said managing director Calvin Chan Jian Chern.
He said the group expected its first Jakarta café to open at Central Park Mall by the end of 2026, followed by outlets in Mauritius and Cambodia.
Once operational, the expansion will give Oriental Kopi a presence in five countries, including Malaysia and Singapore.
Founded in 2020, Oriental Kopi currently operates 41 cafés, comprising 38 in Malaysia and three in Singapore. It also sells packaged products, including instant white coffee and kaya.

Oriental Kopi said the Cambodian agreement was unlikely to materially affect earnings per share, gearing or net assets for the financial year ending September 30, 2027, but was “expected to contribute positively to future earnings”.

67ed45b413a769a0: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 23 — Worldwide Holdings Berhad (WHB), through its subsidiary Worldwide TG12 WTE Sdn Bhd, has been recognised for winning second place for the Highest Investment by Local Companies in Selangor for Services Sector (New Projects 2025) category at the Selangor Investors Appreciation Awards 2025.

The recognition, based on investment data compiled by the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (Mida), reflects WHB’s continued commitment to developing critical waste management infrastructure in Selangor, particularly through its investment in the Tanjung Dua Belas Waste-to-Energy (WTE) project.

The award was presented at a ceremony organised by Invest Selangor Berhad at the Kuala Lumpur Convention Centre tonight, attended by Ng Sze Han, Selangor state executive councillor (exco) for investment, trade and mobility, and investors and key industry stakeholders.

The Tanjung Dua Belas WTE project represents WHB’s third WTE plant and another significant milestone in the Group’s efforts to establish a more sustainable, efficient and long-term solution for municipal solid waste management in Selangor. As one of Malaysia’s leading WTE developers, WHB continues to strengthen its capabilities in modern waste treatment and disposal infrastructure, supporting the state’s transition away from conventional landfill dependency towards a more sustainable and resource-efficient waste management system.

Group Chief Executive Officer of Worldwide Holdings Berhad, Ahmad Zaki Ahmad Zainuddin, said the recognition reflects the importance of sustained investment in infrastructure that addresses both present and future needs.

“We are honoured to receive this recognition from the Selangor state government. It is a strong acknowledgement of our continued investment in developing long-term and sustainable waste management solutions for Selangor.

With Tanjung Dua Belas becoming our third Waste-to-Energy plant, we are building on the experience and capabilities developed over the years to strengthen the state’s waste treatment infrastructure and progressively reduce its reliance on conventional landfills.”

“More importantly, this investment is not just about building another facility. It is about putting in place the infrastructure and capacity that Selangor will need for decades to come, while creating greater value from waste through energy generation and resource recovery.”
Ahmad Zaki added that WHB’s expanding WTE portfolio also reflects its ambition to contribute more broadly to the development of Malaysia’s waste management sector.

“Having established our capabilities in Selangor, we are now extending our experience and expertise beyond the state. We see significant opportunities for Waste-to-Energy to become an integral part of Malaysia’s long-term waste management strategy, and Worldwide Holdings is committed to playing a leading role in that transition.”

WHB’s WTE development journey has progressed with the commencement of commercial operations at its first Jeram WTE plant in May 2026. The group is also expanding its footprint beyond the state through the Bukit Payong WTE project in Johor.

The recognition also saw WHB’s joint venture company, Bestari Solar Sdn Bhd, secured the highest investment position in Selangor, further highlighting the group’s contribution to the state’s renewable energy development.
Together, these investments reinforce WHB’s strategic role in supporting Selangor’s sustainable development agenda, while strengthening its position as a key player in Malaysia’s WTE sector.

2ccc08f42a138644: Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.

Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil.

But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.

Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods.

These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it, which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years.

“There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the big questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.”
How it works

There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks.

The resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon.
If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing.

“Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans.

ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations.

But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.
So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone).
“It’s something the Earth has been doing for billions of years,” says Mary Yap, chief executive and cofounder of Lithos Carbon, an ERW startup. “It can scale. We know it works kinetically.”
“If we can figure out where in the world are the best places to do this and then make that happen,” she adds, “it can help both the communities and also help our atmosphere.”

Enhanced rock weathering could be of particular benefit to farmers who haven’t been able to manage their soil acidity, including many subsistence farmers in poorer parts of the world, says Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, a postdoctoral fellow at the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture. One recent study found that ERW boosted the median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%.
“That is huge for subsistence farmers,” he says.
Agricultural limits
But the new findings, which have not yet been peer-reviewed, suggest there could be a steep trade-off, at a certain point, between benefits for farmers and benefits for the climate.

A number of modeling studies that inform UN climate reports and national climate efforts have estimated that adding crushed rock to agricultural land could store away four to 12 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year (though some estimate lower levels). But the authors state in one of the new papers that these findings don’t account for the ways that significant levels of enhanced rock weathering will alter the pH of agricultural soil over time.

Initially it should merely reduce the soil acidity, but adding too much of these materials would eventually push up the pH beyond neutral and into alkaline territory. That could cause micronutrient deficiencies, disease susceptibility, and other problems for certain crops, potentially reducing yields—and, by extension, food supplies and farm revenue. That would likely force farmers to halt the practice, at least until soil pH returns to favorable levels.

The analysis found that preventing the more extreme effects of soil alkalization could limit ERW’s total potential to around 600 million tons of carbon dioxide removal per year, and even that may push pH levels too high for some crops, Kukla says. That’s a fraction of what some models have estimated.

“All of these models are assuming really, really optimistic things about what enhanced weathering can accomplish,” he says. “And when you just layer in the geochemistry that they’re missing, the numbers not only go down but get really uncertain.”
The researchers intend to submit the papers to peer-reviewed journals.
Rising popularity

Companies have been investing more and more money in ERW. In September, Google announced its largest carbon removal deal, as well as the biggest for this method to date: an agreement with the company Terradot to work with rice farmers in southern Brazil to apply enough crushed rock to their fields to draw down a million tons of carbon by 2040. (The deal includes a separate effort to cut methane emissions by draining the flooded paddies.) Google didn’t respond to an inquiry from MIT Technology Review.

Frontier, a coalition of companies that has committed to purchase $1.8 billion of carbon dioxide removal, has dedicated $121 million to prepurchasing 333,000 tons’ worth through enhanced rock weathering. That includes a $57 million deal with Lithos to remove more than 150,000 tons.
Zeke Hausfather, climate research lead at Frontier, says the early data from their deals has demonstrated consistent weathering of rock across hundreds of fields.

He acknowledges there are remaining uncertainties, including how much of the carbon may be released before it’s permanently sequestered in the ocean. But he adds that those and other issues are all the subject of ongoing studies—including some Frontier has backed—by both ERW companies and academic groups.

All told, companies have committed to spending about $670 million on enhanced rock weathering to date, based on an average cost of about $350 per ton, according to CDR.fyi, a public-benefit corporation that provides independent data on the carbon removal sector. A working group of the UN’s climate panel, the European Commission, and other government agencies are also in discussions about the possibility of incorporating ERW into national or regional climate efforts.
Tempered expectations

The new papers add to a growing recognition that enhanced rock weathering is more constrained and “more complicated than we initially thought,” says Rebecca Neumann, who leads a hydro-biogeochemistry research group at the University of Washington but was not involved in the studies.

In April, researchers at CarbonPlan, the nonprofit that led the new studies, raised concerns about an allotment of carbon credits that Lithos received for this method. The startup claimed to have removed 8.3 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year through ERW, but the CarbonPlan team noted that this figure exceeds around 90% of the rates reported in previously published experiments.

CarbonPlan followed up on that report the following month with an analysis finding that modeling of enhanced weathering has often relied on an equation that could inflate the surface area of the crushed rock—and, in turn, overstate the amount of carbon dioxide removal achieved.

Finally, several studies last year highlighted a known but important issue: Magnesium and calcium ions can get trapped in soil for long periods instead of traveling with the bicarbonate into the oceans. That creates a risk that the bicarbonate will simply dissolve back into carbon dioxide and water again, “resulting in no carbon removed,” explained Robert Höglund, cofounder of CDR.fyi, in an online post. Or it may delay the carbon removal by years to decades.
“I’m not saying it doesn’t work,” Höglund said in an interview. “I’m pointing out there’s a lot of uncertainty about what’s permanent and how we should measure it.”

Lithos’s Yap stresses that the high rate of carbon removal the company reported in that instance simply reflected large applications of more finely crushed rock on farms with favorable soil chemistry, adding that the project applied as much as 10 times more per hectare than some of the studies cited in the CarbonPlan post. She also criticized the nonprofit for not contacting the company before posting its results and for publishing them on a blog instead of in peer-reviewed literature.
Kukla says CarbonPlan did account for higher applications of crushed rock in its analysis.

A few additional findings further underscore the complexity and uncertainty surrounding this approach. For example, a more recent preprint suggests that the equation CarbonPlan critiqued does accurately capture the rock surface area in some cases. Meanwhile, other papers have found that the problem of trapped calcium and magnesium ions could be mitigated through location choices and certain land management practices.
Healthy debate
But all this back and forth raises an obvious question: how can commercial deployments of this practice proceed while the scientific debate is still unfolding?

Kevin Sutherland, a carbon removal scientist at Isometric, one of the first carbon registries to develop methods for certifying how much carbon a project draws out of the atmosphere, says the company accounts for these scientific uncertainties by quantifying the climate benefits of ERW conservatively.

“In practice, this means projects receive fewer certificates than our best estimate of the carbon they remove,” he explained in an emailed response. “We would always rather issue too few certificates than too many.”
Despite the recent findings, Neumann says that ERW is still a promising approach for helping farmers and the climate, even if the carbon removal potential is significantly lower than initially hoped.

Yale’s Suhrhoff, who also read over the new findings but was not involved in the research, says that providing a clearer sense of ideal application levels can help the approach catch on. “If we figure out where enhanced rock weathering makes sense agronomically and how much enhanced rock weathering to do to reach agronomic optimal conditions, I think this can actually greatly improve the realistic uptake speed of this technology,” he says.
Kukla himself stresses that none of CarbonPlan’s research suggests enhanced rock weathering doesn’t work or can’t make a meaningful contribution to slowing down climate change.

But it’s important to understand the potential scale, he adds, because the world needs to know how much we can count on any given form of carbon removal—and how hard we’ll need to pull on other climate levers, including the basic job of cutting greenhouse-gas emissions.
“This is all just about calibrating our expectations and grounding them in the science as best as we can,” he says.

cb733f0aea6c2643: Women in Niger face barriers accessing their rights in disputes over land, inheritance, and child custody
Originally published on Global Voices
Nigerien women gathered at an awareness-raising session on the fight against jihadism. Screenshot via France 24's YouTube channel. Fair use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In 2024, Niger had a population of over 27 million. However, according to the Justice Needs and Satisfaction survey (eJNS) conducted by the Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) and the Ministry of Justice, more than half experienced justice problems that year.

Overall, 61 percent of the population has experienced at least one issue accessing justice. And while men are more likely to report these problems (70 percent) than women (52 percent), this does not in any way mean women suffer fewer injustices. Instead, it underscores the fact that many women either do not recognize their challenges as justice problems or do not advocate for themselves. The survey results therefore indicate that while women need justice just as much as men, they face greater obstacles in obtaining it.

Long before reaching any courtroom, women face barriers not only within their families and communities, but also in the resolution of disputes, often over land, inheritance, and child custody. This survey also shows how the outcome of a dispute can ultimately shape a woman’s income, economic security, and ability to invest in her future.
Invisible problems

Within Niger, the gap between men and women’s rights is obvious. As 41 percent of women say they are unaware of their legal rights, women (38 percent) are more likely than men (34 percent) to drop an ongoing court case. What’s more, almost two-thirds (64 percent) of women also have no formal education, compared to 47 percent of men.

Domestic violence (DV) is the most pressing issue faced by women in Niger, far surpassing crime, neighbor conflicts, and land disputes, with 29 percent saying they have experienced some kind of intimate partner violence. Between 2022 and 2024, domestic violence jumped from the eighth most serious problem for the general population to the third. According to HiiL, this may signal a shift in attitude toward reporting such incidents.

Across different datasets, land disputes over field boundaries, inheritance, contested sales, and crop damage rank second (17 percent) behind crime (23 percent) among the most serious justice problems. In its October 2026 report, HiiL also found that land problems accounted for 23 percent of all recorded justice problems, with a severity score of 7.1.

For women in rural areas, where more than 80 percent of Nigeriens currently live, land provides food, income, and economic autonomy. However, traditional practices, family pressures, and systems where people farm land they do not own keep their access uncertain. HiiL thereby conducted a qualitative study in the Dosso and Tillabéri regions, ultimately producing a best-practice manual for justice practitioners.
Inheritance: A silent injustice

Nigerien statutory law grants women the right to own, use, and inherit land. However, in practice, customary and family rules often deny them what is rightfully theirs. In some areas, once married, women are thought to belong to their husbands’ families, precluding them from inheriting land from their birth families.

In its 2025 Annual Report, HiiL shares real-life stories, such as Saouda’s, exemplifying this reality. Widow and mother of five, Saouda lost access to her late husband’s land when his relatives claimed ownership, but successfully regained it after learning about her rights through an awareness-raising campaign.

This exclusion has a direct economic impact on those women. They not only lose inherited land, but also a source of income, food security, and the ability to invest in livestock, trade, or farm improvements.
Child custody

After a separation, divorce, or the death of a partner, family-made agreements often determine where the children live, who provides for them, and whether their mother can maintain a meaningful relationship with them. These decisions are often made out of court, where customary norms hold considerable sway.

In its report, HiiL highlighted this issue through Amina’s story. Detained following a custody battle over her children, Amina thought her only hope was her family. After being told she could not legally win custody after a divorce under Islam, she had no idea she had such rights.
In this region, customary rulings tend to favor male authority in family matters, with customary chiefs typically awarding custody to fathers on religious grounds.

In 2020, the General Report of the National Consultation on Justice found that women were underrepresented in the judiciary, accounting for just 39 of the 399 magistrates in late 2017. Although customary court hearings may be more welcoming for women, no women sit among the customary assessors, prompting the report to recommend their inclusion.
The social norm burden

For almost a third of women, preserving family relations is the main reason they do not turn to courts or customary authorities. Any woman who claims her share of inheritance or custody of her children could be seen as “causing problems” or dividing her family. Consequently, testimonies gathered across the country tell stories of women fearing they will damage their families’ honor and relatives advising them to stay silent, at the expense of their rights.

Economic constraints only add to their difficulties. Due to insufficient funds, about four percent of women say they did not take action even when they knew their rights were being violated. Financial dependence on their partner or family also limits their ability to pursue legal proceedings. Quoting an NGO official, HiiL shared:
Les femmes viennent souvent nous voir après avoir épuisé leurs maigres ressources. Elles sont alors coincées, incapables de poursuivre leurs quêtes de recherche de solution à leurs problèmes.
Caught in a bind and unable to pursue their search for solutions, women often come to us after exhausting their already limited resources.

About a quarter of women with justice problems choose not to act, believing that legal action will not lead to a fair outcome. Zara, a 25-year-old Nigerien woman unable to afford legal fees and forced to drop a domestic violence case, stated:

Même si je préfère aller devant le juge je ne pourrai pas car je n’ai pas les moyens. Je ne suis qu’une vendeuse d’eau fraîche et de Bissap, même si je sais que je peux aller devant le juge si mon mari ne me nourrit pas, je n’ai pas de quoi supporter les aller-retours et autres frais qu’on demande à la justice.

Even though I would prefer to take my case to court, I can’t afford it. I only sell chilled water and bissap [herbal drink]. While I may be entitled to go to court if my husband didn’t support me, I couldn’t afford the round trips and other legal fees.

Even when women know about their rights, they still tend to choose customary justice over formal justice. Although it is often biased and patriarchal, it is also faster, closer to home, and delivered in their native language. As such, 40 percent of women identify family as a source of support, compared to just 28 percent of men. Meanwhile, only four percent of women and six percent of men turn to formal courts.

According to data published in the daily newspaper Le Sahel in 2024, men (75 percent) take legal action more often than women (71 percent). While this gap may be modest, it nonetheless compounds other obstacles.
Solutions exist

Typically, Nigeriens will seek out informal pathways to settle disputes. In the 2024 Justice Needs and Satisfaction survey, direct negotiation (40 percent), family (33 percent), and customary or traditional authorities (24 percent) were the most commonly cited sources of help, far surpassing formal courts (five percent). HiiL subsequently recommended including these actors in the justice process by conferring full legal status on customary decisions or strengthening mediation and conciliation pathways.

Established under Law No. 2011-42, the National Agency for Legal and Judicial Assistance (ANAJJ) provides free consultations, information on rights, guidance, and legal aid for those in financial need. According to the 2025 statistics, 33,394 beneficiaries received legal assistance, including 8,489 women. Meanwhile, its regional offices awarded 3,747 legal aid grants, including 550 to women.

In December 2025, during the first National Week of Legal and Judicial Assistance for women and children, Minister of Justice Alio Daouda presented different figures. Such discrepancies — at odds with independent NGO and journalistic findings — mean that official administrative reports must be read with caution.

The ANAJJ covers all of the country’s eight regions, but leaves many rural areas underserved. That said, additional initiatives do exist, including those led by the Association of Women Lawyers of Niger, an organization that has offered women and children legal assistance for 35 years.

However, resolution remains a stumbling block. According to the 2024 Justice Needs and Satisfaction survey, 56 percent of justice problems remain unresolved, with 20 percent on hold and 36 percent dropped. Conversely, 72 percent of solutions achieved are considered fair. While taking action significantly improves the chance of resolution, the main challenge is no longer just access itself, but seeing cases through to their conclusion.
Justice for women

The issue is not just the existence of courts, but ensuring women know they have rights, understand how to enforce them, and can do so without fear of rejection from their family or community. Awareness of their rights should go hand in hand with the ability to exercise them and the support of religious and traditional leaders alike.

In rural areas, practical steps are being taken to make this a reality. Traditional, female, and religious leaders have all received training in women’s land rights. After a female leader called for access to a plot of land for her group, the village chief publicly committed to finding one. Radio and theater, in local languages, have also enabled some women to claim their rights. According to HiiL, the objective is not only to recognize their rights in legislation, but to create practical conditions for exercising them.

Achieving justice that truly meets Nigerien women’s needs requires several steps: legal information in local languages, legal clinics in rural areas, training for traditional and religious authorities, protection for women’s inheritance, support in land and family disputes, and the inclusion of women among customary assessors.

As long as land, inheritance, and child custody decisions are made behind closed doors, with no guarantee of fairness, a considerable number of Nigerien women will continue to lose not only their assets but also a significant proportion of their economic independence.
Written (Français) by Jean Sovon
