8f13969a68ed3f91: Having agreed to new peace talks with Ukrainian and American representatives earlier this month, Russian negotiators suddenly wanted to discuss the European security order, too.
It was an obvious attempt to divert attention from the urgent need, after almost five years, for a ceasefire in Russian president Vladimir Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine.
While the inept US negotiating duo of Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff seemed to go along with the Russian proposal, the Europeans saw right through it.
They pointed out that there is already an agreed European security order, to which Russia is a signatory. The only problem is that Russia is blatantly violating it. That is what must be discussed.

The European security order is basically no different from what the United Nations Charter established in 1945. Coming after two bitter, brutal world wars, the UN Charter codified the territorial integrity of all states, and identified the crime of aggression as the ultimate violation of international law.

But the European order that gradually emerged towards the end of the Cold War went further than this. Through the laborious negotiations leading up to the Helsinki Accords in 1975, and through the process that produced the Paris Charter of 1990, Europeans added provisions on democracy, human rights, and economic cooperation to the basic security architecture.

Of course, there were occasional disagreements about how to implement these agreements’ requirements, and in both Georgia and Moldova in the 2000s, Russia openly violated provisions barring the presence of a country’s armed forces on the territory of another without its consent.

These moves sparked bitter debates, with Russia eventually calling for revisions to the European security order. The Kremlin, for obvious reasons, objected to the provisions concerning human rights and elections, and demanded that they be deleted or substantially diluted.

It wasn’t difficult to see why. A series of “colour revolutions” had started to sweep through the region, most notably in Georgia and Ukraine, where protesters demanded democratic reforms, the rule of law, and closer links with democratic Europe.
Upon returning to the presidency after a brief stint as prime minister to circumvent constitutional limits, Putin himself was confronted with huge demonstrations in Moscow.

With a democratic wave sweeping much of the world at the time, the Kremlin understood that the colour revolutions in other countries had inspired pro-democracy demonstrations on its own streets. More to the point, it knew that pro-democratic forces could count on moral support from the West.

Russia tried to force new negotiations to suppress previously agreed commitments on democracy, but no one else would support such an effort. The order that had been established at the summits in Helsinki and Paris stood firm.

More recently, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov has called attention to a provision from a 1999 Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe document, which holds that signatories “will not strengthen their security at the expense of the security of other states”.

Yet he completely ignores another provision from the same document, which reaffirms “the inherent right of each and every participating state to be free to choose or change its security arrangements, including treaties of alliance”.
Such cynical cherry picking is dishonest even by Lavrov’s standards. Membership in Nato or the European Union clearly preserves peace and in no way threatens Russia.

Democratisation in other countries may well inspire those seeking democratic change inside Russia, but that is not the democratising countries’ fault or problem, nor does it endanger Russia’s security.
Putin is now left trying to roll back various European countries’ security choices, and thus their sovereignty. This is obviously a non-starter.

Finland and Sweden chose to enter Nato not to attack Russia, but because Russia had just launched a full-scale invasion of another European neighbour. No sane person is under any illusion about cause and effect.

One hopes that at some point there will be an opening to return to confidence-building and arms-control measures. But with Russian guns blazing and Russian bombs falling over another European country’s civilian centres, now is obviously not the time.

The European security order’s foundational principle is to reject aggression and respect other countries’ territorial integrity. There is no need to revise that order, only to wait for a Russian regime that is willing to accept it.
In the next round of talks, European representatives will demand an immediate end to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. Until that happens, there is nothing else to talk about.
Carl Bildt is a former prime minister and foreign minister of Sweden.

dc93da4cf6a361d8: Over 223,700 children have dropped out of school in Cameroon’s Northwest and Southwest regions, while 2,463 schools are non-operational
Originally published on Global Voices
A general view of Buea's OIC Market in the Southwest Region of Cameroon, where displaced families sell goods to support their livelihoods. Photo by Cynthia Ebot Takang. Used with permission.

For children displaced by Cameroon’s ongoing armed Anglophone conflict, reaching safety has not ended the struggle. In Buea, the capital of Cameroon’s Southwest region, some children are balancing school with market trading to help their families survive.

“At least here in Buea, there are no gunshots, and we do not have to hide in the bush,” says 11-year-old Lorane in an interview with Global Voices, describing the relative safety his family found after fleeing their home in Cameroon’s conflict-affected Southwest Region.

The move brought the children to a calmer environment where they could resume schooling and live with less fear of armed violence. But leaving their communities also meant losing homes, familiar surroundings, friendships and, for some, years of education. In Buea, the struggle to rebuild family livelihoods has introduced another responsibility to their lives: helping their parents earn a living.
A safer place, but a childhood reshaped by displacement

The Anglophone crisis in Cameroon began in 2016, when teachers and lawyers began protesting over the perceived marginalization of English-language education and common-law systems, which they say favored French. This escalated into wider demonstrations and a government crackdown. In 2017, the situation deteriorated into armed conflict between government forces and separatist groups seeking independence for the two English-speaking regions as a state commonly referred to as Ambazonia. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) estimates that between 2.1 and 2.2 million people have been displaced due to the violence and insecurity.

At Buea’s OIC Market, children from displaced families sell bleach, puff-puff, plantains, ginger, garlic, and oranges, particularly during weekends and before school. Some travel from neighboring communities to help their parents sell goods, while others work around family-owned stalls.

For 14-year-old Joy, this means traveling from Mutengene to Buea on weekends to sell sachets of bleach. Her mother buys the bleach in bulk and repackages it into smaller sachets, which Joy sells for CFA 100 (about USD 0.17) each. She says daily sales can reach CFA 10,000–15,000 (about USD 16.81–25.21), helping support the household and her siblings.

Joy has been working since her family fled their village when she was in Class Five. “They were shooting guns in my village, so my mum had to bring us here so we could continue school,” she says. She has since become used to the routine, which allows her to contribute to the family while continuing her education.

For 14-year-old Sidoine, displacement meant losing four years of schooling. Her family fled Ekona after their house was burned while they were away at the farm. She remembers hiding in the bushes when they heard attacks were coming, unsure what would happen next. Her family eventually left their hometown, Ekona, for Buea, joining thousands of others who have had to rebuild their lives away from their roots. A well-wisher eventually helped her enroll in school in Buea.
Although the family sometimes visits their farm to collect food, it has not been possible to return permanently. Sidoine misses her former home and friends.
Rebuilding a family livelihood

For younger children, displacement has also changed family routines. Twelve-year-old Michelle sells plantains while waiting for his mother to return from church. His 11-year-old cousin, Lorane, sometimes accompanies him. The two help their parents attract customers, particularly on weekends.
They also miss people they left behind in Ekona, including their grandmother, who died during a raid as a result of the crisis.

Susan Achuagoh, a mother of five whose house was burned during the conflict, has had to rebuild her livelihood as an orange seller in Buea. She gives her children small quantities of oranges to sell while she remains at her stall. This helps supplement their family income.
“I sell oranges; I give them small things to walk around with while I stay at the stall,” she shared in an interview with Global Voices. “If they do not help like that, it will not go at all.”

Her children’s education was interrupted for more than three years during the conflict. Another mother, Mami Blessing, says her children’s schooling was also disrupted and that they now help her at the market as the family struggles to make ends meet.
The cost of conflict

Godiva Ndang epse Limene, Education and Partnerships Officer at Street Child UK-Cameroon, says the prolonged crisis in the Northwest and Southwest has increasingly become a crisis of childhood, affecting education, protection, and development.

Children exposed to armed violence, displacement, and repeated insecurity may experience anxiety, difficulty concentrating, and social withdrawal. Taking on economic responsibilities can add to these pressures. Ndang says work that takes up time needed for learning, rest, and play can affect children’s cognitive, emotional, social, and physical development.

She stresses that helping in a family business is not automatically child labor. The distinction depends on the child’s age, the nature and duration of the activity, the risks involved, and whether it interferes with education, health, rest, or development.

The right to education is only one of the rights affected. Children also have a right to rest, leisure, and play, as well as protection from economic exploitation. For those uprooted from their communities, maintaining friendships, participating in cultural life, and developing a sense of belonging are also important parts of growing up.
Learning spaces offer a route back to education

The scale of the disruption remains significant. Figures from the Regional Delegations of Basic Education cited by UNICEF in September 2026 show that 223,749 children were completely out of school in the Northwest and Southwest, while 2,463 schools were non-operational. Of these, 2,005 were in the Northwest and 458 in the Southwest.

To educate children in conflict-affected communities, local partners including TeenAlive, the Foundation for Inclusive Education (FIED), Strategic Humanitarian Services (SHUMAS), and the Authentique Memorial Empowerment Foundation (AMEF) support Mobile Neighborhood Learning Corners and Satellite Learning Corners. These are established in accessible locations such as village chiefs’ homes, churches, schools, and community verandas.

The program has supported close to 100 learning corners across the two regions. Other education interventions include help with school enrollment, uniforms, and learning materials, as well as Teaching at the Right Level, a tutoring program.

Street Child also combines education with other forms of support. Its girls’ resilience and empowerment work provides displaced adolescent girls with life skills, literacy, and vocational training, alongside start-up kits and mental health assistance. Its Play for Peace initiative, supported by the FIFA Foundation, uses sports to promote peace, health, and education in conflict-affected communities.

Ndang says children also need psychosocial support, safe learning environments, and opportunities to play and interact with their peers. She adds that helping caregivers rebuild their livelihoods matters because reducing economic pressure on families can lessen the burden on children.
Ambition despite displacement
Despite interruptions to their education and the responsibilities they have taken on, the children interviewed for this story continue to speak about their goals and ambitions.

Eliot, 14, who helps his mother sell oranges on weekends, wants to become an engineer. Sidoine hopes to study law, although she worries about the years she lost in school. Vickians, 12, who fled Lebialem and now studies computer science, wants to become a computer engineer.
On weekends, Vickians sells miondo, a cassava-based delicacy, with her parents. Her family continues to make sacrifices to keep her in school, and she remains determined to pursue her education.

At the start of the 2026–2027 academic year, Southwest Governor Bernard Okalia Bilai said the authorities wanted children across the region to have equal access to education and learning facilities, despite differences in school attendance between urban and rural communities. His remarks, reported in this September 2026 interview on the reopening of schools, underline the challenge facing the region: ensuring that displacement and insecurity do not determine whether children can access education.

Reporting note: The names used for the children in this story are pseudonyms to protect their identities. No photographs of the children have been published. Consent was obtained from parents before the interviews were conducted.

ce467387ca06079a: From Jonathan Edward
The narrative surrounding Chinese industrial overcapacity is being used as a convenient scapegoat for domestic economic stagnation.

The recent comment by Mazli Noor, China’s overcapacity, a test of Malaysia’s resilience, exemplifies this point by suggesting that Malaysia must erect trade barriers, tighten anti-dumping regimes, and mandate local content rules to shield domestic producers from Chinese imports misses the fundamental mechanics of global trade.
If Malaysia wishes to thrive, it must either compete on the same terms through aggressive state-backed industrial policy or pivot towards producing different, higher-value goods and services.
Attempting to insulate uncompetitive industries behind regulatory walls is not a strategy for resilience, but a guarantee for economic obsolescence.
'Overcapacity' is a politically loaded talking point
The very term "overcapacity" is a politically loaded construct designed to frame superior manufacturing efficiency as a market distortion.

In April 2024, former US Treasury secretary Janet Yellen warned that Chinese industrial overcapacity threatened global markets and Western workers - a claim China rejected, crediting its export success to market forces, scale, and supply chain integration rather than unfair manipulation.

State support has undeniably played a major role in China's industrial ascent, yet there is nothing stopping Malaysia from adopting similar measures if it genuinely wishes to dominate heavy industries like crude steel.
If replicating China’s state-capitalist model is neither fiscally practical nor politically desirable for Putrajaya, then market forces must be allowed to dictate the outcome.
The failure of domestic protectionism

Malaysia already knows the consequences of coddling legacy industries. For decades, protectionist policies and selective state support have benefitted a handful of well-connected conglomerates without translating into broader economic dynamism.
Instead, these sheltered entities have repeatedly devolved into sluggish, uncompetitive monopolies that pass higher costs onto Malaysian consumers and downstream businesses.

It is an uncontroversial local reality that shielding domestic firms from foreign competition removes the very pressure required to innovate. Calling for anti-dumping duties and stricter customs hurdles will merely entrench inefficiency while penalising every Malaysian household and manufacturer that relies on affordable inputs.
Moving up the manufacturing value chain

Trying to compete head-to-head with the world’s largest manufacturing powerhouse on basic commodities like crude steel or bulk plastics is economic suicide. Rather than lamenting low capacity utilisation in legacy blast furnaces, Malaysia must upskill and upgrade its industrial base.

Modern manufacturing technologies, such as precision computer numerical control (CNC) machining, industrial 3D printing, and advanced metallurgy, allow smaller, agile firms to produce specialised components and bespoke widgets made from exotic materials.

Instead of churning out raw base stock, Malaysian manufacturers should be supplying precision-engineered parts for global aerospace, medical devices, and specialised equipment for the regional oil and gas sector.
Unlocking agriculture, aquaculture, and services

Malaysia’s economic future does not depend on matching China factory for factory when vast domestic sectors remain chronically underutilised. Consider agriculture and aquaculture, both of which possess immense export potential. For years, prime agricultural land has been squandered on speculative property developments that sit unsold, or cleared under questionable pretexts for logging.

Meanwhile, our rivers suffer from heavy sedimentation caused by upstream deforestation, alongside rampant chemical pollution and garbage dumping. Properly managed, Malaysia’s waterways could anchor a lucrative freshwater aquaculture export industry.

Malaysians are an inventive and entrepreneurial people. We have even successfully bred sturgeon in tropical conditions to produce luxury caviar. Imagine what could be achieved if environmental stewardship and agricultural land reform were treated as national priorities.

Similarly, Malaysia holds substantial natural advantages in high-value services. With a multilingual workforce and established legal and financial frameworks, the nation is well-positioned to expand aggressively into regional tech support, fintech, cross-border legal services, and financial advisory. Competing in brainpower and service delivery bypasses the physical scale advantages of Chinese manufacturing entirely.
Geopolitical hypocrisy and trade realities

Singling out China for its industrial might also ignores the broader geopolitical reality facing Southeast Asia. The US has swung towards unpredictable unilateralism, weaponising tariffs and imposing sweeping restrictions on artificial intelligence chips and advanced technologies. Its actions in the Middle East have kicked off the energy crisis the whole world is reeling from.

At the same time, the European Union is grappling with severe deindustrialisation and has become an increasingly cumbersome trade partner, imposing stringent regulatory barriers that directly threaten Malaysia’s environmental sovereignty and palm oil exports.

Why, then, should Malaysia lecture China for being a cost-effective manufacturer and a vital trading partner when we do not publicly chastise the US for its tech blockades or the European Union for its protectionist green mandates? Criticising the one major power that still possesses the capacity to produce at scale and low cost while offering a massive consumer market for Malaysian exports defies basic economic logic.
Adaptability over obstruction

Complaining about how well-resourced the competition happens to be reflects a defeatist mindset. True progress comes from pulling oneself up, not attempting to drag a competitor down. If Malaysia wants to empower local industry, it should immediately deregulate sectors where bureaucratic red tape suffocates enterprise, slash corporate and manufacturing taxes, and provide agile firms with the land, energy, and capital needed to scale.
Trying to restrain China’s industrial output is an exercise in futility, and attempting to freeze market dynamics is like trying to stop time itself.

Global manufacturing is constantly in motion. When a dominant power shifts its focus towards new frontiers, nimble competitors step in to fill the vacated space. Malaysian manufacturers must embrace this reality, pivot away from lost battles in heavy commodities, and capture the specialised, high-value niches where they can genuinely win.
Jonathan Edward is a media practitioner and an FMT reader.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that dive-bombed our ancestors, brightened the sky, recalled an old tune, and got hosed by marine mucus.

First, scientists discover that eagles are hunting large baboons, hinting that early human relatives once sated ancient avian appetites. Then: star-on-star contact, a musical memory lane, and the secrets of cetacean snot.
As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files.
Eagle-eyeing you…for dinner!
Hobaiter, Catherine et al. “Signs of Eagle Predation on a 22-kg Adult Primate.” American Journal of Biological Anthropology.
Death came from the sky for early humans, according to a new study that suggests giant eagles preyed on our ancestors far more recently than was previously known.

Birds of prey (raptors) have hunted primates for at least 20 million years, including early human relatives, known as hominins. For example, a hominin toddler known as the “Taung child” shows signs of being killed by a raptor roughly 2.5 million years ago. But scientists have assumed that hominins outgrew their status as bird bites since that time, and there are no reports of raptors preying on primates that weigh over 28 pounds on record—until now.

In 2025, scientists discovered that Verreaux’s eagles—one of the largest eagle species in the world—at Ennedi Plateau in Chad are likely hunting adult olive baboons weighing up to 57 pounds. The team found baboon remains among the region’s sandstone cliffs that show signature marks of eagle predation, such as talon punctures on the skull and scrapes to the shoulder bones.

“We cannot definitively rule out scavenging activity, but the severity of punctures is suggestive of lethal interactions through a killing grip,” said researchers led by Catherine Hobaiter of the University of St. Andrews. The team also observed the baboons rapidly retreat when eagles approached, suggesting that they feared aerial attacks.

Some researchers have argued against the “raptor-mediated predation” of the Taung child on the grounds that the hominin would have been too heavy for a bird. The study’s authors get extra points for including a quote from the comedy Monty Python and the Holy Grail on this point: “It is a simple question of weight ratios. A five-ounce bird could not carry a 1-pound coconut.” IYKYK.

However, the laughs stop there, as the team refutes this idea by recounting the grisly “low flight with sustained grip attack” that eagles perform on ungulates, such as antelopes or cattle, which reveal that raptors can kill animals that are many times their own weight with the right approach.

“Briefly, an eagle will land on the back or neck of a moderately large ungulate, gripping it firmly with its talons. If the prey withstands knocking to the ground, the eagle will ride it with wings outstretched and flapping to maintain balance until the quarry collapses, either from exhaustion, shock, or internal injury. A similar tactic is described in the extraordinary report of a Harpy eagle (Harpia harpyja) attacking a 52-kg adult woman.”

Wow, new fear unlocked! Imagine being an early hominin, minding your own business banging rocks together or something, when suddenly a giant bird of prey either pushes you off a cliff or rides you to death. For everyone preparing to eat a huge bird for Thanksgiving next week, be grateful that it’s no longer the other way around.
In other news…
A union made in heaven
Karambelkar, Viraj et al. “An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion.” Nature.
Speaking of unwieldy meals, scientists have captured an unprecedented glimpse of a star eating another star, thereby forming a new mega-star.

Over the past few years, scientists noticed that something weird has been unfolding in a binary star system called AT 2025abao—nicknamed “Bao” (yum!)—in the outskirts of the Andromeda galaxy, which is about 2.5 million light years away from the Milky Way. One of the stars, “Big Bao,” was expanding into its dying red giant phase, which pulled its companion, “Little Bao,” into a deadly spiral. Last year, the system rapidly brightened, signaling that Big Bao had swallowed Little Bao.

“In October 2025, the star underwent a dramatic eruption” and exhibited “a sudden increase in its photospheric temperature to about 8,000 K,” said researchers led by Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University. The system “shows the defining hallmarks of luminous red novae, a class of transients established to arise from impulsive energy injection…during the merger of a star with its companion.”
“This inspiral in such a system has never been observed directly,” the team noted.
Congratulations to the newly-fed couple! Long may Bao shine.
Girl, put your records on / but don’t think you own that song
Turnbull, Cara et al. “Music illuminates sociocultural dimensions of autobiographical memory.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

We’ve all had that feeling of hearing a familiar song and being transported to a specific time and place in our lives. But as it turns out, the recollections stirred by those cherished songs are probably not all that special, according to a new study that surveyed 233 undergraduate students about these so-called “music-evoked autobiographical memories.”

The students (aged 18-23) listened to clips of 32 popular songs grouped into two categories: “new” songs released from 2014 to 2019, during their adolescence, and “old” songs released from 1985 to 1995, before they were born. When asked to reminisce about the songs, students with similar backgrounds were remarkably aligned in their answers.

“Memories evoked by country songs were more strongly associated with very recent time periods (college) and themes relating to family, driving, summertime, romantic partners, and listening to music (particularly music selected by someone else),” said researchers led by Cara Turnbull of Texas Tech University.

“Alternatively, memories evoked by hip-hop songs were most often associated with friends, acquaintances (such as classmates, coworkers, and teammates), dancing, and being at school, while those evoked by pop songs were most associated with middle school, listening at home or by oneself, and singing along,” the team added.

As an elder millennial, it was humbling to realize what counts as an “oldie” these days. I also felt my generation’s soundtrack was done dirty by offerings like “Achy Breaky Heart” by Billy Ray Cyrus or “Whoomp! There it is” by Tag Team. No Stevie Nicks? Madonna? Wu Tang? All I ask of future generations is that you do not judge us solely by the croonings of C+C Music Factory and Bryan Adams, I beg you.
Thar she blows (DNA)!
O’Mahony, Éadin et al. “Breath to Genome: Whole Genome Sequencing of Large Whales From Blow Sampling.” Molecular Ecology Resources.

Join hands, dear friends, for we are about to run directly through majestic fountains of whale snot. Scientists who flew drones through whale “blow”—the mucus-filled vapor exhaled by whales through their blowholes—have successfully sequenced whole genomes from the snotty samples, representing “a major step towards non-invasive cetacean sampling,” according to a new study.

“Preserving biodiversity requires the genetic monitoring of wild populations, which is traditionally done through invasive sampling techniques for DNA collection,” said researchers led by Éadin O’Mahony of the University of St. Andrews. “However, this approach can impact animal welfare or be impossible to implement due to behavioural responses to anthropogenic factors or national/international legislation.”

Indeed, I think that we can all agree that humans have stressed whales out enough as it is. Instead of invasive biopsies of skin and flesh with darts or scrapers, O’Mahony and his colleagues equipped drones with petri dishes and flew them through a total of 58 blows from 26 Northeast Pacific humpback whales in the Gitga'at First Nation territory of northern British Columbia.

The team “established that a whole humpback whale genome can be recovered from exhaled respiratory vapour (‘blow’), marking a significant methodological advancement in non-invasive cetacean genomics.”
While it’s not the kind of blow most people associate with breathing orifices, it just might be what we need to study whales without hassling them.
Thanks for reading! See you next week.
Corrected: A previous version of this story erroneously used "miles" in place of "light years."

4d98effdc3566e59: The dominant Nepali food narrative overlooks the diverse regional histories and culinary traditions of Indigenous communities
Originally published on Global Voices
Timu khole, wild mushroom soup. Photo by Binti Gurung. Used with permission.

Food enriches our soul. It makes us who we are. However, the emergence of cosmopolitanism and global and local food politics has sidelined Indigenous food, not to mention the traditions and rituals associated with them.

“Over the last decades, ever since the country was opened up to the outside world in the 1950s, in search of a national food identity, the staple daal bhaat, a nutrient-dense combination of lentils and rice accompanied by vegetables, has been elevated to Nepal’s national dish,” writes Binti Gurung, a food historian and founder of Natural Roots Foundation, an organization dedicated to documenting, preserving, and promoting Indigenous Himalayan food heritage, traditional recipes, and local knowledge in Nepal. “The national food narrative that is being set completely obscures the varied regional histories and food practices of the Indigenous peoples.”
The Foundation, established in 2017, promotes the many varieties of food that have become neglected in Nepal, especially the plants and herbs that can be foraged in the forests and mountains.

Working with Aama Samuha, a collective of women’s groups set up to maintain cultural traditions and support communal activities in Nepali villages, she has been documenting and archiving the food knowledge primarily held by Indigenous women in Nepal.

The Lekhali Cookbook, authored by Gurung, draws its name from lekh, the high ridges in Nepal, and highlights the rich food tradition shared by women’s groups from Nepal’s Mustang, Manang, Lamjung, and Gorkha districts.
Sanjib Chaudhary of Global Voices caught up with Binti Gurung to talk about her work on food heritage. The interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Sanjib Chaudhary (SC): Can you introduce yourself and tell us a bit about your work?

Binti Gurung (BG): Before talking about the food heritage of Nepal, it’s necessary to mention that knowing the broader political and historical context of the country is important because a lot of what my work looks into connects with understanding of the past.

The pivotal moment can be attributed to the 1950s, when the absolutist regime came to an end. As a country, Nepal had remained closed off to the outside world for so long that very little was understood about Nepali society, particularly its food practices.

Within this environment of reaching out to the past events that happened in this land, uncovering the stories of the people, and mainly breaking down and deconstructing the idea of “Nepali-ness,” lies the understanding of our food heritage.

I myself come from what used to be called a Gurung country until the 1970s. I know something about our collective history as Gurung people, and that my great-grandfather on the maternal side was a mukhiya, a tribal chief somewhere in that Gurung country. There are no written documents about our lineage, apart from the knowledge that remains in the tongue. I take pride in that, but it also means some knowledge has not been transmitted.

My paternal grandfather was the first person to be educated because of his connection to British India, after which he did a lot in his village, which included donating some of his personal land to the village school. Whereas I am the first in my family to go to university, learn English (like the rest of my generation), and read history.
SC: Food sovereignty is a burning issue for Indigenous peoples. Can you give us an overview of what challenges Indigenous communities in Nepal are facing with regard to food sovereignty?

BG: Even though the constitution of 2015 has given recognition to the right to food, how does it translate to the many Indigenous groups accessing their food? Are the Indigenous peoples who have been living by the rivers and the forests able to access the foods that they have learned to process, collect, and eat?

For the communities that still live in or near the forest, how are their relationships affected when forests are turned into national parks? Do the Indigenous peoples who have been relying on these ancestral food practices have access? Can the state recognize and permit it?
When we start to think this way, we go beyond the conversation about food sovereignty because then we have to talk about the land and the peoples who inhabit it, and their connection to it.
The author in conversation with women's group members. Photo via Binti Gurung. Used with permission.

SC: Nepal is a multi-ethnic country, and communities have their own food and agriculture systems. However, food politics is prevalent, with some communities claiming a particular dish as solely theirs. What’s your take on this?

BG: I think it is impossible to claim any particular dish as solely belonging to only one community. After all, we live in a shared world. We are beings in constant interaction with the land. Like any living practice that is evolving, our food practices are also in motion; it is not a static, fixed thing.

What may be helpful is to think about how a dish or food practice evolved. Or even to try to understand how it has evolved the way it has, including the factors of influence. Even though we think of Nepali communities having their own food systems, if we look underneath somewhere, we can find some similar practices.

One example is the way food is harvested from the forest; this particular practice, whether in the high mountains, hills, or the Terai, remains similar. Of course, how this practice is treated by those not practicing is an entirely different thing.

SC: It’s high time we promote Indigenous food in a global space. Can you tell us about your recent book “The Lekhali Cookbook: Indigenous Food Heritage from the Highlands of Nepal” and the dishes you’d like to share with a wider audience?

BG: This book has been in the making for a very long time. When I started doing this work in 2017, at some point it felt very urgent to understand the issues around it, and gradually it became important to start documenting in a written way because a lot had been unknown.
The cover of The Lekhali Cookbook. Photo by Sanjib Chaudhary. Used with permission.

There may be many factors why the conversation around food heritage has remained so obscure, but one that I attribute strongly to is our own political history that has shaped the Indigenous experiences.

For many Indigenous communities, the problem has also been due to others writing about their history. Of course, there are some very rare scholars who have done a fine job, but in the case of our own history, there is now an immense effort to establish or re-establish our origin account. It’s very saddening to have to read about some of these accounts. And then there is also the process of verifying and fact-checking, and that takes a lot of time.

The Lekhali Cookbook came into being due to a generous grant from the British Council. A lot of the work had been conducted prior to receiving the grant, but it allowed us to visit the villages in the central Himalayas and work with aama samuha [translated as “mothers’ groups,” acting as local women’s collectives] who are heavily involved in the food production process. Based on the consultation with the groups, we collected the recipes of the eight villages of Lamjung, Manang, Mustang, and Gorkha.

In the book, we have some unique recipes that many people do not know, such as the foraged panyu (wild rhubarb), kru (yak sausage), yak curry with satu, or farsi ko bhat eaten with sattu up in the high Gorkha hills.
SC: What do you think the future of Indigenous food will look like in a decade's time? What should Indigenous communities, in your opinion, do to preserve and promote their food heritage?

BG: I think we have immense challenges ahead of us. Every year, these challenges seem to be only growing more and more. We only have to look at the recent disasters; it’s quite terrifying for the people who are living in these landscapes.

For several reasons, it’s crucial that we recognize that our situation is changing and that it is very fragile, and we have to be alert to this changing situation. So much has already changed, and within this framework we have to think of how we are going to adapt to our new circumstances, whether it is living in the city, establishing a relationship with urban life, learning to operate in a language that is not your mother tongue, learning technology, issues of sustainability, and so on.

In the midst of this vast change from our previous ancestral way of life, how are we going to hold ourselves as people with a distinct way of living, language, and culture? Moreover, how are we going to maintain the values that have been passed down to us from our ancestors? How willing are we to work for our collective welfare to protect our cultural and food heritage in this sea of change? Because without addressing these questions or without internalizing them, we cannot have real progress.
Written by Sanjib Chaudhary

b59750cc64703019: Muhammad Fajri/GettyAfter a year of record-breaking weather and a “super” El Niño underway, there’s no doubt climate extremes are wreaking havoc across the globe. For decades, scientists have warned us this would happen. Their research made the case for reducing fossil fuel dependence. And we’ve relied on their expertise to assess the severity and extent of climate change. But a small bloc of fossil fuel-producing countries is now obstructing the publication of a key scientific report from the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). This threatens global cooperation on tackling the climate crisis. And it has created deep concern at the COP31 climate summit, currently in its final hours in Turkey, also known as Türkiye. A truly global report First, it helps to understand why this report is so significant. The IPCC is the UN body for assessing the science related to climate change. Established in 1988, it provides political leaders with independent scientific assessments on climate change and strategies for response. This panel has produced six pivotal reports to date, which have collated and reviewed the latest knowledge on climate change science. And over the past two years, more than 640 experts from around the world have been meeting to write the seventh. The authors are leading researchers who volunteer their time. More than half of the authors working on the current seventh report, called the Seventh Assessment Report, or AR7, are from developing countries. I am a lead author for the Sixth and Seventh Assessment Reports in the working group that looks at impacts, vulnerability and adaptation. Work on this seventh report kicked off in December 2024, and its timeline for completion was never officially finalised. What’s the hold-up? Originally, the plan was for the seventh report to be released in 2028. But five countries are objecting to this timeline and pushing for a later release in 2029. India, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Kenya and China are ostensibly arguing that countries from the global south lack the resources and capacity to meet the current deadline. However, these countries also happen to be among the world’s largest fossil fuel producers. If recent reports are anything to go by, the evidence of global warming in this seventh report is likely to be alarming. It will highlight the evidence for much greater action, including deep and urgent reduction in fossil fuel production and use. Extending the release date means IPCC contributors would have even more information they would have to assess. This delay would increase, not alleviate, the demands of authorship and reviewing for those contributors from developing nations. The disagreement resulted in the suspension of the latest IPCC meeting in October in Ethiopia, with no confirmed timeline for the report release or budget for 2027. This threatens the very existence of the IPCC. Nations seeking delay argue that tight timelines are unfair to developing countries. But the least developed countries (LDC), a group comprised of 44 nations, expressed “deep disappointment” when the meeting in Ethiopia was suspended. Why the deadline matters Every five years, the UN’s climate body does a global stocktake of how effectively the world is responding to climate change. Intended to ramp up climate action, these stocktakes take a long hard look at the state of the planet, identify the gaps in our approach and suggest a path forward. To be truly effective, these must be based on the latest science. Delaying the seventh report would mean the most recent science is not fed into the 2028 global stocktake. This has grave implications for future climate action, and any delay in our response could have catastrophic effects on the wellbeing of planetary and human health. Science vs politics While major fossil-fuel-emitting countries often attempt to impede phaseout efforts, undermining the IPCC follows a recent trend of discrediting science for political ends. After a UN report in September found that limiting global warming to 1.5°C was no longer possible, Saudi Arabia jumped to question the credibility of the science, contending the research was not peer-reviewed. In fact, the report had been written over the course of a year by 44 experts, and reviewed by a further 44. Conflict at COP31 Despite opposition to delaying the IPCC report, those pushing for it have remained unmoved at COP31. Speaking to media at the summit, former US Vice President Al Gore accused Saudi Arabia of trying to sabotage the IPCC’s work. “Saudi Arabia is trying to destroy the IPCC in order to prevent the next global stocktake from using the accurate scientific data on fossil fuels,” he said. At climate negotiations where the phrase “fossil fuels” is routinely vetoed from the text, finding a resolution to the IPCC issue has even broader implications. If countries can’t agree on this, how will nearly 200 countries agree on a robust final COP31 outcome? Seeking resolution While the clock ticks down on the COP31 negotiations, a resolution to the IPCC issue is unlikely in Turkey. However, it is hoped a timeline and budget can be nailed down at meetings in early December. As the world’s most authoritative global body on climate change, the role the IPCC plays in driving climate action is critical to our future wellbeing. And the science in this seventh report will be fundamental to a truly effective global stocktake. In a time when the world often feels divided, settling this issue amicably and in good faith would offer countries a much-needed reminder that we are capable of cooperation in pursuit of a better future. She is affiliated with the Port Philip EcoCentre and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), where she is a lead author for the Sixth and Seventh Assessment Reports (Working Group II - Impacts, Vulnerability and Adaptation). b6a152aa5fb65c1a: The state welcome accorded to French president Emmanuel Macron at Dataran Merdeka on Nov 17 reflected Malaysia’s growing strategic importance to France, a European country that is also an Indo-Pacific power.

France is not merely an external observer of the Indo-Pacific. Through its overseas territories, maritime interests, military presence and extensive exclusive economic zones, France has a permanent stake in the region. Malaysia, meanwhile, occupies one of Asia’s most consequential geographical positions.
It sits between the Straits of Malacca and the South China Sea, two maritime spaces indispensable to international commerce, energy security and regional stability.
The convergence of French strategic interests and Malaysia’s geographical significance creates opportunities for both countries to deepen their partnership.
France is an Indo-Pacific power

France possesses overseas territories in the Indian and Pacific Oceans, including Réunion, French Polynesia and New Caledonia. These territories give France a permanent population, maritime jurisdiction and security responsibilities across the Indo-Pacific.

Unlike European countries whose regional engagement depends primarily on diplomacy or commercial investment, France maintains a continuous physical presence. Its naval forces, surveillance capabilities and defence partnerships enable Paris to contribute to maritime security across vast distances.
Yet the Indo-Pacific cannot be secured through military deployments alone. The region requires diplomacy, economic connectivity, institutional cooperation and respect for international law.
This is where Malaysia becomes important.
Malaysia’s strategic geography

The Straits of Malacca is among the world’s most important maritime arteries. It connects the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea and the wider Pacific, facilitating trade between Europe, the Middle East, South Asia and East Asia.
Any serious disruption here would affect shipping costs, energy supplies and global supply chains. Malaysia shares responsibility for the security of this passage with Indonesia and Singapore.

Malaysia is both a maritime trading nation and a claimant state in the South China Sea. Its economic interests depend on freedom of navigation, uninterrupted commercial activity and the peaceful management of maritime disputes.

France therefore has compelling reasons to strengthen relations with Putrajaya. Malaysia offers Paris a diplomatic interlocutor linking the Indian and Pacific Oceans, while France gives Putrajaya another avenue for cooperation without excessive dependence on Washington or Beijing.
Beyond great-power rivalry
Competition between the US and China increasingly shapes the Indo-Pacific. Reducing the region to a binary confrontation, however, would be shortsighted.

France has traditionally emphasised strategic autonomy, even while remaining a member of Nato and a close US ally. Malaysia similarly values strategic independence and constructive relations with competing powers.
Both countries should recognise that smaller and medium-sized powers cannot be expected to surrender their national interests to the preferences of larger states.

Asean must remain central to regional diplomacy. France can support Asean-led institutions, including the East Asia Summit and Asean Regional Forum, while respecting the sovereignty of Southeast Asian countries.
The objective should not be to militarise the Indo-Pacific, but to strengthen a rules-based regional order through dialogue, confidence-building measures and practical cooperation.
Malaysia as a Europe-Asean bridge

This is where Malaysia can assume a more consequential diplomatic role. Its value to France should not be measured only by geography or bilateral trade. Malaysia can also serve as a bridge between European strategic interests and Asean's regional priorities.

Malaysia’s long-standing participation in Asean gives it an understanding of the region’s diplomatic sensitivities and diversity. Since Southeast Asian countries do not always share identical views on major-power competition or maritime disputes, European engagement must be based on consultation and respect for Asean centrality.

France can use its relationship with Malaysia to deepen its engagement with Southeast Asia. Putrajaya can help explain Asean's preference for inclusive dialogue and practical cooperation, while conveying European perspectives to regional partners.
This does not mean Malaysia should speak on behalf of every Asean member. Rather, it can help create channels through which European and Southeast Asian policymakers better understand one another.

The opportunity extends beyond France. As an EU member, France can contribute to stronger Asean-EU relations in maritime cooperation, digital governance, clean energy, education and resilient supply chains. These are areas of shared interest, but cooperation must be shaped around local needs and mutually agreed priorities.

Malaysia’s engagement with the EU provides a foundation. Stronger ties with France can connect governments, universities and businesses, turning diplomatic goodwill into sustained exchanges and practical projects.
A partnership across two strategic seas

Acting as a diplomatic bridge requires Malaysia to preserve its strategic autonomy, maintain constructive relations with major powers and remain committed to Asean-led processes. Its credibility rests on showing that cooperation need not force Southeast Asian countries into rival camps.

For France, this means engaging Malaysia as a partner with its own agency, not simply as a gateway for French influence. For Malaysia, it means widening its diplomatic and economic options while reinforcing Asean voice.

Ultimately, the significance of Macron’s visit should not be measured solely by the agreements announced. Its longer-term importance lies in whether Malaysia and France can build a partnership connecting two strategically important regions.

At the crossroads of the Straits of Malacca and the South China Sea, Malaysia can do more than safeguard maritime interests: it can help bring Europe and Asean closer through dialogue and practical cooperation.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
669406732a3f4212: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”
A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”
“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.
A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.
The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.
In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.
“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”
The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.
f4cc3245def3a5b6: Negeri Sembilan menteri besar Ismail Lasim's statement following his audience with Yang Dipertuan Besar Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir should put to rest any uncertainties and mark the end of a protracted crisis.

Ismail has made it clear that he will abide by the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang decisions and procedures in all matters concerning customs and administration. Party politics should have no place in such matters.
However, the end of this constitutional crisis may spark another - one that concerns not only the people of Negeri Sembilan but the entire country.
A crisis of integrity involving Umno’s top leadership, particularly those who also hold senior positions in Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Cabinet.
A setback that could lead to public calls for Umno to quit the government for attempting to remove a legitimate and just state ruler.
(Calls that could easily drown out chants of "bubar" (dissolve Parliament) that were heard following Umno's convincing victory in the Melaka state election.)
To re-cap, Ismail has denied submitting or agreeing to a resignation letter as menteri besar, contrary to what was announced by Barisan Nasional secretary-general Zambry Abdul Kadir.

His denial raises serious questions. Why was the letter made public? Who prepared it, and on whose authority was it submitted? Why did the process appear to move ahead without first obtaining the Yang Dipertuan Besar’s consent?
These questions should not be directed at Zambry, who is also the higher education minister, alone.
Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, who is also the deputy prime minister, has also offered an explanation that now appears to contradict Ismail’s own account.
Now, if Zahid and Zambry only held posts in Umno, this controversy could be easily reduced to internal strife within the party or dismissed as another political dispute in Negeri Sembilan.
But they don't.
Which is why any reservations about their honesty, transparency and credibility cannot be taken lightly.
There are three key questions that need to be answered.
First, who actually prepared the resignation letter for Ismail that Zambry announced?
Second, did Ismail really not provide any reason for supposedly stepping down as menteri besar as Zahid claimed?
Or was this simply a tragic case of a misunderstanding or misinformation?

Third, why did Zahid and Umno submit a candidate for the menteri besar's post to the state ruler, following Ismail's resignation, despite Tuanku Muhriz allowing the Juasseh assemblyman to continue in his role?
I sincerely hope Zambry and Zahid will provide clear, comprehensive and convincing answers to all three questions.
Such explanations are important, not just to protect their reputations, but also to restore public confidence in the integrity of leaders entrusted with governing the country.
I still want to believe that there are capable Malay leaders whom the people can rely on. Leaders who also respect the royal institution, the Malay rulers, and the constitution.
But political statements alone won't win new converts or retain the current devotees. Instilling such belief requires honest and responsible action.

In examining the Negeri Sembilan crisis, another question deserves closer attention. Was everything that happened part of a deliberate plan, or was it simply the result of misunderstandings and poor communication among those involved?
If it was merely a misunderstanding, a sincere explanation and an apology should be enough for everyone to move forward.
But if the crisis is proven to have been orchestrated, whether by political figures, customary authorities or both, the consequences would go far beyond a power struggle in a single state.
It could undermine public confidence in customary institutions, the supremacy of the constitution, and the integrity of a Malay party with a long history in the formation of this nation.

Politicians should remember that in today's world, backroom dealings are harder to conceal, thanks to social media. A seemingly innocuous remark by a lowly clerk could create a butterfly effect that threatens a powerful party leader.
Once trust erodes, even loyal supporters may become disillusioned, while political allies may choose to distance themselves.
This is why integrity cannot be an afterthought in politicking.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
73927cb8c81d9316: Kenyataan Menteri Besar Negeri Sembilan Ismail Lasim selepas menghadap Yang Dipertuan Besar Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir semalam, pada hemat saya, menandakan berakhirnya kemelut yang mencetuskan persoalan mengenai kedudukan pemerintah negeri serta keabsahan pelantikan Undang.

Ismail dengan jelas menyatakan pendiriannya untuk akur kepada keputusan dan tatakelola Dewan Keadilan dan Undang dalam segala urusan berkaitan adat dan pentadbiran. Politik kepartian pula tidak seharusnya mencampuri urusan berkenaan.
Alhamdulillah, sebagai rakyat yang mengikuti perkembangan ini, saya bersyukur kerana kebenaran akhirnya mendapat tempat, sekali gus meredakan kekeliruan yang sekian lama menyelubungi Negeri Sembilan.
Namun, berakhirnya kemelut perlembagaan ini membuka satu lagi persoalan yang tidak kurang serius, bukan sahaja kepada rakyat Negeri Sembilan, malah seluruh negara.
Persoalan itu menyentuh integriti pucuk pimpinan Umno, khususnya mereka yang turut memegang jawatan penting dalam Kabinet Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim.

Jika sebelum ini kedengaran laungan 'bubar, bubar' selepas kemenangan besar pada PRN Melaka, jangan sampai rakyat pula mula melaungkan 'keluar, keluar' terhadap Umno apabila integriti kepimpinannya dipersoalkan susulan kemelut yang turut dikaitkan dengan usaha menyingkirkan pemerintah negeri yang sah selain memerintah dengan baik, adil serta saksama.
Lebih membimbangkan, persoalan ini timbul daripada kenyataan Ismail sendiri, bukannya khabar angin atau dakwaan pihak ketiga.

Ismail secara terbuka menafikan beliau pernah menghantar atau memberikan persetujuan terhadap surat peletakan jawatan sebagai menteri besar yang diumumkan Setiausaha Agung Barisan Nasional (BN) Zambry Abdul Kadir.

Penafian itu menimbulkan persoalan besar. Mengapa surat berkenaan diumumkan kepada umum? Siapa yang menyediakannya dan atas kuasa siapa ia dikemukakan? Mengapa pula proses itu seolah-olah mendahului perkenan Yang DiPertuan Besar?
Persoalan ini tidak wajar dipertanggungjawabkan hanya kepada Zambry yang juga menteri pendidikan tinggi.
Presiden Umno Zahid Hamidi yang juga timbalan perdana menteri, turut memberikan penjelasan yang kini menimbulkan percanggahan dengan pendirian Ismail sendiri.
Sekiranya kedua-dua pemimpin itu sekadar memegang jawatan dalam Umno, mungkin kemelut ini boleh dianggap sebagai masalah dalaman parti atau isu politik Negeri Sembilan semata-mata.
Namun, hakikatnya kedua-duanya memegang amanah besar dalam pentadbiran negara. Justeru, sebarang persoalan mengenai kejujuran, ketelusan dan kewibawaan mereka tidak boleh dipandang ringan.
Sebagai rakyat Malaysia, saya mempunyai rasa hormat terhadap kedua-dua tokoh ini. Namun, perkembangan terbaharu menyebabkan saya tertanya-tanya tentang kewajaran tindakan dan penjelasan mereka.
Ada tiga persoalan utama yang perlu dijawab secara terbuka.
Pertama, siapakah sebenarnya yang menulis atau menyediakan surat peletakan jawatan Ismail yang diumumkan Zambry?

Kedua, benarkah penjelasan Zahid bahawa Ismail tidak memberikan sebarang alasan kepadanya berhubung peletakan jawatan itu? Atau adakah penjelasan tersebut berpunca daripada salah faham atau maklumat yang tidak tepat?

Ketiga, mengapakah Zahid dan Umno masih mengemukakan nama calon menteri besar baharu untuk perkenan Tuanku Muhriz, sedangkan terdapat kenyataan bahawa baginda memperkenankan Ismail meneruskan tugasnya?
Saya amat berharap Zambry dan Zahid dapat memberikan penjelasan yang jelas, menyeluruh dan meyakinkan terhadap ketiga-tiga persoalan ini.
Penjelasan itu penting bukan semata-mata untuk mempertahankan nama baik mereka, tetapi juga bagi memulihkan keyakinan rakyat terhadap integriti pemimpin yang diberikan amanah untuk mentadbir negara.
Saya masih mahu percaya bahawa orang Melayu mempunyai pemimpin berwibawa yang mampu menjadi tempat rakyat bersandar, selain menghormati institusi Raja-raja Melayu dan prinsip perlembagaan.
Namun, kepercayaan itu tidak boleh dipertahankan dengan kenyataan politik semata-mata. Ia mesti disokong oleh tindakan yang jujur dan bertanggungjawab.

Dalam menilai kemelut Negeri Sembilan ini, satu lagi persoalan perlu diperhalusi. Adakah segala yang berlaku berpunca daripada perancangan tertentu, atau sekadar salah faham dan kegagalan komunikasi antara pihak berkepentingan?
Jika benar ia hanya salah faham, penjelasan yang ikhlas dan permohonan maaf sepatutnya memadai untuk membolehkan semua pihak bergerak ke hadapan.
Tetapi jika terbukti kemelut ini dirancang, sama ada oleh pihak politik, pihak adat atau kedua-duanya, kesannya jauh lebih besar daripada sekadar perebutan kuasa di sebuah negeri.
Ia boleh meruntuhkan keyakinan rakyat terhadap institusi adat, keluhuran perlembagaan dan integriti sebuah parti Melayu yang mempunyai sejarah panjang dalam pembentukan negara.
Saya ingin mengingatkan ahli politik semua bahawa this is a different age altogether. Perbuatan tersembunyi sukar ditutup dengan kewujudan media sosial dan maklumat digital.
Maklumat daripada seorang kerani sekalipun boleh membuka ruang kepada pendedahan yang akhirnya menggugat kedudukan pemimpin besar sesebuah parti.
Apabila kepercayaan mula terhakis, penyokong sendiri boleh menjadi serik, manakala rakan politik pula mungkin memilih untuk menjauhkan diri.
Sebab itulah integriti tidak boleh dianggap sebagai perkara sampingan dalam percaturan politik. Ia merupakan asas kepercayaan rakyat terhadap seseorang pemimpin.

Kalau nak 'bubar-bubar' lebih baik 'keluar-keluar' kerana kami perlukan pemimpin yang boleh dipercayai dan berintegriti kepada sumpah khidmat kepada rakyat semua dan sumpah ketaatan kepada Raja Melayu.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
b894a0e31143a149: When Southeast Asia’s leaders link arms for their customary family photo at the Asean Summit in Manila on Nov 16–18, the show of unity will belie the fact that, on the eve of the organisation’s 60th anniversary, the group is more divided and less effective than ever.
Amid a fracturing global order, Asean has a choice: turn its convening authority into concerted action or be reduced to an arena for great-power rivalry.
The fault lines are numerous. Indonesia’s wildfire haze has choked Singapore and Malaysia in recent months. Thailand and Cambodia fought border skirmishes that came close to outright war last year.

Myanmar is led by a putschist-turned-president who wants his seat back at the leaders’ table. And the Philippines, the summit’s host, is locked in a standoff with China that most of its neighbours would rather avoid.
And yet Southeast Asia needs Asean more than ever because it gives member countries visibility and a voice on the global stage.

To be sure, Asean is not in danger of collapse. The risk is subtler. Each fissure exposes an institutional shortcoming. On Myanmar, it is enforcement: Min Aung Hlaing, the general who ousted and detained the democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi in February 2021, signed Asean’s Five-Point Consensus in April of that year, only to disregard it. The group responded by barring the junta leader from attending Asean summits.

But after winning Myanmar’s military-organised elections—with voting confined to junta-controlled areas, excluding large swaths of the country—in December and January, Min Aung Hlaing swapped his general’s uniform for civilian garb in April.
Hard-headed realpolitik compelled China and India to recognise him, while half of Asean members, led by Thailand, have also now officially received him, amounting to de facto normalisation.
Likewise, the Thai-Cambodian conflict exposed the limits of Asean’s much-touted capacity to sustain peace. Fighting in July 2025 killed dozens and displaced some 300,000 people.

The first ceasefire came after US president Donald Trump threatened tariffs, leading to the “truce for trade” accord signed in October 2025. But it unraveled only a couple months later, with border clashes uprooting many more people.

Without pressure from the US, Asean could not end the fighting on its own. Both sides are now using the “compulsory conciliation” process under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea to resolve their bilateral conflict.

Meanwhile, tensions in the South China Sea reveal the absence of common external positions in Asean. China exploits member states’ differing views of it to pursue its maritime claims, leaving the Philippines exposed, particularly given America’s unpredictability under Trump.

The Philippines wants to complete a long-promised code of conduct for the South China Sea at this month’s summit. But even if the code is finalised, a text without teeth will not do much to stop China’s incursions.

Indonesian peatland fires have exposed the most telling rift, because great powers play no part in it. The haze closed schools in Malaysia and resulted in Singapore’s longest period of toxic air since 2015, triggering consumer boycotts, ministerial barbs, and a reduction in Indonesia’s pipeline gas exports to Singapore.
But Indonesia alone cannot address the problem. The Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution has been in force since 2003, yet its 2020 target for a smoke-free region was pushed back to 2030.

Singapore has issued notices to ten locally-based companies over their links to the fires causing the current haze. A treaty that fails to reach those boardrooms will do little to protect the region’s people from hazardous smoke.

These fault lines matter more than ever because the US-China contest has turned coercive, with tariffs, export controls, critical minerals, and supply chains wielded as weapons, at the same time as the multilateralism that once cushioned smaller countries is being eroded.

Here Asean’s value as a buffer, bridge, and broker is easily overlooked. Despite lacking a unified foreign policy and a joint military, Asean serves as a single interlocutor representing nearly 700 million people and some US$4 trillion in output. It also brings together the US, China, Russia, Japan, India, and others at its East Asia Summit and related forums.

While leaders call for like-minded countries to form coalitions of the willing amid a “rupture” in the global order, Asean member states have already started hedging: Indonesia is now a full member of BRICS, while Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam are partner countries. But these countries need an anchor at home, lest diversification turns into fragmentation. The task now is to demonstrate Asean’s centrality.
Singapore’s 2027 chairmanship offers an opening for several major reforms. Asean should hold fewer summits, with one leaders’ meeting per year and ministers held responsible for delivery.
The group also should hire a secretary-general based on merit and for shorter, performance-dependent contracts, rather than appointing someone for a five-year term, based on alphabetical rotation.

And flexible participation should be the norm, extending the “Asean Minus X” formula used for economic integration to coalitions of the willing on issues such as maritime security, haze enforcement, and scam centres.
Asean would also benefit from empowering past, present, and incoming chairs to mediate conflicts, advance existing agreements, and launch new initiatives.

Lastly, Myanmar’s return to the leaders’ summit should be tied to measurable benchmarks, such as an end to air strikes on civilians, humanitarian access, the release of political prisoners including Aung San Suu Kyi, and an envoy acceptable to all sides.

The aim is not to turn Asean into a supranational authority or geopolitical bloc, but to recover the founding aspiration of 1967, when five wary neighbours judged their quarrels less dangerous than facing outside pressure alone.

Their number has since grown to 11, and member states must remember that endurance does not amount to agency; the choice now is between strengthening their partnership or being picked apart one by one.
Thitinan Pongsudhirak, a professor at Chulalongkorn University’s Faculty of Political Science, is a senior fellow at its Institute of Security and International Studies.
