48a4b14c4a193313: Philadelphia workers who work for a private company with more than 10 employees may be entitled to paid sick leave. andresr/E+ Collection via Getty ImagesWhat do you do when you wake up with a runny nose and a cough? If you work in Philadelphia, you might have the legal right to a paid sick day. There is no federal right to paid sick leave. However, Philadelphia, like a growing number of states and cities nationwide, requires certain employers to provide paid time off when workers get sick. In Philadelphia, these requirements apply to private-sector employers with more than 10 employees. In theory, under these laws, sick workers have time to recover and avoid spreading germs, and they don’t have to choose between a sick day and a paycheck. For immigrant workers, though, it may not be that easy. I study restaurant work, an industry that depends on the labor of people who are foreign-born. Philadelphia’s award-winning dining scene wouldn’t be the same without the creativity and hard work of people from countries such as Mexico, Honduras and Guatemala. I studied this industry during the COVID-19 pandemic by working in a restaurant from 2021 to 2022, as well as by interviewing restaurant workers, managers and owners from 2021 to 2024. Some interviews were also conducted by my then-fellow Temple University graduate students Andrew Chelius and Camila Franco Rodríguez. Philadelphia’s paid sick leave law has been around since 2015. During the COVID-19 pandemic, federal and local laws temporarily expanded those protections. The Families First Coronavirus Response Act, a federal law which was passed on March 18, 2020, and amended by the CARES Act later that same month, required private-sector employers with less than 500 employees to provide 80 hours of paid sick time each year, on top of their existing paid leave policies, to full-time employees. A 2022 temporary expansion of the local paid sick leave law in Philadelphia, meanwhile, required private-sector employers with 25 or more employees to provide 40 hours of additional paid sick leave to eligible employees. What I found, though, was that several factors could make it hard for workers to take advantage of these policies. Immigrant workers faced unique, additional barriers. ‘$300 for a simple flu’ Our interviews and my immersion in restaurant work showed me that even during a pandemic, restaurant workers had to deal with employers skirting the law or misunderstanding policies. Workers were also impacted by long-standing service industry norms that discourage calling in sick, even when they’re under the weather. Many bosses required doctor’s notes, too, before they paid out any sick time – as I heard from bosses themselves. The local law says, however, that employers may require “reasonable documentation” – but only after an absence of more than two days. Immigrant workers, meanwhile, experienced additional hurdles. Take the example of doctor’s notes. Seeing a doctor is more affordable when you have health insurance. If you’re an undocumented immigrant, getting health insurance is difficult and expensive. Undocumented people are not eligible for Medicaid and are excluded from the Affordable Care Act marketplace. Only a few states try to mend the gap by offering health insurance for low-income people ineligible for Medicaid. Pennsylvania is not one of them. Bill – a pseudonym, like the other participants’ names in this article – is originally from Mexico, and he was a server at an Italian restaurant in Philadelphia’s Center City during the pandemic. When he got sick, his attitude was: “Keep the money. Don’t pay me for sick days.” What kept Bill from claiming sick pay? His employer required him to turn in a doctor’s note before he could receive paid sick leave. However, Bill was undocumented and did not have health insurance. “I wasn’t going to go to the doctor and spend US$300-$400 for a simple flu,” he said. Gaps arise when restaurants have different policies for front-of-house workers, who interact with customers, than back-of-house workers, who staff the kitchen. Willie B. Thomas/DigitalVision Collection via Getty Images Different policies for back-of-house workers In the restaurant where I worked, meanwhile, it was harder for immigrant workers to get sick days than nonimmigrant workers, based on my observations and interviews. This was not necessarily due to ill will toward immigrant workers. But there was a stricter policy around paid sick leave in the kitchen, which was staffed mostly by immigrants from Latin America. The chef who managed the kitchen described his policy like this: “If you bring me proof that you went to the doctor, and the doctor gave you a day or two days of rest, OK, that’s fine.” Those days would be paid. In the customer-facing front of the house, though, where a different manager was in charge, workers – including me – weren’t told they needed proof. These workers were almost all nonimmigrants and mostly white. I heard from Socorro, a prep cook who worked at a different restaurant, that managers where she worked were stingier with sick days for kitchen workers than for servers. “The servers were given their sick leave days and paid them. They’d say, ‘Oh no, my head hurts. I’m not going to work.’ But we couldn’t. ‘Oh, your head hurts? You have to put up with it and come to work.” In that workplace, Socorro said, immigrants also mainly worked in the kitchen, while servers were mostly U.S.-born. Fear of retaliation Immigrant workers in Philadelphia restaurants – both those with and without legal status – also weighed the risks they could face if they asked for paid sick days. These were not risks their nonimmigrant co-workers generally worried about. Claudia, a restaurant worker from Mexico, worked with a local organization called El Comité de Trabajadorxs de Restaurante – the Committee of Restaurant Workers – to educate her peers about paid sick leave. She found that immigrants were really scared of losing their jobs if they spoke up for themselves. “The majority – 80% if not 90% – even if they know they have paid sick hours … they don’t ask for it,” she said. “They don’t claim it, because [they think], ‘Oh, I am an immigrant and they are going to fire me.’ Or, 'Where am I going to get another job?’” Healthy workers, healthy public My research suggests that immigrants in Philadelphia face a gap between the promise and the reality of the city’s paid sick leave policies. These barriers might also help explain gaps in paid sick leave access between foreign-born and U.S.-born workers in other places that require it, like New York City or California. Gaps in access based on immigration status are an equity issue. But beyond that, research suggests that everyone wins if it’s easier for workers to get paid sick leave. Paid sick leave makes for healthier workers, and healthier workers make for a healthier public. e853741b74a166f4: Now that Ismail Lasim sudah buat pengakukan terbuka bahawa beliau tidak pernah letak jawatan menteri besar Negeri Sembilan, persoalan penting ialah siapa yang mengutus ‘surat peletakan jawatannya’ kepada Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan?
Persoalan ini amat penting kerana pada hemat saya pihak yang mengutus surat itu telah membohongi atau cuba membohongi Tuanku Muhriz Tuan Munawir.
Apa tidaknya kerana pihak itu telah memaklumkan perkara yang nampaknya tidak benar dan mahu baginda mempercayai isi kandungan surat itu mengenai peletakan jawatan menteri besar.

Orang atau orang-orang yang terlibat dengan penghantaran surat itu saya kira tidak sangka akan reaksi Yang Dipertuan Besar sebaik menerima surat itu. Atas kebijaksanaan Tuanku Muhriz, Istana Negeri Sembilan menegaskan (ketika itu) belum mengesahkan ketulenan surat itu meskipun menurut Setiausaha Agung BN Zambry Abdul Kadir ia telah ditandatangani Ismail.
Sebelum berbicara lanjut elok kita imbau kembali kenyataan Pengelola Bijaya Diraja Istana Negeri Sembilan Azizi Mohamad Ali yang dikeluarkan 17 Nov lalu berbunyi begini:
“Istana Negeri Sembilan mengambil maklum akan kenyataan Zambry Abdul Kadir, Setiausaha Agung Barisan Nasional berhubung peletakan jawatan Ismail Lasim sebagai menteri besar Negeri Sembilan.
Kenyataan itu dimuat naik di media sosial pada 10 malam 16 Nov dan kelihatan berdasarkan salinan surat peletakan jawatan yang berada dalam milikan beliau.
Surat peletakan itu telah dihantar ke Istana Hingap Seremban pada 12.16 pagi 17 November”.

Bagi saya ini amat janggal. Zambry telah menghebahkan ‘peletakan jawatan’ Ismail pada malam 16 Nov tetapi ‘surat peletakan jawatan’ Ismail dihantar ke Istana Hinggap hanya pada keesokan hari yakni 17 Nov.
Bukankah ini bermakna Zambry sudah mengumumkan peletakan jawatan Ismail long before Yang Dipertuan Besar dimaklumkan? Is this proper dalam urusan dengan istana?

Berbalik kenyataan Pengelola Bijya Diraja Istana Negeri Sembilan yang disebut tadi: “Surat itu diserahkan oleh seorang individu yang memperkenalkan dirinya sebagai Hamidi daripada firma guaman Shahrul Hamidi & Haziq"
Aneh. Jika saya mahu letak jawatan misalnya daripada syarikat tempat saya bekerja, saya akan umum sendiri my resignation. Bukan orang lain yang umum.
Dan surat peletakan jawatan akan saya serah sendiri kepada majikan bukan meminta pihak lain melakukannya.
Dalam kes ‘peletakan jawatan’ Ismail adakah ‘molek’ menyerahkan surat kepada Yang Dipertuan Besar menerusi third party? Dan tidak menghadap untuk mempersembahkan surat personally?

Ada lagi yang dihuraikan Pengelola Bijaya Diraja Istana Negeri Sembilan. Menurut beliau: “Pada jam 6.38 petang,semalam (16 Nov 2026 ) Setiausaha Sulit Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan telah menyampaikan kepada Ismail melalui aplikasi WhatsApp perkenan Tuanku Muhriz untuk menghadap seperti yang dipohon oleh menteri besar itu.
Perkara tu telah diakui terima oleh Ismail dan acara menghadap telah ditetapkan pada pukul 10 pagi Jumaat (20 Nov).
Perkenan untuk menghadap itu telah diberikan 80 minit lebih awal sebelum siaran media Zambry yang memaklumkan peletakan jawatan itu.
Aneh dan pelik. Ismail yang memohon menghadap bertindak ‘meneruskan hasrat letak jawatan’ (yang diumum Zambry) setelah tahu Yang Dipertuan Besar telah perkenankan permohonannya?

Berbalik pula kepada kenyataan setiausaha agung BN itu. Kata Zambry pengerusi gabungan itu Zahid Hamidi sudah menerima salinan suara peletakan jawatan Ismail yang diutuskan kepada Yang Dipertuan Besar.

“Pengerusi Barisan Nasional akan mengemukakan cadangan calon menteri besar yang baharu untuk dipersembahkan ke hadapan Duli Yang Maha Mulia Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilsn selaras dengan peruntukan Undang Undang Tubuh Kerajaan Negeri Sembilan”.

Zahid insisted Ismail resigned voluntarily. Beliau juga memberitahu media hanya satu nama akan dipersembahkan. Ini menurut saya tidak beri Yang Dipertuan Besar banyak pilihan. Atau tidak beri pilihan langsung.

Apa pun itu sudah tidak terpakai kerana hari ini Yang Dipertuan Besar bertitah supaya Ismail teruskan tugas sebagai menteri besar. Ini kata Ismail pada sidang medianya selepas menghadap Tuanku Muhriz.
Saya ulangi apa kata Ismail pada sidang media itu “Saya tak pernah setuju surat ini dihantar dan saya pun tak hantar sendiri surat ini kepada Tuanku. Saya hanya tahu melalui media sosial.”
Namun Ismail mengaku surat peletakan jawatan semenagnya ada dalam simpanan pimpinan parti namun tidak dinyatakan sebabnya.
Setahu saya ada parti mewajibkan Ahli Parlimen dan Adun yang mewaklinya menandatangnai surat melepaskan jawatan atau kedudukan dalam usaha memastkan mereka tidak lompat parti.
The pre signed resignation letter will be released in the event of crossing over to other parties. Ini amalan lazim sebelum ada anti hopping law.
Bagaimanapun boleh dirumuskan penjelasan Ismail diterima Yang Dipertuan Besar pada upacara menghadap semalam. Lantas baginda mahu Ismail kekal sebagai menteri besar.
Bagi saya episod Negeri Sembilan tamparan hebat kepada BN khususnya Umno yang selama ini megah mendakwa ia mempertahakan Raja-Raja Melayu dn kedaulatan Istana.
Di Negeri Sembilan tidak boleh dinafikan Umno mendekati (bersekongkol?) kumpulan yang cuba menurunkan Tuanku Muhriz daripada takhta dan gagal.
Kesimpulan terbaik saya kira dibuat oleh Naib Pengerusi DAP Syahredzan Johan “Semua tindakan ini adalah berasaskan suatu perkara yang terbukti tidak benar. Ismail Lasim tidak pernah letak jawatan.”
Adakah Umno cuba untuk memperdayakan Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan dan rakyat dalam hal ini?
Nota kaki: Terbaharu, lewat petang ini Azizi mengeluarkan kenyatan menyatakan Ismail perlu menunjukkan beliau mendapat sokongan majoriti Adun untuk terus memegang jawatan menteri besar.
Kenyataan itu juga berkata tidak tepat dan tidak berdasarkan fakta untuk mengatakan Istana mahu Ismail kekal sebagai menteri besar memandangkan beliau sendiri menegaskan tidak meletakkan jawatan.
Menurutnya, pihak Istana akan mematuhi sepenuhnya konvensyen dan peruntukan perlembagaan.

2b876ce610b840bc: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
What we learned when our Roundtables explored the quest to make minds immortal

To preserve our sense of self, some scientists are working on ways to keep our brains going—even beyond death. In their quest for cognitive immortality, these “mind savers” are exploring everything from head transplants and brain freezing to conscious software avatars.

In the latest MIT Technology Review Roundtables event, senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado joined science editor Mary Beth Griggs to examine these ideas. After following the money, the science, and the philosophy, he came back part skeptical, part awestruck. Here’s a taste of what Antonio found—and what he made of it.

Not all the projects are quite what they seem: A $190 million US government program to develop replacement brain tissue is officially about treating stroke, but “it’s also a fig leaf for the actual ambition”: living forever.

AI could lead to convincing mind clones: Large language models are making it possible to build AI copies of people that act quite like the real thing. “This digital avatar might not be good enough for you, but what if it’s good enough for me?”
Immortality can be a hard sell: One company, Nectome, wants to preserve brains within 12 minutes of medically assisted death. “If you’re selling a hot product, this is not it.”
It’s not always clear what we’re trying to preserve: “I’m not even sure that I have a very good claim to be myself.”
There’s an upside to life as a brain in a jar: “You can surf the internet. I do that pretty much 12 hours a day, anyway.”
To find out which of these ideas might actually work, subscribers can now watch the full conversation on demand.

c1cb73c3d8571045: From Kua Kia Soong
The controversy over the RM1,000 land premium for the 99-year lease renewal of the Kuala Lumpur and Selangor Chinese Assembly Hall (KLSCAH) has become another occasion for racial politicking.
Some have portrayed the decision as an unjustified privilege for a Chinese organisation, while others have defended it as a concession to the Chinese community.
Both sides are missing the bigger issue: whether Malaysia genuinely respects its historical and cultural heritage or allows commercial development and political expediency to take precedence.

Established in 1923, KLSCAH is more than a Chinese communal building. It has played an important role in Kuala Lumpur's political, social and cultural history and has been used by Malaysians of different ethnic groups and political affiliations.
Its significance should be assessed in the context of national history, rather than reduced to the racial identity of its users.

The controversy also raises a more fundamental question: why is the preservation of historical buildings and cultural institutions in Malaysia so often treated as an inconvenience rather than a public responsibility?
Monorail and disregard for historical landmarks
Consider the fate of Kuala Lumpur's historic temples.

The Guan Yin temple, established in the 1890s or possibly earlier, is one of the city's historic places of worship. Located beside the Maharajalela Monorail station, its historical setting and architectural character are overshadowed by the surrounding concrete infrastructure.
The temple has survived fires, Kuala Lumpur's transformation and generations of change. Yet how much consideration was given to its historical setting when the monorail infrastructure was introduced?
Modern public transport is undoubtedly necessary. But must modernisation mean historical buildings are reduced to insignificant structures dwarfed by concrete and steel?
This is not an argument against public transport, but for intelligent urban planning that allows modern infrastructure and historical landmarks to coexist.
The Sydney Monorail, for instance, was decommissioned in 2013 and dismantled in 2014 as part of the city's transition to light rail.
Another new development now threatens the Guan Yin temple. The authorities should assess its impact on the historic precinct before any damage becomes irreversible.
The wider Chinese community should also be asking why more has not been done to protect such landmarks.
Kuala Lumpur is destroying its own history
The fate of other historical buildings in Kuala Lumpur should prompt reflection on our priorities.
Pudu Jail, built in 1895, was once among the city's most recognisable landmarks. Its imposing walls and famous mural formed part of Kuala Lumpur's physical and social history.
The prison complex was demolished in stages, with most of the buildings gone by 2012. Only sections of its exterior wall and entrance were retained.

Whatever one's views on the colonial prison system, Pudu Jail was part of our history. Its preservation could have provided an important historical and educational site. Instead, most of it disappeared.
Then there was Bok House, a neo-classical mansion built in 1929 by businessman Chua Cheng Bok along Jalan Ampang. It also housed the well-known restaurant Le Coq d'Or.

Despite appeals by heritage advocates, the mansion was demolished in 2006. The argument that it lacked sufficient historical value illustrated how little importance was attached to architectural heritage.
The Cathay cinema, another familiar Kuala Lumpur landmark, also disappeared in the name of urban redevelopment.
How many more buildings must we lose before we realise that a city is not defined merely by its shopping malls, luxury condominiums and skyscrapers?
The Sultan Abdul Samad Building, Central Market and historic buildings around Dataran Merdeka have fortunately survived.
But their survival should not be an excuse for complacency. They require continued conservation, proper maintenance and protection from insensitive development.
Malaysia's collective memory under threat
This is not simply a Chinese community issue.

Malaysia's heritage includes Malay villages, traditional wooden houses, mosques, Indian temples, colonial buildings, indigenous settlements, archaeological sites, historic cemeteries and natural landscapes.

The demolition of the Sri Uchimalai Muniswarar Temple in Rawang in February was another painful reminder of the vulnerability of places of worship with longstanding community ties. The temple was demolished after the landowner sought possession of the site.

The controversy over the 130-year-old Dewi Sri Pathrakaliamman Temple on Jalan Masjid India, Kuala Lumpur, also raised fundamental questions about how development should accommodate historic places of worship.

Although the authorities subsequently identified a replacement site, the episode showed how vulnerable such institutions can be when land ownership and development interests take precedence over historical continuity.

We should also remember the traditional Malay kampungs lost to urban redevelopment, indigenous communities displaced by development projects and historic landscapes sacrificed to commercial interests.
The heritage of the Orang Asli and indigenous peoples of Sabah and Sarawak deserves the same protection as Kuala Lumpur's old temples and shophouses.
A nation that remembers only the history of its politically powerful communities has a distorted understanding of itself.

Developers should be required to assess the historical, cultural and social significance of buildings and places of worship before obtaining development approvals. Where possible, they should preserve these sites in their original locations rather than treating relocation as the default solution.

In the latest KLSCAH controversy, critics who believe public institutions should not receive special consideration for heritage preservation must explain why the same principle should not apply to every other historic building, temple, mosque, church, traditional settlement and cultural institution in Malaysia.

Should a historic Malay institution be required to pay commercial land premiums even when its land is designated for institutional use? Should an Indian temple be denied consideration simply because its preservation benefits a particular religious community?
We must reject this absurd racial arithmetic.
The question is not whether KLSCAH is Chinese, Malay or Indian. It is whether the institution has historical, cultural and public significance that deserves protection.
Kua Kia Soong is a former MP and a former director of Suaram.

b00d2094481c93e7: Now that the Melaka state election is done and dusted, here are six harsh truths Malaysians need to confront.
The first is this: like it or not, the Barisan Nasional (BN)-Perikatan Nasional (PN) bloc won resoundingly.
There is no other way to describe it.
Many of the majorities recorded were astronomical, suggesting that Malay voters remain firmly behind these two coalitions, particularly Umno and PAS.
The prospect of BN and PN forming the next federal government, aided by voter transference between the two coalitions, appears increasingly likely with each passing day.
The second harsh truth is one we are often reluctant to acknowledge: many Malay voters appear largely indifferent to corruption.
The Tabung Haji and Felda controversies associated with Umno barely registered at the polls and did little to dent the party's support.

Meanwhile, PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang, who commands considerable influence among the religious electorate, continues to advance the narrative of Malay-Muslim political dominance with relatively little challenge.
It is a simple yet powerful message. The idea that Malay-Muslims must remain in power is easy to understand and sell.

Against such populist narratives, the Madani government's successes in attracting investments, creating jobs and improving fiscal management have struggled to gain traction, even when the achievements of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's administration were communicated effectively.
The third harsh truth is for a specific group of Malaysians: those in Bersama.
Twice now, despite their hard work, sincerity and idealism, they have come away empty-handed.
Bersama may yet have something to learn from Umno and PAS and their marriage of convenience.
The relationship between the two parties is far from a fairy-tale partnership. I suspect there remains deep distrust between them. After all, what became of Muafakat Nasional?
Nevertheless, both parties recognised that cooperation was necessary for political survival.

Rafizi Ramli may have serious differences with Anwar, but if the PKR president was once able to set aside his differences with mentor-turned-nemesis Dr Mahathir Mohamad to wrest Putrajaya from BN's iron grip in 2018, why can't Rafizi do the same?

There is also a reason figures such as Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, Mahathir, Hadi and Anwar have remained relevant for decades. Rather than dismissing them as political dinosaurs, Bersama might do well to study the lessons they offer.
The fourth harsh lesson is for PKR itself.
The time has come for Anwar to do something bold if the party hopes to survive the next general election.
He must begin laying the groundwork for a new generation of leaders and gradually step back from centre stage.
Unless fresh faces are given room to emerge, public enthusiasm for PKR may continue to fade.
There is little point talking about a second term for Anwar and his administration if the party remains unwilling to reinvent itself.
The fifth lesson is that Pakatan Harapan must strike meaningful deals with the ruling coalitions in Sabah and Sarawak.
Those arrangements must go beyond simply addressing demands under the Malaysia Agreement 1963.
Anwar still possesses something neither BN nor PN is likely to offer: the possibility of an East Malaysian prime minister.
Such a commitment could fundamentally reshape the political landscape.
The sixth and final harsh lesson concerns voter turnout.
During the Melaka election, it was reported that about 80% of Malay voters turned out, compared with only 60% of Chinese voters.
Overall turnout stood at 70%.
If Malaysia is to chart a different course, every vote matters. An 85% turnout, especially if it includes stronger participation from non-Malay voters, could significantly alter electoral outcomes.
I hope the Election Commission will make every effort to help the roughly one million Malaysians living overseas cast their ballots wherever they reside.
The higher the voter turnout, the greater the chance that Malaysia's future will be determined by the broadest possible expression of its people's will.
We are heading into stormy waters. We need to be honest with ourselves if we are to avoid the maelstrom that could engulf us all.

b9181880dad68760: The last few weeks haven’t been good for the US tech industry. The recent US midterms elections signalled strong pushbacks against AI, data centres and big tech in general. Then there’s last week’s breakdown of Microsoft services followed almost immediately by an outage that grounded civilian flights across the US for hours.

Donald Trump's aggressive policies in his second presidency – tariffs, embargoes, sanctions and even military actions against many countries including those once considered allies – are beginning to register loudly in the risk assessments of many countries. The latest incidents bring even more intense focus on this matter.

China was the first to face US actions on its tech sector, especially those involving semiconductors, software and AI. However, China has the resources to deal with this. Chinese companies such as Huawei and DeepSeek are successfully overcoming these obstacles and showing they’re good at converting these problems into opportunities.

Europe is a bit late to the party, taking longer to realise they aren’t high on the US list of friends and allies any more. The inertia and in-fighting in its huge coalition of disparate European nations slowed things down a lot. But even there the logjam is breaking.

A particular shock was Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The Trump administration's overt siding with Russian president Vladimir Putin is unnerving Russia’s European neighbours. They realise they depend too much on the US, whether for office productivity tools, weapons, satellite capabilities or semiconductor chips that power their AI ambitions.
A wake-up call

The recent incidents where SpaceX withheld its Starlink and Starshield services to Ukraine’s war efforts are wake-up calls on the perils of depending too much on an increasingly unreliable partner. The same goes with the repeated US threats of annexation of Canada, Greenland, Panama as well as the de facto annexation of Venezuela.
There’s a growing international desire to reduce dependence on US technology, especially critical ones for defence, finance and businesses.

That we can have service breakdowns such at Microsoft and at the US Federal Aviation Administration shatter the decades-old illusions of the superiority, invincibility and desirability of American technology.

Now Malaysia is not China. We don’t have the resources to build cutting-edge tech we can use for ourselves and perhaps sell to the world. But neither do most countries out there,for that matter. We still have to rely on external technologies and services for many areas, even critical ones.
But change must happen. While we’re good at producing everything from agricultural commodities to manufactured goods, we have never been known for being particularly technologically innovative.

But given Asean’s 700 million people and over US$4.5 trillion in GDP, and given the need for economic and security blocs to deal with aggressive and even predatory superpowers, we have the ability, resources and motivation to achieve our goals.

That the overheating global AI markets could crash has been on everybody’s mind lately. Recent events, such as grave warnings about the potential dangers of AI going rogue and harming humanity, coming from AI's biggest boosters themselves, as well as scandals and personnel changes that can potentially alter the tech landscape, may accelerate such an economic scenario.

What’s not on anybody’s bingo cards, however, were the Microsoft and FAA outages. They reveal the dangers of both transitioning complex current systems to new technologies as well as concentrating it in the hands of a handful of American tech giants so much of the computing power that the world needs.
Computing as a service

Over the past few decades the world had increasingly relied on computing hardware and software being made available on subscription from remote data centres owned and operated by mostly US tech giants. Such “cloud computing” means users rent computing services rather than owning the hardware and software themselves. They’ve become tenants rather than landlords, and their landlords have a near-monopoly.

We are seeing the perils of being tied to massive, remote cloud computing capabilities, as when Ukraine and Iran bombed some of Russia’s and the US’s data centres. We’ve always thought having giant tech companies offering capital, expertise and multiple redundancies would guarantee us from those dreaded “single points of failure”.

We were wrong. We are now seeing how single points of failure can and do indeed fail and shut things down. And the human part of the deal – a president or a CEO – can actually be that single point of failure and cause havoc such as we’ve never planned for or insured against.

Another lesson over the recent past has been that middle powers – such as Ukraine and Iran – that had their backs against the wall can show amazing resilience and innovation. They are both successfully holding back global superpowers, lobbing actual bombs and missiles at them, and even bloodying up some noses in return.

There are no reasons that Malaysia, already a reasonably-sized economic middle power, can’t create the tech and infrastructures that can provide us with some sovereignty and hence protection against hostile nations. If Malaysia is to be Boleh at anything, this is certainly an area where we must Boleh.

Meanwhile, I came across a wonderful term used to describe the ability of some systems to degrade under attack but still provide some reduced, predictable functionality, rather than totally collapsing like what happened at Microsoft and the FAA. It's called graceful degradation, a term I wished I’d invented to describe myself growing old.
I'm degrading for sure, with the occasional outage, though whether it's graceful or not still remains to be seen!

b9b68b51845fc3b9: Japan is yet to establish the Human Rights Protection Bill and a independent national human rights institution
Originally published on Global Voices
Anti-immigration policy protest in Oct 2026. Screen capture from the Japan Unfiltered YouTube Channel. Fair Use

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.
A newborn Black baby delivered at a clinic in Tokyo’s Meguro Ward became the target of a barrage of racist harassment online.

The clinic published the baby’s photo with a congratulatory message on its social media account as part of its routine “babies born this month” photo series. A screenshot of the post spread widely on X, gaining more than 1.3 million views within a day. The post attracted many hateful comments loaded with anti-immigrant sentiment and racial discrimination against non-white and non-Japanese people. Some of the hateful comments received thousands of likes.
All comments have since been removed from the post, and the clinic has disabled commenting on its Instagram.

This incident sheds light on two issues within Japanese society. On one level, it reflects how racist hate speech still remains rampant in Japan. But more broadly, it exposes a missing layer of justice infrastructure: Japan has no independent human rights commission empowered to handle discrimination complaints, no enforceable national hate speech law, and no effective way to force platforms to remove hate speech targeting entire groups.

While some cultural critics argue that the widespread racial discrimination in Japan stems from the younger generation’s inadequate interest in foreign cultures and development, others argue that the prevalence of online hate speech is to a large extent related to a lack of effective domestic legislation and human rights education.

Despite being a signatory to the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD) since 1995, Japan has not passed the Human Rights Protection Bill or established an independent national human rights institution to investigate human rights violations and penalize perpetrators. While there have been numerous attempts to pass such a bill, it was tabled multiple times in the 2000s and early 2010s. Critics say the efforts failed because the public feared it could violate the freedom of speech protected by the Constitution.
Toothless anti-discrimination national laws

Thus, instead of passing a comprehensive set of laws, it addresses discrimination and human rights through issue-specific laws, such as the Act on the Promotion of Human Rights Education and Human Rights Awareness-Raising (2000), the Act for Eliminating Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities (2013), the Act on the Promotion of Efforts to Eliminate Unfair Discriminatory Speech and Behavior against Persons with Countries of Origin other than Japan (2016), the Act on the Promotion of the Elimination of Buraku Discrimination (2016), as well as the Act on the Promotion of Public Understanding of the Diversity of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity (2023), which aim to raise public awareness about human rights and providing government support rather than criminalizing hate speech and discrimination.

For example, while the Hate Speech Elimination Act was enacted to curb xenophobic street rallies that terrify ethnic minorities residing in Japan, such as the series of protests against Kyoto Korean Elementary School between December 2009 and March 2010, it does not declare hate speech illegal, nor penalize offenders with fines or jail sentences.

Moreover, the law only protects foreigners with a legal status, but excludes undocumented migrants, asylum seekers, and Indigenous peoples, including the Ainu and Ryūkyūans. The law’s legal scope is at odds with the United Nations’ recommendations, which state that a signatory of the ICERD must “ensure legislative guarantees against racial discrimination apply to non-citizens regardless of their immigration status, and that the implementation of legislation does not have a discriminatory effect on non-citizens.” Legal experts have criticized the restrictive clause of the law for, as Shuji Oda, president of the Dai-Ichi Tokyo Bar Association, says, “giving rise to a false reverse implication that hate speech directed at individuals without legal residency status is permissible.”

The toothless anti-discrimination laws only manage to contain explicit discriminatory actions against disabled people, Burakumin (feudal outcasts), LGBTQ+ people, and foreigners with legal status; they have not eliminated hate speech. Meanwhile, street rallies against immigrant and imported labor have surged amid stagnant local wages, inflation, and rising living costs. Though these protests are usually small in scale, they attract a large number of social media comments, with plenty of discriminatory remarks and hate speech against foreigners.

Additionally, none of the aforementioned laws has a mechanism to force internet platforms to remove harmful content; this results in the spread of xenophobia, homophobia, hatred against social minorities, and a racist online culture.
Kawasaki model

As Japanese national politics has stalled the enactment of the Human Rights Protection Bill, some local governments have started building the legal framework from the bottom up to address local unrest targeting ethnic minorities.

Kawasaki City, which is home to a large Zainichi Korean population in Kanagawa Prefecture, was the first municipality in Japan to introduce punitive local laws to curb protests that “injure the human dignity of others,” as described by the city’s Justice Department.

Since the national Act on the Promotion of Human Rights Education and Awareness was passed in 2000, the city enacted its own Children’s Rights Ordinance in 2000 and Human Rights Ombudsperson Ordinance in 2001, which paved the way for the establishment of a local independent Human Rights Ombudsperson system for receiving and investigating complaints on bullying, abuse, and discrimination.

Following a surge of demonstrations calling for the exclusion of people of foreign origin around 2013, the city enacted the Ordinance for the Creation of a City that Respects Human Rights and is Free from Discrimination in December 2019, which prohibits discrimination based on race, nationality, ethnic origin, gender, sexual orientation, and disability. The ordinance also bans using loudspeakers, placards, or flyers that induce hatred against people originating from outside Japan and their descendants. Under the Ordinance, repeat offenders would have their identities publicly disclosed, and they could be fined up to JPY 500,000 (approximately USD 3,130). The city would also keep a record of hate groups and ban them from using public facilities, such as sports venues and parks.

Furthermore, the ordinance established an expert panel empowered to review hate speech and instruct online platforms to remove extreme content targeting a specific group of people and disclose the abusers’ identities.

While the ordinance has managed to reduce discriminatory protests against Korean-Japanese communities within Kawasaki City, it is powerless when the protests take place in neighboring jurisdictions. Moreover, thus far the criminal penalty of the local ordinance just punishes abusers targeting people originating from outside of Japan; LGBTQ+, disabled, and indigenous communities have remained unprotected. It cannot penalize landlords or employers who discriminate and has limited power over online abuse, as internet companies are not legally bound by local laws.
Human rights education translated into moral education

Various UN bodies have repeatedly criticized Japan for failing to enact a comprehensive anti-discrimination law and establish an independent commission to investigate and prosecute abusers in line with the “Paris Principle,” the official international standards for national human rights institutions. Yet, to date, Japanese society still lacks the consensus and determination to pass the Human Rights Protection Bill.
While proponents of stalling the legislation cite potential violations of free speech, a deeper reason relates to local xenophobia and perceptions of human rights.

The concept of human rights was introduced to Japan about 150 years ago, during the Japanese modernization period beginning in the late Edo and early Meiji era. However, when the Constitution of the Empire of Japan was promulgated in 1889, it defined citizens’ rights not as inherent human rights, but as “rights of subjects” granted by the Emperor.

Only after World War II was the concept of universal human rights re-introduced and localized to criticize Japan’s wartime militarization of society and crimes against non-Japanese people. Yet, human rights education in schools is often confused with conventional moral education, which emphasizes individual responsibility to family, society, and the country, and the need to maintain harmonious human relations through interpersonal politeness and consideration.

However, the individual morality approach overlooks the structural causes of discrimination and fails to empower individuals as rights-holders to address the problem of systematic discrimination, as pointed out by a group of Japanese teachers from the Institute of Global Education and Culture in a proposal to better integrate moral and human rights education in 2014:
日本では人権教育・啓発の場で「おもいやり」「やさしさ」などが強調される一方で、権利そのものを学習することは低調である。[…]
[…]具体的な「権利」という側面も、また「社会的に」問題を解決しようという側面も極めて弱い。「思いやり」を強調する抽象的・心情主義的教育は、私的な人間関係の中での問題解決ばかりを強調し、権利を具体的に考え実現しようとする力をむしろ弱めているといえる。
In Japan, human rights education and awareness-raising campaigns have kept emphasising concepts like ‘consideration for others’ (omoi-yari) and ‘kindness’ while downplaying education on rights. […]

It’s extremely weak in addressing different aspects of individual rights and the social resolution of rights-related problems. The emphasis on ‘understanding’ is both abstract and sentimental; as such, education relies solely on problem-solving within private interpersonal relationships and will hence weaken the ability to think concretely about rights and exercising one’s rights.

Earlier this year, Human Rights Watch urged the newly elected prime minister Sanae Takaichi to legislate a comprehensive anti-discrimination law and create an independent national human rights body to address the rise of xenophobic sentiments against immigrants. Although the right-leaning government has no intention of resurrecting the Human Rights Protection Bill, a civic coalition has formed to advocate for an independent National Human Rights Institution with investigative and corrective powers to address discrimination and human rights abuses by 2028.
Written by Jo Carter
